articles.title: Zelenskyy In Canada Seeking Support Amid Destructive Russian Attacks
articles.body:
PAVLOHRAD, Ukraine -- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ottawa will provide Ukraine with air defense support as he visited Canada in an attempt to shore up support from the country's allies amid deadly Russian drone and missile attacks.
"This is a very important package of air defense," he told reporters on September 10, adding that Canada will also provide aid to Ukraine's energy industry. He provided no further details.
The Ukrainian president arrived in Canada's western city of Calgary a night earlier after a visit to Norway for the funeral of King Harald V and talks on air defense support.
His plane was delayed on its way to Oslo after an alert in Moldova that a Russian drone had entered the nearby airspace.
"Canada remains one of our closest partners," Zelenskyy wrote on X after his arrival in Canada. "We value the support of the Canadian people and the decisions that help Ukraine to withstand the war and to protect our people."
Zelenskyy's visit came as Russia continued to launch intense air attacks on Ukraine, with fresh strikes reported on September 10 in Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Mykolayiv regions.
At least 10 people were killed in Russian strikes across these regions, while more than 100 others were injured, including children.
In Dnipro, the capital of the east-central Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian forces struck a food-industry facility that had already been damaged in an earlier attack the same day, while in neighboring Pavlohrad, a shopping area and cars caught fire after an evening strike.
"There was a hit in central Pavlohrad by a Shahed drone," RFE/RL Ukrainian Service correspondent Roman Pahulych reported from the aftermath site, adding that another strike followed less than a minute later.
"There are shopping premises here. There was heavy traffic here -- a bus stop is located here," he added, as he filmed devastating images showing ruined buildings and burnt-out cars.
Farther east, in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region, regional authorities said Russian forces had struck four times, with impacts reported near educational facilities and a multistory residential building.
Russian air strikes also hit the southern port city of Mykolayiv, as well as civilian and industrial infrastructure in the surrounding region.
Moscow has stepped up its air war in recent months, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones that have taken advantage of Ukraine's dwindling air defenses. Among other targets, the attacks have hit Ukraine's power grid ahead of the upcoming fifth wartime winter.
Since the beginning of its invasion, Russia has sought to paralyze Ukraine's energy system, leaving thousands of people across the country with no heating and electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued its own long-range strikes inside Russia.
Overnight on September 9-10, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala in Daghestan. Elsewhere, Russian authorities reported one person died and two were injured in another attack in the Voronezh region. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.
The intensifying exchange of strikes has put air defense and the protection of Ukraine's energy infrastructure at the center of Zelenskyy's trip.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement on September 9 that Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."
"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," the statement said, adding that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."
Renewed Diplomatic Efforts
As fighting remains intense, Zelenskyy's latest international trip comes amid renewed US-mediated efforts to find a path toward ending the war.
After months of stalled talks aimed at ending the conflict, US special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv and Moscow over the past weekend in what appeared to be the latest attempt to narrow the gap between the two sides' negotiating terms.
Days later, Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump, a conversation the Kremlin described as "constructive and quite frank."
"We had a great conversation. He [Putin] is wanting to make a deal, and if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump told reporters on September 9, adding, "These are two people that are tired of fighting."
Putin has given no sign he is ready for a cease-fire unless Kyiv makes major concessions it has rejected, including ceding territory in the eastern Donbas region that Russian troops have been unable to take by force.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov suggested Putin told Trump that an immediate cease-fire could be secured if the United States would end all support for Kyiv.
On September 9, the Financial Times reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a bigger role in US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, citing unnamed sources the paper said indicated the roles of US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner might be scaled back to make room for Ratcliffe.
In a post on X, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly called the FT story "incorrect and ridiculous." CIA spokeswoman Liz Lyons, also on X, wrote: "This reporting is false."
Witkoff and Kushner have led the talks with Moscow and Kyiv for the last year and a half.
According to the FT, officials close to Ratcliffe have told their European peers that in addition to maintaining contact with intelligence agencies in both Russia and Ukraine, the CIA director would now play a more active role in shuttle diplomacy.

articles.title: Poland Expects Russia to Target Its Border Crossings With Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland believes Russia may target its border crossings with Ukraine, after Warsaw averted a threat to one of its own crossings overnight.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk made the remarks at a press conference in Bratislava, Slovakia on Thursday, Sept. 10, according to Reuters. Overnight from Tuesday into Wednesday, Sept. 8-9, Russian drones struck the Ukrainian side of the Tudora-Starokozache crossing, killing two Ukrainian nationals and injuring seven people, including a Moldovan national.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to one of the border crossings was averted,” Tusk said.
“As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border crossings – for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” he continued.
Tusk cites CIA warning
Tusk said he had also received what he described as “a fairly precise report directly from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months,” which he said matched warnings he had issued for months about Russian provocations.
He also urged Poland and the rest of Europe to prepare for a range of scenarios, not only along the Ukrainian front but also across the eastern flank, echoing his previous warnings that Russia may attack NATO.
Moldova crossing struck two days earlier
On Wednesday, Moldova accused Russia of deliberately Tudora-Starokozache border crossing and using false claims about weapons shipments to Ukraine to justify the strike and civilian deaths.
Russian Strikes Kill 7, Injure 120 Across Ukraine
Russia’s defense ministry confirmed the attack, saying Moscow had struck logistic facilities that were allegedly being used to transport military cargo to Ukraine.
The incident followed a series of Russian attacks on Moldovan-Ukrainian crossings in August.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu accused Russia of deliberately sending some of the drones into Moldova’s airspace.
“Judging by the trajectory of those drones, we can say which are sent intentionally and which are there by chance,” Sandu said, adding that in both cases, the drones violate the country’s airspace, Sandu said on Aug. 17.
“And the only one who is guilty, the only party that is guilty of these things, is the Russian Federation, which started this war,” she continued.
Poland sees little hope for recent Ukraine peace talks
Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing the country’s special services, has met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe over fears that Russia may attack NATO.
Siemoniak confirmed the meeting with Ratcliffe on Tuesday, which was held at the agency’s headquarters near Washington.
Ratcliffe had traveled to Moscow on Aug. 25, in his first visit to Russia during his tenure in the agency, where he held talks with Sergei Naryshkin, head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), and Alexander Bortnikov, director of the Federal Security Service (FSB).
Although further details of the talks were not made publicly known, Politico reported on Aug. 26 that Ratcliffe warned Putin against attacking a NATO member, with the discussion centering on the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Putin was reportedly also warned against providing military and economic support to Iran, which Moscow views as an ally and has received Shahed drones from.
US President Donald Trump dismissed the possibility of Russia attacking NATO on Aug. 27, while rejecting reports that Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow to warn the Kremlin against such a move. Separately, he downplayed the visit by calling it “semi-routine,” before saying that his administration was “working very hard to get that war ended.”
On Sunday, Sept. 6, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time as Washington’s intermediaries, where where they held bilateral talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky and the American emissaries, followed by a multilateral session that included national security advisers from the UK, France, and Germany.
The two also traveled to Moscow and held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday evening, Sept. 5, subsequently having an informal working dinner.
Despite the weekend meetings being described as substantial and productive, and despite the Kremlin signaling openness for further trilateral talks, Russia continues to conduct large-scale attacks on Ukraine, with the latest attacks killing seven and injuring at least 118 nationwide on Thursday.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, speaking in Latvia on Wednesday, said he was not optimistic regarding the prospect of peace negotiations, adding that Moscow has not softened its military aims and continues to reject ceasefire proposals.

articles.title: Ukraine nearly out of F-16 missiles used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones – The Economist
articles.body:
Ukraine nearly out of F-16 missiles used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones – The Economist
Ukraine is nearly out of US-made AIM-120 and AIM-9 missiles for F-16 fighter jets, which are used to intercept Russian cruise missiles and new jet-powered drones.
Source: The Economist
Details: Ukrainian air defence lacks sufficient missiles to intercept the new Russian Geran-4 and Geran-5 UAVs, which can fly at speeds of up to 600 km/h, while Russia is producing around 3,000 of them a month.
Their turbojet engines are mostly supplied from China, although some components are manufactured directly in Russia using smuggled Western 3D printers. Alongside the larger Banderol drones, these UAVs are increasingly resembling inexpensive cruise missiles, leaving F-16 fighter jets critically short of AIM-120 and AIM-9 missiles to intercept them.
Ukraine is developing its own interceptor drones to counter Russian UAVs, but the situation with defence against ballistic weapons is even more difficult.
Ukraine's stockpile of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems is now also nearly depleted. New large-scale deliveries from the US are unlikely because American stockpiles have been depleted by the war with Iran.
Meanwhile, Russia has increased ballistic missile production to around 100 a month: 60 Iskander-M missiles and 40 RM-48U missiles.
There are some expectations surrounding the planned delivery of several older French-Italian SAMP/T air defence batteries, along with Aster missiles, to Ukraine by the end of 2026. Next year, Ukraine is due to receive eight of the latest SAMP/T NG systems.
Quote: "The new system has a more advanced radar for the final stage of guidance and can handle multiple manoeuvring ballistic missiles, such as Russia's Iskander-M. The Aster has a warhead that explodes next to the incoming missile, rather than the PAC-3's 'hit-to-kill' impact. But French army sources claim it outperforms the Patriot in some respects. It is also less than half the US$7m price of the latest export version of the PAC-3."
Details: Germany plans to produce up to 200 less powerful PAC-2 missiles a year under licence, some of which could be supplied to Ukraine with the agreement of NATO countries.
A joint European-Ukrainian project called Freyja is intended to fundamentally change the situation. Its ambition has been compared with that of a "moonshot" programme. Its goal is to provide Ukraine and its European allies with a significantly cheaper and higher-volume alternative to PAC-3 missiles compatible with NATO-standard radars and data-link systems.
The planned interceptor is based on the Ukrainian FP-7 short-range ballistic missile. Sensors, guidance and control systems will be supplied by 12 European defence companies, including France's Thales, Italy's Leonardo, Germany's Diehl and Sweden's Saab.

articles.title: Trump was warned: Iran war could last until end of his term in 2029
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump made an intriguing statement Wednesday night, saying the war with Iran would end “immediately” after the midterm elections, which will be held November 3. But The Wall Street Journal reported overnight between Wednesday and Thursday that senior officials had warned him the conflict could instead continue until the end of his term in 2029.
U.S. officials who spoke with the newspaper said the warning had also been voiced by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who cautioned in closed-door discussions that Tehran could withstand U.S. pressure, both from the blockade and from “other military tactics” — a scenario that could prolong the confrontation beyond the inauguration of the next president in January 2029.
The report was published hours after Trump’s surprising declaration, which came after he was asked about the surge in oil prices following the renewed escalation with the Islamic Republic, as crude oil prices crossed the $100-a-barrel mark Wednesday. Trump said the price would fall — but only after the midterms.
His remarks came against the backdrop of assessments previously voiced by commentators and Israeli officials that after the elections — once the political pressure on Trump to avoid price increases that could hurt Republicans’ chances of preserving their narrow majorities in both houses of Congress has eased — the president may resume intensive military action against Iran.
Speaking with reporters before departing for a Republican conference in Dallas ahead of the elections, in which control of Congress is at stake, Trump was asked why he believed the war would end immediately afterward. In response, he attacked Democrats hoping to regain control of the House and Senate.
“Because they [the Iranians] can’t hold on anymore. They’re desperate to try to influence the election, so that we get a nice, weak group of people in there [meaning the Democrats], who will leave them alone and allow them to get their nuclear weapon. All they want is a nuclear weapon, and if they get a nuclear weapon, the whole world will be in very serious trouble.”
Before boarding his new Air Force One — the aircraft he received as a gift from Qatar — Trump was forced to wait about 10 minutes while the plane’s emergency slide was inspected after it deployed in front of photographers covering the president.
Trump was asked about it and said “they were just doing a check.”
“They checked it earlier, and they wanted to make sure. I assume they’ve already put it back up, they wanted to see that everything works perfectly,” he said.
Asked whether it was safe for him to board the aircraft — against the backdrop of the unusual incident in July in which he was secretly transferred by truck from the Qatari aircraft to an alternate plane in Turkey, out of concern over an Iranian attack — he replied: “Yes, otherwise I wouldn’t be on it.”
Oil prices climbed about 3% Thursday following the renewed escalation with Iran, which is believed to be seeking to intensify the confrontation in an effort to raise the price Trump pays for the blockade he is imposing on it, as he tries to force Tehran into submission by worsening its economic distress.
Iran has escalated its recent actions and, according to reports, is now trying, unlike in its previous attacks during the war, to hit U.S. warships as much as possible. In recent days it has fired ballistic missiles at them several times, so far without success.
The United States has vowed to respond to each such attack by destroying Iranian oil tankers in retaliation and on Wednesday struck five such tankers, disabling them, after attacking three more tankers on Saturday.
Iran responded by launching 20 missiles at U.S. targets in Jordan, and the interceptions over Jordan were visible from Israel.
The Jordanian military said it intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles, and U.S. officials told The New York Times on Thursday evening that “minimal” damage had been caused to U.S. military equipment at a base in the kingdom. The officials added that there were no known casualties, though soldiers could report injuries in the coming days.
Historic move at IAEA, with Putin and China providing protective umbrella
Meanwhile, for the first time in 20 years, the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) voted Thursday evening to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council after determining that Tehran was violating its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
The move is not expected to have practical consequences such as new sanctions, because any such proposal would almost certainly be blocked by Iran’s allies China and Russia, which hold veto power on the Security Council. But referring the issue to the U.N.’s highest body is viewed as a diplomatic escalation by the West, and Tehran has threatened to respond.
The proposal to refer Iran to the Security Council was led by the United States, Britain, France and Germany and was approved by 23 of the IAEA Board of Governors’ 35 member states.
According to reports, only three countries — Russia, China and Niger — voted against the measure at IAEA headquarters in Vienna. Eight abstained and one did not participate in the vote.
The move is a direct continuation of a previous IAEA resolution from June 12, 2025 — one day before Israel launched Operation Rising Lion against Iran, at the end of which the United States bombed Iran’s main nuclear facilities — which determined that Iran was violating its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Those violations relate to IAEA investigations that have been underway for years into traces of uranium found at several undeclared nuclear sites in Iran. The investigations began following the Mossad’s exposure of Iran’s “nuclear archive” in 2018, and the suspicion is that the sites were previously used for Iran’s military nuclear program, a program Tehran officially denies ever having operated.
It was previously reported that the program was shut down in 2003, but Israel has accused Iran of continuing it afterward.
Iran has previously expressed anger over IAEA resolutions against it, claiming they effectively provided Israel with a pretext to attack, and dramatically curtailed cooperation with nuclear inspectors, who have not been permitted to visit the nuclear sites since they were bombed last June.
Iran’s refusal to cooperate with the IAEA and allow its inspectors access to nuclear facilities has now become a new focal point of friction, leading to another resolution against the Islamic Republic in June this year, in which the Board of Governors demanded that Iran reveal what happened to its enriched uranium stockpile.
Before Operation Rising Lion, Iran had 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% — very close to the 90% level required for nuclear weapons — an amount estimated to be sufficient for at least 10 nuclear bombs.
It was previously reported that a large portion of the enriched material had been buried deep underground near the nuclear facility struck in Isfahan. But Iran has not allowed the IAEA to access that site or the other facilities attacked, Natanz and Fordow, where enriched uranium may also have been buried.
The question of the enriched uranium has remained a central issue since the outbreak of Operation Lion’s Roar at the end of February this year, and the fact that it remains deep underground in Iran is seen as a significant failure to achieve one of the war’s main objectives — destroying the Iranian nuclear threat.
The concern is that Iran could retrieve the material from underground and, relatively simply and quickly, enrich it to weapons-grade levels at a secret location — perhaps the facility at “Pickaxe Mountain,” which has been dug to great depth and may therefore be protected from bunker-busting bombs.
Although the referral to the Security Council is not expected to have practical consequences, Iran threatened Monday to retaliate against such a decision.
So far, the ayatollah regime has not announced any concrete response, but Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi criticized the move.
“They attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, which are under safeguards, disrupt the proper verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution at the Board of Governors. Through such maneuvers, you will not be able to compensate for the failure of your policies and actions, nor achieve any results at the Security Council.”
A statement issued Thursday evening by Iran’s mission to the IAEA also made no mention of any retaliatory action.
“Once again, a political resolution concerning Iran has been adopted by the IAEA Board of Governors without consensus,” the Iranian delegation to the international nuclear agency said.
“The current situation was created solely by the criminal acts of aggression of the United States and the Israeli regime. The delusional goal of the United States, to force the great Iranian people into ‘surrender’ and plunder its oil, will never be realized,” the statement added.

articles.title: North Korean leader salutes ‘overseas’ troops
articles.body:
This picture taken on February 25, 2026 and released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on February 26, 2026 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un (R) and his daughter Kim Ju Ae attending the military parade to commemorate the 9th Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea at Kim Il-sung Square in Pyongyang. (AFP Photo/KCNA via KNS )
Leader Kim Jong Un praised troops in “overseas military operations” during a speech marking North Korea’s founding anniversary, state media reported on Sept. 10, an apparent nod to Pyongyang’s assistance in Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, North Korea has become a key ally of the Kremlin, sending troops to support Moscow’s war effort in return for economic benefits and military technology, analysts say.
During comments marking North Korea’s Sept. 9, 1948 founding, Kim hailed overseas compatriots but paid special tribute to troops deployed abroad, the official Korean Central News Agency reported on Sept. 10.
“I also extend my special gratitude and profound respect to the commanders and soldiers of our military participating in overseas military operations,” said Kim on the nation’s the 78th anniversary.
“Our ideal is being realized rapidly thanks to patriotism, voluntary service and devoted contributions by all citizens praying for the country’s prosperity,” he added.
According to South Korea, some 2,000 North Korean troops have been killed in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine claimed that Moscow had launched North Korean ballistic missiles in a strike that killed at least nine people and wounded dozens.
Kiev has also said that up to 50,000 North Korean troops are due to deploy to Russia, although it has provided no evidence to back the claim or a timeframe for the deployment.
In making the claim, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky asked Seoul to supply air defense systems to protect against Russian missiles, a request that has gone unanswered by the South.

articles.title: Canada joins Ukraine’s effort to counter Russia’s growing ballistic missile threat: the FREYJA program
articles.body:
Editor's note: this article has been updated with new information.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Canada will contribute technology to Ukraine’s European FREYJA anti-ballistic defense program and provide additional military assistance as Russia maintains near-constant ballistic missile and drone attacks.
Russia has ramped up ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent months, increasingly combining them with large waves of drones and other weapons. The strikes have damaged civilian infrastructure and caused growing casualties, while Ukraine faces a shortage of the air defense systems and interceptor missiles needed to counter the evolving threat.
Zelenskyy made the announcement on 10 September during a visit to Canada, where he met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. He said the talks focused on winter support, energy, Ukraine’s financial needs, and defense cooperation.
“Mark assured me that Canada is ready to join our European anti-ballistic program FREYJA with its technologies,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a necessary and timely step.”
Zelenskyy also said Canada had made an “important decision” on a major air defense assistance package, adding that there is a global shortage of air defense systems and missiles.
Update: Canada and Ukraine sign 100-year partnership declaration
Update 23:00: Zelenskyy and Carney also signed a declaration establishing a 100-year partnership between Ukraine and Canada, setting out long-term cooperation between the two countries.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine and Canada had reached agreements worth more than $2 billion, including more than $1 billion in government defense assistance.
Canada will also contribute $40 million to a new Ukrainian veterans fund, while the two countries reached agreements on energy cooperation ahead of winter.
Zelenskyy said Canada’s support will strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses and its fighter aircraft, including those being used to intercept Russia’s jet-powered Geran drones. He added that 21 Ukrainian pilots are currently training in Canada.
Russia is changing its aerial attacks
The additional air defense comes as Russia has significantly expanded and adapted its aerial campaign against Ukraine.
Russia is launching increasingly large waves of drones, including faster versions of the Shahed/Geran attack drone, while combining them with ballistic and other missiles. The changing speed, volume, and composition of attacks are putting greater pressure on Ukraine’s air defenses and interceptor stocks.
Zelenskyy said he had also discussed with Carney Russia’s “virtually constant” strikes with ballistic missiles and drones.
The Russian attacks increasingly reach deep into Ukraine, targeting cities, energy facilities, transport and logistics infrastructure, and industrial sites far from the front line.
That makes layered air defense increasingly important. Ukraine needs systems capable of intercepting different types of threats, from relatively slow attack drones to much faster ballistic missiles.
Air defense becomes critical ahead of winter
The need for additional air defense is particularly urgent as Ukraine approaches another winter under Russian attack. Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s energy system during previous winters, damaging power generation and distribution and threatening electricity, heating, and water supplies.
Ukraine therefore needs not only more interceptor missiles but additional systems and technologies capable of dealing with the increasingly complex mix of Russian aerial weapons.
Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia’s new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter
Zelenskyy said Canada would also provide additional defense supplies and that the two countries were working on a broader “Drone Deal” covering defense cooperation.
He thanked Canada for its support throughout the war, saying Ukraine needs to remain strong to achieve a “strong and lasting peace.”

articles.title: Can’t intercept the missiles? Hit the factories—Ukraine’s other way to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine has nearly run out of the one weapon that reliably stops Russia's ballistic missiles, and no replacement is close, according to The Economist. Now it is betting on cheaper homemade interceptors—and on hitting Russian missiles before they launch.
Russia has spent this year rebuilding its arsenal around the weapons Ukraine can least often intercept and aiming them at cities and the power grid, so the race to field cheap defenses will help decide how many people survive another winter of strikes.
Ukraine's homemade bet
Kyiv is building its own answer. The pan-European Freyja project, led by Ukrainian firm Fire Point with 12 European defense companies, aims for an interceptor near $700,000. That is a fraction of a $7 million export Patriot round. The second track is "left-of-launch": hitting the factories and launchers before missiles fly. In March, Ukraine struck a Bryansk plant making Iskander components. It also hopes to add its own Sapsan and FP-series missiles within months, though catching Russia's mobile launchers is a tall order.
Europe’s answer to the Patriot costs $700,000 a shot—and no foreign government can switch it off
Faster drones, less warning
Russia sends waves of jet-powered Geran-4 and -5 drones to swamp Ukrainian radar, then fires ballistic missiles behind them. The drones fly at up to 600 kph, and 3,000 leave Russian factories each month. Over five days to 1 September, Russia hit Kyiv almost hourly. The barrage paused on 6 September for the visit of American envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who had just met Putin in Moscow. The day after they left, Russia killed three civilians. Ukraine's F-16s, meanwhile, are running low on the American air-to-air missiles they need against cruise missiles.
The shield is empty
Ballistic missiles are the class of Russian weapon Ukraine's air defenses stop least often, which is why Brussels recently cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American interceptors for the winter, and why a cheaper homemade fix carries so much weight.
1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses
Of 57 ballistic missiles fired in the first eight days of August, Ukraine intercepted only one. Kyiv has almost nothing left of the PAC-3, the one interceptor that reliably downs them. Russia now turns out about 100 of its deadliest missiles a month, 60 of them Iskander-Ms. Resupply looks unlikely, because US President Donald Trump's war on Iran drained America's own Patriot stocks, and no ally wants to give up interceptors it cannot replace.

articles.title: Ukraine and Canada signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership
articles.body:
Ukraine and Canada signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine and Canada agreed to jointly produce drones, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition. The parties are also preparing a Drone Deal and defense supplies.
Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the "Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership," which provides for a long-term partnership in the defense industry to jointly produce unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic-warfare capabilities, as well as ammunition. The parties are also working on the Drone Deal. This was reported by the Government of Canada, according to UNN.
"On September 10, 2026, Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Calgary and signed the "Declaration on a 100-Year Partnership," in which they expressed their intention to elevate relations between their countries to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership and confirmed their alignment," the statement said.
It is noted that, based on the Letter of Intent on joint production signed in Kyiv on August 24, 2025, Canada and Ukraine will establish a long-term partnership in the defense industry to jointly produce unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic-warfare capabilities, as well as ammunition, supported by scientific research and technology transfers.
"They will promote predictable procurement of jointly produced equipment and work with partners to establish a Defense, Security and Resilience Bank. Canada and Ukraine will expand trade and investment under a modernized Free Trade Agreement, promote the development of public-private partnerships, and mobilize the capital and risk-mitigation solutions necessary to support Ukraine's recovery and reconstruction. Canada will cooperate with the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support macroeconomic stability and mobilize private capital," the Canadian government said.
It is also noted that both countries will deepen cooperation in the areas of energy security and critical minerals, industry and sustainable forest-resource management, as well as strengthen ties between innovators and researchers in the fields of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, space, biotechnology, and digital governance.
Zelenskyy said that, together with Prime Minister Carney, they had discussed opportunities to ensure Ukraine's financial resilience for this year and the next.
"Thank you for your willingness to help find the funding necessary for the needs of the budget and our soldiers. I also spoke about Russia's virtually constant ballistic missile and drone strikes. Mark assured me that Canada is ready to join our European FREYJA anti-ballistic program with its technologies. This is a necessary and timely step. There will also be additional defense supplies. Of course, we also had a substantive discussion of promising bilateral projects in defense and the economy. In particular, our teams are currently working on the Drone Deal. We expect that in the near future we will be able to reach a full-fledged agreement," Zelenskyy said.
It should be recalled
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Canada had decided on a "very important package of assistance for air defense".

articles.title: Timeline: How a Russian drone nearly hit Zelenskyy's plane in Moldova
articles.body:
Russia’s latest drone incursion into Moldova and NATO airspace comes as Moscow increasingly deploys jet-powered attack drones, blurring the line between traditional UAVs and low-cost cruise missiles and making them much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was preparing to leave Chișinău for Oslo on Tuesday afternoon when Moldova’s military detected an unmanned aerial vehicle in the country’s airspace.
What initially appeared to be another Russian drone incursion took on greater significance the following day, when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre revealed that Zelenskyy’s plane had almost been hit by a drone.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in,” Støre told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
The timeline shows how the events unfolded.
Moldovan military first detected an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle at 4:20 pm EEST (3:20 CEST).
Moldovan officials confirmed to Euronews that the country’s airspace was closed shortly after 4:30 pm.
“The airspace was closed to protect the aircraft flying over Moldova at the time - three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result.”
By 4:37 pm, Romania’s Defence Ministry said the drone crossed into Romanian — and therefore NATO — airspace.
Two minutes later two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced Air Policing mission took off to monitor it.
The jets did not intercept the drone. Romanian radar continued to track it until 5:02 pm, when contact was lost.
Five minutes later at 5:07 pm the drone was detected again over Moldova, where it later crashed about 25 km east of the Romanian border.
According to Moldovan officials, the flight restrictions were lifted after 5:20 pm, when authorities confirmed the drone had come down and exploded near Mihăilenii Vechi, in the Râșcani district, about 160 km from Chișinău International Airport.
“For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took off from Chișinău International Airport later than scheduled," officials said.
According to monitoring channels, Zelenskyy’s plane took off from Chișinău around 5:57 pm.
For much of Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine that began in early 2022, Zelenskyy has travelled abroad primarily through Poland, with Rzeszów serving as a regular departure point.
In recent months, however, his presidential aircraft has also begun using Chișinău more frequently for foreign trips.
What type of drone was it?
The exact model of the drone involved in Moldova and Romania has not been officially established.
Ukrainian open-source monitoring channels identified it as a Geran-4, one of Russia’s newer jet-powered attack drones.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 are among the newest additions to Russia’s expanding Geran family, although they differ significantly in design and capabilities.
The Geran-4 has a wingspan of about three metres and is roughly 3.5 metres long. Its maximum take-off weight is around 450 kilograms.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Geran-4 can reach speeds of up to 500 km/h and carry a warhead weighing between 50 and 90 kilograms.
Russia has recently stepped up its use of jet-powered drones, including in complex barrages alongside ballistic and cruise missiles designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.
Their speed makes them much harder to intercept than conventional Shahed-type drones, particularly for the mobile fire groups and other relatively inexpensive systems Ukraine has relied on to counter slower-moving UAVs.
Ukraine is instead forced to use scarce and considerably more expensive air-defence missiles against the faster threats, putting additional pressure on already limited interceptor stocks.
Several Ukrainian companies have reportedly begun testing missiles specifically designed to shoot down the new jet-powered Geran models.

articles.title: Timeline: How a Russian drone nearly hit Zelenskyy's plane in Moldova
articles.body:
Russia’s latest drone incursion into Moldova and NATO airspace comes as Moscow increasingly deploys jet-powered attack drones, blurring the line between traditional UAVs and low-cost cruise missiles and making them much harder to intercept.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s plane was preparing to leave Chișinău for Oslo on Tuesday afternoon when Moldova’s military detected an unmanned aerial vehicle in the country’s airspace.
What initially appeared to be another Russian drone incursion took on greater significance the following day, when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre revealed that Zelenskyy’s plane had almost been hit by a drone.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in,” Støre told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
The timeline shows how the events unfolded.
Moldovan military first detected an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle at 4:20 pm EEST (3:20 CEST).
Moldovan officials confirmed to Euronews that the country’s airspace was closed shortly after 4:30 pm.
“The airspace was closed to protect the aircraft flying over Moldova at the time - three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result.”
By 4:37 pm, Romania’s Defence Ministry said the drone crossed into Romanian — and therefore NATO — airspace.
Two minutes later two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced Air Policing mission took off to monitor it.
The jets did not intercept the drone. Romanian radar continued to track it until 5:02 pm, when contact was lost.
Five minutes later at 5:07 pm the drone was detected again over Moldova, where it later crashed about 25 km east of the Romanian border.
According to Moldovan officials, the flight restrictions were lifted after 5:20 pm, when authorities confirmed the drone had come down and exploded near Mihăilenii Vechi, in the Râșcani district, about 160 km from Chișinău International Airport.
“For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took off from Chișinău International Airport later than scheduled," officials said.
According to monitoring channels, Zelenskyy’s plane took off from Chișinău around 5:57 pm.
For much of Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine that began in early 2022, Zelenskyy has travelled abroad primarily through Poland, with Rzeszów serving as a regular departure point.
In recent months, however, his presidential aircraft has also begun using Chișinău more frequently for foreign trips.
What type of drone was it?
The exact model of the drone involved in Moldova and Romania has not been officially established.
Ukrainian open-source monitoring channels identified it as a Geran-4, one of Russia’s newer jet-powered attack drones.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 are among the newest additions to Russia’s expanding Geran family, although they differ significantly in design and capabilities.
The Geran-4 has a wingspan of about three metres and is roughly 3.5 metres long. Its maximum take-off weight is around 450 kilograms.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Geran-4 can reach speeds of up to 500 km/h and carry a warhead weighing between 50 and 90 kilograms.
Russia has recently stepped up its use of jet-powered drones, including in complex barrages alongside ballistic and cruise missiles designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.
Their speed makes them much harder to intercept than conventional Shahed-type drones, particularly for the mobile fire groups and other relatively inexpensive systems Ukraine has relied on to counter slower-moving UAVs.
Ukraine is instead forced to use scarce and considerably more expensive air-defence missiles against the faster threats, putting additional pressure on already limited interceptor stocks.
Several Ukrainian companies have reportedly begun testing missiles specifically designed to shoot down the new jet-powered Geran models.

articles.title: RM-48U for the S-400 Carries a 199-kg Warhead — DIU Reveals Features of Russian Missile
articles.body:
Russian RM-48U ballistic missiles for the S-400 air defense system carry 199-kg high-explosive fragmentation warheads.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine announced this, with the relevant information published on the War&Sanctions website.
These missiles can strike ground targets up to 400 km away.
The DIU also revealed the component base, the companies involved in its production, and the foreign equipment they use.
Despite its Russian origin, the RM-48U missile incorporates many foreign-made components, with 117 foreign electronic components identified in its design.
The majority came from the United States, with 95 components. Another four originated in Taiwan, three in Switzerland, two each in Germany, the Netherlands, Japan, and South Korea, and one component came from France.
Key components include the ZYNQ XC7Z010 microprocessor and FPGA, a Micron memory chip, Analog Devices and Texas Instruments analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters, as well as transceivers, operational amplifiers, voltage regulators, and other U.S.-made electronics.
Under Swiss marking is the M10050-KB GNSS module manufactured by u-blox, part of the Kometa-R12 satellite navigation system.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Russia is refurbishing decommissioned surface-to-air guided missiles and target missiles from the S-400 system and upgrading them for use against ground targets.
The RM-48U is equipped with a solid-fuel motor from the 48N6DM surface-to-air guided missile used by the S-400. Its tail section comes from the 48N6E2 export missile, which is used with the S-300PMU1/2 and S-400 systems. The RM-48U’s instrument section contains components from the 9M96 and 48N6E2 missiles.
The missile has a single-stage design and follows a ballistic trajectory at a speed of Mach 4–6.
According to the DIU, the production of the RM-48U involves at least 63 Russian enterprises taking part in manufacturing the missile itself and its key components.
One of the main participants in the production chain is JSC Aerospace Defense Concern Almaz-Antey, the primary developer and manufacturer of the RM-48U. Another key enterprise is JSC VNIIR-Progress, which manufactures the Kometa-R12 satellite navigation system incorporated into the missile.
JSC Research and Production Association Poisk, named after V. I. Rdultowsky, also produces individual components. The company manufactures the 9E134 safety and arming mechanism installed in the RM-48U warhead.
Russian enterprises also produce the missile’s solid-fuel motor. The FSE Kamensky Combine supplies the 87B6 motor charge, while the FSE Plant Named After Y. M. Sverdlov manufactures components for the warhead and motor, including the 87B6 and 28A6 charges.
For more information, look into the feature article “RM-48U Missiles for the S-400 Cannot Be Launched Without Foreign Components: How Russia Depends on the West for Its New Ballistic Missiles.”

articles.title: Zelensky arrives in Canada to discuss Ukraine's air defense needs
articles.body:
Ukraine, Canada sign 100-year partnership agreement as Zelensky and Carney discuss air defense
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.
Canada and Ukraine signed a declaration establishing a 100-year partnership and agreed to deepen cooperation in defense, energy, technology, trade, and reconstruction following President Volodymyr Zelensky's talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sept. 10.
Zelensky arrived in Canada on Sept. 9 as he seeks support for Ukraine's air defenses and preparations for the winter. He is also expected to hold "important meetings" aimed at strengthening the countries' strategic partnership for years to come.
"We're talking today about a winter support package and energy. This is very important. Today, Canada is making a significant decision — a very important aid package for air defense," the president said in a social media post. "There is a major global shortage of such systems and the missiles for them."
Carney and Zelensky announced agreements and investment commitments worth more than $2 billion following talks in Calgary on Sept. 10.
"This relationship has flourished for over a hundred years and it will flourish in the century ahead, long after this war ends. Ukrainians helped build Canada, and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine," Carney was quoted as saying.
Canada and Ukraine also agreed to pursue the joint production of drones, counter-drone technologies, and munitions under a new long-term defense partnership, while Ottawa said it was prepared to contribute Canadian technology to the European Freyja anti-ballistic missile program.
Canada is preparing a new sanctions package for the fall aimed at hampering Russia’s production of ballistic missiles.
Carney also announced a $253-million package of critical air-defense interceptors to be delivered through the U.S. Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline. Canada will provide an additional $311 million in loan guarantees to help Ukraine secure natural gas supplies for the winter.
Ukraine’s state nuclear energy company Energoatom and Canada’s Cameco will deepen their strategic partnership on long-term uranium supplies and conversion services through 2035. Export Development Canada will provide a further $144 million to support projects including Ukraine’s hydropower infrastructure.
As part of the visit, the Ukrainian delegation, led by Zelensky, plans to attend an off-site meeting of the Canadian government. First Lady Olena Zelenska is also expected to meet with Canadian philanthropists supporting Ukraine.
The visit follows Zelensky's trip to Norway, where he and the first lady attended the Sept. 9 funeral of King Harald V.
In Oslo, Zelensky also met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store to discuss strengthening Ukraine's air defenses and advancing the Freyja anti-ballistic missile program.
Ukraine aims to have a working prototype of Freyja ready in the first half of 2027. The project brings together Ukraine and nine European countries, including Norway, as well as several European defense manufacturers.

articles.title: Zelenskyy’s big bet: Ukraine can outlast Russia
articles.body:
A helicopter flies past smoke billowing from a Russian e-commerce warehouse near St. Petersburg after a Ukrainian drone strike on July 24, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is gambling that taking the fight deeper into Russia will put enough pressure on Vladimir Putin to force him to get serious about peace talks.
For much of the war, the Russian president has been able to shield ordinary Russians from the worst of the conflict. The Ukrainian leader is now trying to break that insulation — disrupting air travel and striking refineries, factories, warehouses and other targets deep inside Russia.
The logic is brutal but simple: Raise the economic and political cost of the war for Russians faster than Putin can raise the military and civilian costs for Ukrainians with his escalating air assaults.
Advertisement
With that aim in mind, Ukraine mounted in August one of its heaviest waves of strikes on Russia since the war started more than four years ago.
The campaign expanded quickly to target not just conventional military facilities but also oil refineries, factories, and the vast warehouses of Russia’s online retail behemoths, Wildberries and Ozon. And ordinary Russians have expressed frustration at the domestic fuel shortages, the disruption of air travel and the upending of Russian e-commerce. Ukraine has scaled up domestic production of its attack drones as it tries to make the war unsustainable for Moscow.
But there is little evidence yet that the disruption poses any serious threat to Putin’s hold on power. Coups have been forecast before. European spymasters, Ukrainian officials and Russian exiles have issued numerous predictions that Putin’s days are numbered, that Russians will turn on him or he’ll be ousted in a Kremlin uprising by oligarchs and Russia’s elite.
Nonetheless, Putin has endured.
What Ukraine’s air campaign does appear to have done is make the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore. That’s significant given how the Kremlin has succeeded largely in silencing public dissent and has Russian-based media on a tight leash.
“I don’t think the authorities’ approval rating can fail to decline when people go outside and see a huge column of smoke rising over the city, or when they arrive to a gas station and there’s no fuel, while on television they’re being told that Russia is a great oil power,” said Ian Matveev, a Russian political analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny.
Advertisement
Matveev added that Zelenskyy’s air campaign has exposed how the Russian military can’t fully protect the country.
That was underscored in May when the Kremlin reluctantly pared back the Victory Day jamboree celebrating the Red Army’s defeat of Nazi Germany.
Shortly after, in June, Ukraine repeatedly struck Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, including around Moscow. In July, Ukrainian drones reached the Omsk refinery in Siberia, Russia’s largest, about 2,700 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory, reportedly using an upgraded drone.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrives to attend the pared-back Victory Day military parade at Red Square in Moscow on May 9, 2026. | Pool photo by Alexander Kazakov via AFP/Getty Images
By then, Ukrainian strikes had hit many of Russia’s major refineries, oil terminals and fuel-storage facilities. At the same time, Ukraine launched an operation against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black and Azov seas, targeting more than 200 vessels, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Russian media has reported on the impact of the strikes at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses on small businesses, with sellers of clothing and electronics lamenting that they’ve lost years of work, even their livelihoods. Pro-war military bloggers have not held back on their criticism, faulting the Russian armed forces for ineffectiveness.
But are these complaints enough to alarm Putin and prompt him to stop the war?
Advertisement
The strikes are clearly embarrassing the Russian autocrat, said John Lough, a former NATO official who is now at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a think tank founded by exiled Russian businessman and prominent opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
“These attacks are damaging for Putin — more in terms of his credibility with the elites than with the population at large,” Lough said. “They can see increasingly that the war is not winnable on the terms advertised and that he has damaged rather than improved Russia’s security.”
Lough said he doesn’t see a revolution or coup around the corner. “But if the fuel problems continue and more warehouses burn down, there will be more questions from the population about how long this is all going to last and why it started in the first place,” he added.
To ramp up the pressure, Zelenskyy and his tacticians are now eager to make Russia’s commercial airspace increasingly difficult to use.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” the Ukrainian leader said last week. He warned foreign airlines to stay clear as the skies over Russia would become increasingly unsafe because of Ukraine’s drone operations. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he added.
Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat, described Ukraine’s air campaign as “ very, very successful.” But Ukraine’s position as it enters into another wartime winter is more desperate than Russia’s, he feared.
Advertisement
“I think Kyiv is terrified about going into another winter, and this time without any means to defend itself against ramped up Russia’s ballistic missile attacks,” he said.
Putin is unlikely to have missed that vulnerability. Nor have Ukraine’s allies.
During a meeting with Zelenskyy and top security officials from Britain, Germany and France last week, much of the focus was not on the peace deal recently proposed by a U.S. delegation fresh from a visit to Moscow.
It was, according to a senior Ukrainian official who spoke to the AP, on “how to get through the winter.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Arctic attack extends Kyiv’s strike reach into Russian gas heartland
articles.body:
- 
  Ukraine’s special forces said they attacked two crucial natural gas plants in the Arctic about 3,000km (1,800 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border. Both lie in the heartland of Russian gas production: Novy Urengoy is Russia’s unofficial gas capital, located in the Yamal-Nenets region in north-western Siberia. The other plant is in the Purovsky district of Yamal-Nenets. A Ukrainian statement described the two plants as “crucial for the gas condensate industry … Previously, this was considered an absolutely safe area away from the front for the aggressor.”
- 
  Fire Point, a Ukrainian company that makes deep-strike weapons including the Flamingo cruise missile, posted: “Guess who just travelled over 3,300km and successfully hit the target?” Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, praised the strikes for their effect on the Russian economy. The Russian regional governor confirmed the attack and said the damage was being assessed. About 80% of all natural gas in Russia is extracted in the Yamalo-Nenets region, according to the Interfax news agency.
- 
  Ukrainian forces also targeted Novorossiysk, a Black Sea port in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The attack hit the Russian naval base, including a terminal used to load oil, military port facilities, and warships carrying cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said.
- 
  Ukraine and neighbouring Moldova played down reports that a plane carrying Volodymyr Zelenskyy was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo. In fact, Zelenskyy’s departure for Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldovan airspace due to a drone alert, a Moldovan government spokesperson said. The president’s plane was cleared for take-off from Moldova on Tuesday once it was established that the drone had come down. In all, three departures and four arrivals were delayed. Norway’s prime minister was among those who thought Zelenskyy’s plane had been attacked.
- 
  The Moldovan president, Maia Sandu, denounced the drone intrusions as a “serious threat to people’s lives” and condemned an earlier Russian drone attack on a border crossing with Ukraine that killed two people. Three other people were injured in the strike on the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova. One person was killed and at least four people injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Kyiv, while more strikes were reported in Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr. A Russian drone strike on a shopping centre in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy killed two people and injured 20, four of them seriously, said the regional governor.
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared “there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes”. He added: “A response is needed – Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences. The aggression must be stopped here and now, before it spreads any further.” He called for “effective” sanctions against Russia and support for Ukraine, saying “the partners who can help know exactly what is needed every day”.
- 
  A Ukrainian couple got married anyway after a Russian air raid on the eve of their wedding wrecked their Kyiv apartment. Before going to bed, Liudmyla Ryzhak had hung on the bedroom door her dress, white skirt and her soldier fiance Leonid’s traditionally patterned shirt. As they slept a Russian strike hit a warehouse across the street from their building. They fled with Liudmyla’s six-year-old daughter and two guinea pigs to a bomb shelter – but soon returned to dig their wedding clothes out of the rubble of their ruined apartment. In the morning, amid more air raids, they forged ahead with the ceremony – only possible after Leonid had been able to make it back from the frontlines in eastern Ukraine. “If God gave me a continuation of life, then why should I put it off?” the bride said. “At least for now, I have the right to be happy. Both him and me.” – Associated Press
- 
  Russia’s arms production poses a future threat that goes beyond the war in Ukraine, the German defence minister, Boris Pistorius, warned on Wednesday. “Moscow uses large parts of its budget … to fill its inventories for future conflicts, not to deploy weapons to the frontline in Ukraine,” he told the German parliament. “On average, only 80 of the 150 short and medium-range missiles that Russia can produce per month are being deployed to Ukraine.”
- 
  In the UK, a man has been charged after allegedly assisting Russian spy services in planning a sabotage operation, Raphael Boyd writes. Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested in Swindon on Friday 4 September. Scotland Yard said it relates to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that has been accused of engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies. Cammidge would appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday, police said.
- 
  Moscow wants peace talks to take place in Abu Dhabi, the UAE capital, said a Kremlin aide, Yuri Ushakov. Ushakov also said the US should halt aid to Kyiv if the fighting is to stop. Moscow has been indignant throughout the war about Ukraine being able to defend itself with military aid from its allies. Another Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, cited a “confirmed political will” for the talks and suggested prisoner exchanges between the US and Russia might be part of the picture. Peskov was responding to a comment by the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, about a possible roadmap to restart talks. There have been no talks between Russia and Ukraine since February.

articles.title: Tanker war between Iran and US expands, strikes on Sirik
articles.body:
This live blog is now closed.
Please follow our new blog for the latest Middle East developments.
Hello and welcome to our live updates on the Middle East conflict.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they hit a US unmanned vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media.
Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles from existing components while working in underground facilities, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, citing officials from the United States and the Middle East.
The missiles are being assembled in more limited quantities than before the war, the report added.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz, after they seized the key Red Sea city of Mocha.
"The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel said.
The Houthi military spokesman added that Saudi Arabia launched 64 strikes on Yemen in 24 hours.
The leader of Yemen's internationally recognised governing council on Thursday urged Arab and other nations to help protect the country's coasts, after the Iran-backed Houthis seized control of the key Red Sea city of Mocha.
"The protection of Yemen's coasts and the restoration of state control over its territory, ports and waters is a joint Yemeni, Egyptian, Arab and international interest," said Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, during a meeting with Egypt's ambassador.
Houthis take over port city in Yemen vital to control of Red Sea shipping, two officials have said.
Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a U.S. official told Reuters.
The U.S. military suffered material damage even before Iran's strikes on Tuesday. This includes the destruction of more than two dozen drones, Iran striking fighter jets, and aircraft being lost to accidents.
A U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran's attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service.
Iran's strike on the U.S. base in Jordan came after U.S. forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. The U.S. said its strikes were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the previous two days.
A spokesperson for Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait remain safe and uninterrupted.
The spokesperson also said the group’s current operations are limited to specified targets and are defensive in nature.
The US-led coalition has begun withdrawing from Iraq's Kurdistan region ahead of a deadline to end their mission in the country, a Kurdish official said Thursday.
They had already completed their withdrawal from other bases in Iraq in January and are now only present in the northern autonomous Kurdistan region.
They are scheduled to complete their withdrawal by September 30, having concluded their mission against the Islamic State group (IS) in Iraq, according to a 2024 agreement between Baghdad and Washington.
"Under the existing agreement, these forces must leave by the end of September, and they have in fact already begun doing so," Kurdistan's interior minister Rebar Ahmed told journalists.
"The process has started also in the Kurdistan region, with those forces transferring daily to other locations outside Iraq," he added.
A senior Iraqi official confirmed to AFP that coalition forces had begun withdrawing from Kurdistan, and were now only deployed at Erbil international airport.
The coalition forces exited Syria earlier this year.
Two people have been arrested in London as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act offences linked to Iran, British police said on Thursday.
London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement: "The investigation is not connected to any of the incidents or attacks earlier this year that have been targeted at various venues and buildings linked to Jewish and Iranian communities across London."
Western media's coverage of Israel's invasion of Lebanon echoed many of the same patterns seen in Gaza, writes Assal Rad.
Read more below:
A vessel reported being approached by an unidentified skiff 98 nautical miles southwest of Yemen's Al-Mocha on Thursday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said.
The incident comes as fighting intensifies in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and forces affiliated with the Saudi-backed government.
Iran has temporarily suspended a 10% charge on freight fees for foreign vessels carrying imported or exported oil, gas and liquid petroleum products to and from Iran, the semi-official Fars news agency reported on Thursday.
A US naval blockade has sharply disrupted the country's seaborne oil exports.
The presidential legal deputy ordered the collection to stop until the government approves and publishes a list of products subject to the charge, Fars said.
Fars said the charge had increased the cost of transporting oil, gas and liquid products, and suspending the levy could reduce transportation costs and encourage foreign fleets to carry goods to or from Iran.
Algeria has cut diplomatic relations with the UAE after years of mounting tensions, accusing Abu Dhabi of "provocative or hostile" actions.
The UAE ambassador was summoned by the foreign ministry and given 48 hours to comply with the decision.
President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has repeatedly accused the UAE of interfering in Algeria's affairs and destabilising countries across the region.
The Houthis have seized the strategic Yemeni port city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, according to government sources.
The capture marks a major advance for the group after weeks of escalating attacks across western Yemen and brings it closer to the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.
Local sources told The New Arab that large numbers of residents were fleeing Mocha towards the southern city of Aden.
The development comes as fighting intensifies across Yemen's western coast, with government-aligned forces suffering heavy losses and regrouping following Houthi breakthroughs on several fronts.
The European Central Bank looks set to raise interest rates on Thursday for the second time this year, seeking to head off an energy-driven surge in inflation triggered by the Iran war.
Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the U.S. and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets. That has sent oil prices above $100 a barrel again and revived fears about a wave of price hikes in the fuel-importing euro zone.
Economists expect the ECB to respond by raising its policy rate to 2.50% from 2.25% and signal it is ready to tighten further if the inflation outlook does not improve.
"A September hike looks all but locked in," Alessia Berardi, head of global macroeconomics at the Amundi Investment Institute, said. "Inflation remains elevated and should stay sticky over the next few months before easing toward the second half of next year."
Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammed Ishaq Dar has spoken over the phone with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on bilateral relations and regional developments.
In a statement posted on X, The Pakistani Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that both sides affirmed their position on Palestine and their support for the joint statement by the eight Arab-Islamic countries on the UK’s decision to ban illegal Israeli settlement imports.
Both countries also "emphasised the importance of maintaining close consultation on regional matters" including the Regional Four (R4) framework they’ve done with Saudi Arabia and Egypt.
Britain's new measures against illegal Israeli settlements mark a significant shift, but questions remain over how far Europe will follow, Sam Hamad.
The Iran-backed Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha, closing in on the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, three Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Thursday.
Multiple American military aircraft suffered damage in strikes overnight on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, CBS reporter Jennifer Jacobs said on Wednesday on X.
One A-10 Thunderbolt, known as the Warthog, was struck and left with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were placed back into service, she added.
he Mecca agreement, signed between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia last month, is a "defensive alliance" and there are no plans to expand it at the moment, Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesperson said on Thursday.
The statement came in response to a question at a weekly briefing on how Pakistan plans to fulfill its obligations under the accord after Saudi Arabia was attacked by the Houthis.
Yemen's Houthi rebels reported about 40 airstrikes launched by Saudi forces on Thursday in a fresh salvo following attacks by the Iran-backed group against the kingdom.
"The Saudi enemy's air force conducted around 40 strikes in recent hours in the governorates of Taiz, Hodeida, Al-Jawf and Marib," Houthi news agency Saba said.
An Israeli strike in Gaza on Thursday killed a family of four including two children, Palestinian hospital and security sources report.
"The bodies of four members of the Ahmad family were recovered in pieces after an Israeli strike hit a house in the Beit Lahia Project area in the northern Gaza Strip," an official at Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City said, identifying the children as aged 12 and eight.
A Palestinian security source in Gaza said that Israeli warplanes struck after midnight in Beit Lahia and separately in the heart of the Jabalia refugee camp, with Israeli forces also firing on tents of displaced people and ambulances.
"Israel continues its violations in the Gaza Strip," the security source said.
Israel in October last year agreed to a ceasefire brokered by the United States but since then has advanced further into Gaza and continued to kill Palestinians in near-daily strikes.
President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the United States may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, urging Tehran to be cautious.
"We notice there's a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard," Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention.
Pickaxe Mountain, located near Iran's heavily damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility, is a fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes.
Trump has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.
The rise in oil and gas prices due to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which began in February, has become a major issue for Trump and his Republican Party in the lead-up to the midterm U.S. elections in November.
Preliminary data tracking ship movement showed a decline in the number of ships that crossed the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, Wednesday, to 7 ships, compared to 12 ships the previous day, and below the average of the past ten days of 14 ships.
According to the data, 4 ships left the strait and 3 entered it, while the statistics do not include ships sailing through the waterway after turning off their transmitters and receivers.
