Matveev added that Zelenskyy’s air campaign has exposed how the Russian military can’t fully protect the country.
That was underscored in May when the Kremlin reluctantly pared back the Victory Day jamboree celebrating the Red Army’s defeat of Nazi Germany.
Shortly after, in June, Ukraine repeatedly struck Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, including around Moscow. In July, Ukrainian drones reached the Omsk refinery in Siberia, Russia’s largest, about 2,700 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory, reportedly using an upgraded drone.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrives to attend the pared-back Victory Day military parade at Red Square in Moscow on May 9, 2026. | Pool photo by Alexander Kazakov via AFP/Getty Images
By then, Ukrainian strikes had hit many of Russia’s major refineries, oil terminals and fuel-storage facilities. At the same time, Ukraine launched an operation against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black and Azov seas, targeting more than 200 vessels, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Russian media has reported on the impact of the strikes at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses on small businesses, with sellers of clothing and electronics lamenting that they’ve lost years of work, even their livelihoods. Pro-war military bloggers have not held back on their criticism, faulting the Russian armed forces for ineffectiveness.
But are these complaints enough to alarm Putin and prompt him to stop the war?
Advertisement
The strikes are clearly embarrassing the Russian autocrat, said John Lough, a former NATO official who is now at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a think tank founded by exiled Russian businessman and prominent opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
“These attacks are damaging for Putin — more in terms of his credibility with the elites than with the population at large,” Lough said. “They can see increasingly that the war is not winnable on the terms advertised and that he has damaged rather than improved Russia’s security.”
Lough said he doesn’t see a revolution or coup around the corner. “But if the fuel problems continue and more warehouses burn down, there will be more questions from the population about how long this is all going to last and why it started in the first place,” he added.
To ramp up the pressure, Zelenskyy and his tacticians are now eager to make Russia’s commercial airspace increasingly difficult to use.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” the Ukrainian leader said last week. He warned foreign airlines to stay clear as the skies over Russia would become increasingly unsafe because of Ukraine’s drone operations. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he added.
Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat, described Ukraine’s air campaign as “ very, very successful.” But Ukraine’s position as it enters into another wartime winter is more desperate than Russia’s, he feared.
Advertisement
“I think Kyiv is terrified about going into another winter, and this time without any means to defend itself against ramped up Russia’s ballistic missile attacks,” he said.
Putin is unlikely to have missed that vulnerability. Nor have Ukraine’s allies.
During a meeting with Zelenskyy and top security officials from Britain, Germany and France last week, much of the focus was not on the peace deal recently proposed by a U.S. delegation fresh from a visit to Moscow.
It was, according to a senior Ukrainian official who spoke to the AP, on “how to get through the winter.”

articles.title: Putin dismisses rumors of another mobilization as ‘nonsense.’ But can Russia keep fighting without another draft?
articles.body:
Putin dismisses rumors of another mobilization as ‘nonsense.’ But can Russia keep fighting without another draft?
Vladimir Putin and his subordinates have recently been actively denying rumors of an impending mobilization. This has only made many people more anxious: trust in official statements is low, and speculation about plans to forcibly draft hundreds of thousands of recruits into the army shows no sign of letting up. Meduza’s Razbor (“Explainer”) desk has tried to answer the main questions surrounding mobilization. Why has the frenzy picked up specifically toward fall? Is it true that Ukrainian authorities are waging an information attack on the Kremlin with these rumors? And are there objective grounds for mobilization?
Why fall is the predicted timing for mobilization, and how the rumors snowballed
One fact is worth remembering up front: the “partial” mobilization Vladimir Putin announced on September 21, 2022, technically remains in effect. He never signed a decree ending it. The forced draft that sent hundreds of thousands of Russians into the army has ended only in name. Even today, authorities could legally issue someone a mobilization summons.
In practice, though, no one has been drafted that way since late fall 2022. But rumors of a “new wave” of mobilization keep resurfacing with striking regularity. Rather than catalog every failed forecast from 2023 through 2025, this piece focuses on the current “wave.”
Russian officials routinely accuse Ukraine of fueling these rumors to destabilize the country. Kyiv’s motive isn’t hard to explain: Ukrainian military strikes on oil refineries and market warehouses appear, at least in part, to serve the same purpose. The more Russians feel the war’s practical consequences — and the anxiety over a possible draft — the greater the odds of a social explosion and public pressure to end the fighting.
Public opinion polling shows no sign of a “pacifist” trend: data from the Levada Center shows the share of Russians who favor peace talks has been falling since February and March, while the share favoring continued war has been climbing. Still, polling conducted in a country under wartime censorship deserves considerable skepticism.
Either way, Ukrainian officials have genuinely kept the mobilization talk alive. The most prominent voice is President Volodymyr Zelensky, who has made more than a dozen public predictions over the past six months about an impending forced draft into the Russian armed forces. Sources in Western intelligence agencies and government bodies have repeatedly echoed him behind closed doors.
- In mid-April 2026, Zelensky linked the Kremlin’s decision to block Telegram in Russia to an anticipated forced draft of hundreds of thousands of Russians. He later repeated the point publicly: internet blackouts, he said, are a tool for preventing a “revolt” over the coming mobilization.
- Later that same month, Zelensky said the head of Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) had briefed him on Russia’s mobilization plans.
- In mid-May, Zelensky cited HUR figures putting Russia’s mobilization need at 100,000 people. European intelligence services lent support to the rumors around the same time: sources told The Wall Street Journal the move reflected the Kremlin’s desire to expand the conflict beyond Ukraine. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the outlet: “If you just mobilize for this war, then you would send a signal that you are not really winning this war. So […] they need to escalate in order to justify the mobilization. And that’s a very dangerous point.”
- Later that month, Zelensky clarified that additional mobilization in Russia would affect “at least tens of thousands of people” and said Russian authorities had stepped up issuing mobilization notices. Around the same time, the first leaks surfaced suggesting the Kremlin might take the unpopular step in the fall, after elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, according to European officials who told The Washington Post as much on condition of anonymity.
- Zelensky’s next reference to mobilization in Russia came in early June, in his widely covered open letter to Putin, where he described his opponent’s intention to “launch a second wave” of forced conscription.
- In mid-July, Zelensky offered another forecast, this time about the possibility of “increased mobilization” after the State Duma elections.
- By the end of the month, Zelensky made a statement saying a faction within Putin’s inner circle was pushing him toward expanding mobilization, then followed up with another prediction of “a fairly significant wave” of recruitment into the Russian armed forces.
- A few days later, Zelensky added details, saying mobilization could happen in October and that the number mobilized could reach half a million people, or amount to at least 300,000. Soon afterward, sources in Washington backed the rumors for the first time: anonymous American officials told The Wall Street Journal they didn’t rule out the Kremlin soon having no way to reach its battlefield goals except through forced conscription.
- In early August, Zelensky again repeated his estimate that Putin needs half a million troops at the front, though he allowed that there might be no official mobilization announcement at all: recruitment could instead happen through “shadow” contracts. He followed that with a clarification: the information, he said, came from certain “internal Russian documents” obtained by Ukrainian intelligence.
- By the end of the month, the Ukrainian president gave a more detailed picture: “peripheral” mobilization in Russia “will not take place in major cities” and will be capped at 300,000 recruits in 2026 before continuing into 2027. Around the same time, The Wall Street Journal, citing Western intelligence sources, reported that Russia’s armed forces were intensifying drills for mobilization procedures.
- Zelensky’s last remark came on September 8: he continues to forecast 300,000 mobilized “after the elections,” whether in “covert or overt” form.
How justified are these forecasts, and does Russia’s military actually need mobilization?
One caveat upfront: we don’t have clear answers to either question, and in all likelihood, neither do the people making these forecasts.
Let’s start with the official denials. Since roughly midsummer, Russian lawmakers, diplomats, and top officials have regularly accused Ukraine of “planting” disinformation, waging “information attacks,” and otherwise trying to “destabilize” the country. Members of the State Duma’s defense committee have said as much, as has Russia’s U.N. envoy, Vasily Nebenzya; presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov; the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev (more than once); and, of course, Vladimir Putin himself.
But these denials shouldn’t be taken as reassuring. Nebenzya, for one, said mobilization isn’t needed “at this moment.” Putin, in his last statement, ruled out the scenario only “for today.” Hedges like these would let the authorities walk back their assurances after the State Duma elections — exactly what happened in 2022, when State Duma defense committee chairman Andrey Kartapolov assured Russians two days before the “partial” mobilization was announced that they had no reason to fear “general” mobilization. “General” mobilization indeed never happened, only because the authorities hid it behind the euphemism “partial.”
There are other, indirect reasons to suspect that mobilization plans are being concealed.
- Since 2022, Russia has passed numerous laws closing loopholes for potential draft dodgers ahead of any future wave of forced conscription — though that alone doesn’t mean specific plans exist.
- Many observers have viewed this summer’s roundups of men in the Penza region as a testing ground for a coming “peripheral” mobilization. Local authorities there detained potential recruits under all sorts of pretexts and, through various methods — including violent ones — forced them to sign contracts and go to war. But an equally or even more likely explanation is that local officials were simply trying to catch up on contract-soldier quotas handed down from Moscow: sources who spoke to the Financial Times put the overall recruitment target at 409,000 people for 2026. What happened in Penza may reflect “excesses on the ground” by a region falling behind on its quota, rather than a model to be replicated nationwide. (In fairness, similar detentions have occurred in other Russian regions as well.)
- Possible mobilization preparations have also been linked to drills for mobilization procedures in the Kaliningrad region, an increase in job postings for military registration specialists, the distribution of mobilization notices Zelensky mentioned, and other developments. As with the laws above, none of this directly indicates whether mobilization will actually happen.
One argument deserves closer scrutiny: the central case Ukraine has been making for months. Zelensky and other Ukrainian military and political leaders have insisted that Russia needs mobilization not to expand its force at the front, but simply to replace its losses there. According to Kyiv’s account, that’s tied to the Ukrainian military’s success inflicting casualties on Russian forces. In this telling, the Ukrainian army has learned to kill or severely wound more Russian soldiers each month than Russia’s military can recruit.
Is that actually true? Probably not, though we can’t say for certain. There’s no reliable estimate of Russian military losses for 2026. The dispute centers on a benchmark figure of 30,000 people a month; Ukraine claims Russia loses more troops than that. This fall, we’ll test that estimate as part of a new round of our research into Russian military losses, drawing on data from the Registry of Inheritance Cases and named lists of the dead. But none of our previous rounds have come anywhere close to that level.
In August, German economist Janis Kluge wrote that the influx of new recruits into Russia’s armed forces in the second quarter stood at roughly a thousand people a day — the same 30,000-a-month figure. Kluge draws on regional budget data, which fund the large lump-sum payments made to contract soldiers and offer one of the most reliable metrics for tracking Russian army recruitment. In his view, the need for a new mobilization isn’t as acute as Ukrainian and Western sources claim.
But Putin may not be guided solely by “objective” criteria for maintaining the status quo. To reach the “victory” he envisions in the war, he could well opt for a “proactive” buildup of the army through mobilization.
We’ve already described the problems with this step in a recent series of answers to readers’ questions about the war.
- Formations and larger units — brigades, divisions, corps, armies — need support elements: air defense, electronic warfare, logistics, artillery, and so on. Contract-soldier recruitment quotas are set at their current level because that’s how many people the army can actually “absorb,” meaning train and equip. Units fight, not individual soldiers, and those units need officers — both combat and staff officers. There are now also drone-operator units numbering in the thousands.
- The Kremlin has already seen forced mobilization spark public discontent and drive people to flee the country. The social and political risks are real. There’s a financial dimension too: for, say, 300,000 newly mobilized troops, the federal budget alone would have to pay out more than a trillion rubles in the first year alone, by a conservative estimate, in signing bonuses, salaries, supplemental payments, and death and injury benefits.
Despite those risks, Russia’s Defense Ministry may well have a clear interest in mobilization: it appears dissatisfied with the recruits it’s currently getting. It’s hard to build the high-tech units of the “army of the future” out of people who risked their lives for money out of financial desperation, and without mobilization, there’s no alternative to them.
- Over the past year, Russia’s military has tried to recruit several tens of thousands of drone operators from among students and other young people, promising a guaranteed short-term contract with no possibility of transfer to other branches of service. Students apparently didn’t trust the military, and the campaign fell flat.
- The Defense Ministry has similarly tried to recruit people for mobile firing teams that combat drones in the rear, this time prioritizing cost. It tried to staff the teams with reservists — people who receive small payments from the army in exchange for short annual training stints. That campaign hasn’t shown signs of success either, though some reservists do turn up in mobile firing teams.
The Kremlin could well conclude — especially if Putin himself favors the idea — that mobilization would solve the recruit-quality problem. But that, too, remains purely speculative for now.
One last point: alarmism versus rationality.
The 2022 mobilization inflicted deep trauma on Russian society. Hundreds of thousands of people were sent to the front; hundreds of thousands of their family members lost loved ones (named lists alone show more than 20,000 mobilized soldiers have already died in the war, and the true toll is likely far higher); and hundreds of thousands fled the country in a hurry, with nowhere to go. Almost no one wants to relive that experience, save for a small camp of the war’s most die-hard supporters. Even reporting the news triggers irritation among Russians. We feel it every time we’re accused of alarmism after publishing an article, a YouTube show, or an Instagram post about mobilization.
Unfortunately, we can’t say for certain that this anxiety is entirely unfounded, if only because we don’t know what’s going on inside the head of Vladimir Putin, the main (and perhaps only) “decision-making center” on the Russian side. One can only assume he’d suffer serious reputational damage if, after soothing statements dismissing mobilization rumors as “utter nonsense,” he turned around and announced a forced draft of hundreds of thousands of recruits.
But does Putin actually care about his reputation? Is he guided by rational arguments in pursuing his goals, and what does he even want the war to achieve in the end? Only he knows the answers. And the vertical power structure he has built over the course of the war has done a great deal to ensure that any new mobilization goes as “seamlessly” as possible — for the authorities, if not for citizens.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
articles.body:
Moldova closed its airspace on the afternoon of 8 September and delayed the plane carrying Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Norway after a Russian drone crossed into the country, its government said in a statement to Reuters. The aircraft was cleared for takeoff once officials established that it had come down on Moldovan territory. Norway's prime minister described the episode as a near-miss, and neither government has said how close the drone came.
Russia runs three things at once along the EU's eastern frontier—mass drone attacks on Ukraine, drones crossing into Moldovan and Romanian airspace almost weekly, and strikes on the border checkpoints tying the three countries together—and states without interceptors can answer only by closing their skies.
What happened, and when
Moldova's National Army detected a Shahed-type drone entering from Ukraine at 16:20, the country's Defense Ministry reported. It flew toward Bender, a city in the Russian-backed breakaway region of Transnistria, then turned toward the capital, Chișinău, by 16:32. At 16:37, it left the country over western Moldova and headed into eastern Romania, across the Prut river border.
Controllers restricted the airspace over central Moldova at 16:30. The same drone came back from the Romanian side, crossed the north of the country, and came down outside a village in the northwest, near the Romanian border, setting dry vegetation alight, according to the log. Nobody was hurt, and the airspace reopened at 17:39, more than an hour after it closed. The BBC's Ukrainian service placed the crash near a different northern village, without naming a source, so the exact spot is unsettled.
The violation fell in the window when Zelenskyy's aircraft was preparing to take off, Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The civilian airport he was leaving from suspended operations and the border service closed the nearby crossings, the outlet added. Three departures and four arrivals were delayed in all, Reuters said.
A drone nearly hit Zelenskyy’s plane taking off from Moldova on his way to a king’s funeral, Norway’s PM says
How the plane and the drone crossed paths
Zelenskyy flies an Airbus A319 corporate jet, and the threat to it probably came from a jet-powered Geran drone that crossed Romanian and then Moldovan airspace at around 17:00 that day, Militarnyi wrote, publishing the drone's track from the monitoring channel Oko Hora. That fits the return leg in the army's log, though no authority has tied a specific aircraft to the delay.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told the broadcaster NRK the plane was almost hit as it prepared to leave, without naming his source. His office later described a danger recorded in Moldovan airspace that forced the delay. Norway's Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg said Zelenskyy recounted the details himself at a closed meeting in Oslo.
Zelenskyy and First Lady Olena Zelenska attended the farewell ceremony for King Harald V, who died on 28 August. Around it, the president worked on air defense, meeting Støre and then executives of defense companies from partner countries about the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, which Norway's government casts as a cheaper alternative to the Patriot.
Trending Now
The next night, the border crossing
Overnight on 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing on Ukraine's border with Moldova, killing two people and injuring three. The dead were Ukrainians, and a Moldovan citizen was among the injured, Moldova's Foreign Ministry told the broadcaster TV8. Border guards reopened the crossing that afternoon.
Russia claimed it had struck the crossing because it was used for military logistics. Moldova's Foreign Ministry rejected that outright, saying no weapons move through its territory, and that the people crossing there are families, children with their mothers, and the elderly. It is one of the working crossings on the Odesa Oblast stretch of the Ukrainian-Moldovan border, where the heaviest traffic runs through Palanca and Giurgiulești.
Moldova's President Maia Sandu condemned both the strike and the Geran-type drone that had forced her country to close its airspace the day before, and said the events show Ukraine needs more air defense.
Moldova is investing in air defense against the Russian drones crossing from Ukraine—Romania shoots down the ones that reach it
The pattern, and Moldova's empty sky
Russia has hit at least five checkpoints on Ukraine's western borders since late August, four of them facing Moldova and one facing Romania, and the drone that struck the Kotlovyna crossing on 20 August flew in through Moldovan airspace. Euromaidan Press has covered part of that campaign, including burned food cargo near the Giurgiulești crossing in August. The State Border Guard Service has called such strikes an act of terrorism, because people are present at the crossings when they are hit.
In the air, Moldova can do little. It is still buying its first serious air defenses, so it restricts airspace and waits while Romania scrambles jets against the drones that reach its side. It logged three airspace breaches in nine days in August, and more than 100 drones were detected near Romania in four days that month.

articles.title: USA Used More Than 60 Patriot Missiles to Repel Iranian Attack
articles.body:
The United States used more than 60 anti-aircraft missiles during Iran’s missile strike on a U.S. base in Jordan.
OSINTtechnical published footage of the massive deployment of Patriot missiles.
On September 9, a spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces stated that air defense systems intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two munitions fell in uninhabited areas.
Given that each PAC-3 MSE interceptor costs approximately $4 million, the missiles used during this operation likely cost between $240 million and over $400 million.
Footage of an American Patriot SAM battery engaging a massive incoming salvo of Iranian ballistic missiles over Jordan earlier tonight. pic.twitter.com/qGaTrbxsUE
— OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) September 9, 2026
“Iran’s response proved ineffective against an integrated air and missile defense system… Iran fired missiles toward Jordan. U.S. forces bear 100% responsibility for all facilities on Jordanian territory,” an unnamed U.S. official shared with ABC News.
Given current rates of stockpile depletion, repeated attacks could quickly deplete the stockpiles, which would take years of production to replenish.
The Iranian missiles targeted Muwaffaq Salti, also known as Al-Azraq Air Base, where U.S. aircraft and personnel are stationed.
Iran launched the strike after the U.S. military attacked five Iranian oil tankers in response to strikes by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on a U.S. Navy ship.
Iran’s missile strike on the base in Jordan damaged nine U.S. Air Force aircraft.
According to a July study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), amid the U.S. war with Iran, the stockpile of missiles for the Patriot systems has dwindled to fewer than 1,000 units.
In July, amid ongoing concerns about the depletion of anti-aircraft missile stocks due to the war with Iran, the U.S. military purchased new PAC-2 missiles for the first time in over 30 years.
On August 31, the Pentagon signed 7-year agreements to triple production of PAC-3 MSE missiles for the Patriot missile defense system.

articles.title: Kyiv couple marries after Russian strike ruins their home
articles.body:
A Russian strike hit a warehouse across the street from Liudmyla and Leonid Ryzhak's Kyiv apartment overnight into 8 September, sending a blast wave through their home hours before they were due to get married, the Associated Press reported. Leonid, 43, a soldier on leave from the front, had come back for the wedding.
Ukrainians keep marrying and rebuilding through a war that keeps interrupting both. More than 79,000 couples registered their marriages in the first half of 2026, 16% more than in the same period last year, nearly 40% of them online, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice figures. In July alone, the UN counted 437 civilians killed across the country, the deadliest month since May 2022.
The explosion blew out the windows, scattered furniture, and left the apartment uninhabitable. The couple fled to a shelter with Liudmyla's 6-year-old daughter and two guinea pigs. Their cat hid and could not be found. A second strike hit after they reached the shelter.
Neighbors clearing debris stopped to congratulate them.
“We should all be celebrated, that we survived,” Liudmyla replied.
They dug their wedding clothes out of the debris. Liudmyla, 33, shook broken glass from her white tulle skirt, which had small holes. Leonid could not find his dress trousers, so he wore army trousers with his embroidered shirt and sneakers.
The strike was part of a mass Russian attack on Kyiv that came once US peace envoys left the capital, ending a lull that had held for three days. Russia launched 166 drones and 32 cruise missiles at Ukraine overnight, along with ballistic and anti-ship missiles, and air defenses downed 142 drones, 31 cruise missiles, and two ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Three people were killed in Kyiv, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said.
The couple arrived at the registry office on time, at 10:40, but another air-raid siren sounded soon after and the office closed. They waited in the courtyard for almost three hours as explosions hit the surrounding districts.
Eventually, the alert ended, and the couple went inside.
"If God gave me a continuation of life, then why should I put it off?" Liudmyla said. "At least for now, I have the right to be happy," she added.
They got married.

articles.title: What Putin Hopes to Gain From BRICS in India – and Why He May Not Get It
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday ahead of a two-day BRICS summit expected to be dominated by Russia’s war against Ukraine, the expanding conflict in the Middle East, and mounting economic challenges.
Putin landed at Palam Air Force Station, where he was greeted by Indian Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, AFP reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The gathering brings together the leaders of an expanded BRICS at a moment when geopolitical conflicts are testing the group’s ability to maintain a common position. Originally founded in 2009 as a platform for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions traditionally dominated by Western powers, the bloc has expanded to 11 members, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Beneath the choreography of the New Delhi summit, however, lies a coalition divided by competing national interests, territorial disputes and, increasingly, differing approaches toward Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Why BRICS became more important to the Kremlin
For Moscow, the summit provides Putin another opportunity to demonstrate that Russia retains influential partners outside the West despite its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Since February 2022, BRICS has taken on greater economic and political importance for the Kremlin. Western governments have imposed sweeping sanctions on Russian banks, companies and individuals, while major Russian financial institutions have been cut off from the SWIFT messaging system.
Zelensky Signs Historic 100-Year Partnership Agreement With Carney, Advances Drone Deal, FREYJA Support
Russia responded by redirecting trade toward countries that did not join Western sanctions, particularly China and India, and by pushing greater use of national currencies and alternative payment mechanisms.
BRICS offers Moscow a ready-made platform for that effort.
Russia redirected huge volumes of oil toward Asian markets after Europe sharply curtailed purchases. India became one of the largest destinations for Russian crude, often taking advantage of substantial discounts as Moscow searched for buyers.
That trade helped Russia preserve an important source of export revenue even as Western governments sought to squeeze the Kremlin’s ability to finance its war.
But Moscow’s ability to turn BRICS into a broader challenge to the Western-led financial system remains limited.
India, which chairs BRICS this year, is pushing to improve links between members’ central bank digital currencies to make cross-border transactions faster and cheaper. New Delhi, however, has explicitly distanced that initiative from an attempt to replace the dollar as the world’s reserve currency.
While Moscow may see it as protection from Western financial pressure, India presents it primarily as a mechanism for facilitating trade.
Unease within the ranks
Russia and China have promoted BRICS as part of a broader shift toward a multipolar international order, but India has resisted treating membership in the group as a choice between the West and the rest.
New Delhi continues to deepen economic, technological and security relations with the US, Europe and other Western partners while simultaneously maintaining its longstanding relationship with Moscow.
That makes India important to Putin – but not a reliable partner in forging a united anti-Western front.
Expansion has made that problem even more pronounced.
The Middle East conflict is expected to dominate much of this year’s summit, particularly because BRICS members hold sharply different positions on the fighting involving Iran, the US and Israel.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s visit marks his first to India and comes as Tehran seeks diplomatic backing from partners outside the West.
BRICS expansion has also brought rivals into the same grouping. The sharpest divide at this summit is between Iran and the UAE, which suspended trade and financial transactions with Tehran after being hit by Iranian missiles during the Iran-US war.
Those tensions have already complicated efforts to reach consensus, with BRICS foreign ministers failing to agree on a joint statement in May.
Competing ambitions of the Bloc’s giants
The other major fault line runs between the bloc’s two Asian giants.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected in New Delhi for his first visit to India since 2019, marking another step in the cautious thaw between the two countries following years of tension after their deadly 2020 border clash.
Yet the improvement should not be mistaken for strategic alignment.
Deep mistrust persists over their disputed Himalayan frontier, trade imbalances, Chinese investment and the two countries’ competing regional ambitions.
One of the clearest examples is Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative.
India has consistently refused to endorse the project, objecting in particular to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, which passes through Pakistan-administered Kashmir, territory claimed by India.
New Delhi considers the project an infringement on its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The dispute illustrates a broader problem for BRICS: its members may agree that the international system should give emerging powers greater influence, but they frequently disagree over what that new order should actually look like.
Kyiv offers India another strategic track
India’s relationship with Ukraine further complicates Moscow’s narrative.
New Delhi has not abandoned its decades-long partnership with Russia, but it has gradually broadened its engagement with Kyiv beyond diplomatic calls for peace.
During Modi’s visit to Ukraine in August 2024, the two countries signed four agreements covering agriculture and the food industry, medical-product regulation, cultural cooperation and humanitarian grant assistance.
The humanitarian framework established a mechanism for India to finance community-development projects in Ukraine. Projects can include infrastructure in areas such as health, education, agriculture, renewable energy, transport and communications, providing Indian companies with opportunities to participate in Ukraine’s recovery.
That should not yet be confused with a large-scale reconstruction boom for Indian companies. But it gives New Delhi a concrete economic foothold in Ukraine at a time when governments and businesses are positioning themselves for the country’s eventual rebuilding.
Defense provides another potential area of cooperation.
Ukraine has long supplied technology and equipment important to India’s military, particularly marine gas turbines used aboard Indian naval vessels. Ukrainian manufacturer Zorya-Mashproekt has supplied propulsion systems to India for decades, creating a practical defense relationship that predates the current war.
Indian officials have also identified defense as one of the areas for possible expansion in bilateral relations with Kyiv.
Ukraine’s rapid development of battlefield technologies since Russia’s invasion – particularly drones, electronic warfare and other unmanned systems – adds another potential dimension to that relationship, although no major India-Ukraine drone technology-transfer agreement has yet been announced.
The result is a relationship driven by more than symbolism. India has strategic reasons to preserve ties with Ukraine even while Moscow remains one of New Delhi’s most important defense and energy partners.
Public pushback: How Modi ruined Putin’s scripted unity
Russia nevertheless remains deeply important to India.
Moscow has been a major supplier of military hardware for decades, while discounted Russian oil transformed the economic relationship after the invasion of Ukraine.
Yet New Delhi is increasingly demonstrating that maintaining those ties does not mean automatically supporting Moscow’s political narrative.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 and met Modi again during the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
During that meeting, Modi publicly urged Putin to move away from what he called an “endless war,” stressing that disputes should be resolved through peaceful dialogue and emphasizing the human cost of continued fighting.
“We need to move from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities,” Modi told the Russian leader.
The unusually direct appeal put Russia’s war against Ukraine at the center of an otherwise friendly meeting between the strategic partners.
For Putin, it also exposed the limits of Moscow’s ability to present close relations with India as evidence that major powers outside the West accept Russia’s continued war.
India has meanwhile continued high-level contacts with Kyiv. External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Ukraine earlier this month, where President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed New Delhi’s diplomatic efforts to help end the war.
“I am grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war,” Zelensky said.
That is the contradiction Putin brings with him to New Delhi.

articles.title: Iran nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What now?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran's nuclear file is back at the UN Security Council. What will happen next?
The International Atomic Energy Agency's Board of Governors has referred Iran to the UN Security Council over its alleged failure to comply with nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first such referral in 20 years.
The 35-member board adopted the resolution on Wednesday by 23 votes in favour, with Russia, China and Niger voting against and eight countries abstaining.
Submitted by the United States, Britain, France and Germany, the resolution follows an earlier decision in June 2025 that found Iran to be in "non-compliance" with its obligations.
The latest move represents a significant diplomatic escalation between Tehran and Western powers, but with Russia and China holding veto power at the Security Council, it remains unclear whether it will result in any concrete action against Iran.
So why has Iran been referred, what could happen next, and what does it mean for Tehran's nuclear programme?
Why has Iran been referred to the Security Council?
The referral stems from the IAEA's previous finding that Iran had failed to comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations.
The agency's concerns predate the latest US-Iran war and centre partly on Tehran's failure to provide satisfactory explanations for traces of uranium found at undeclared Iranian sites that the IAEA had spent years investigating.
The Board of Governors ruled in June 2025 that Iran was in "non-compliance", but referring the matter to the Security Council on that basis required a separate resolution.
Wednesday's resolution also builds on a more recent decision calling on Iran to declare its remaining enriched uranium stockpile and allow IAEA inspectors to verify it.
What exactly does the new resolution do?
The resolution asks IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to report on the latest decision and previous resolutions to all IAEA members, as well as to the UN Security Council and General Assembly.
Unlike a consensus decision, the resolution was put to a vote. Twenty-three countries backed it; Russia, China and Niger opposed it; and eight abstained.
It was submitted by four Western states: the US, Britain, France and Germany.
The referral itself does not impose new sanctions or other penalties on Iran. Instead, it formally brings the issue before the Security Council and increases diplomatic pressure on Tehran.
Why is the decision significant?
It is the first time Iran's nuclear file has been referred to the Security Council on non-compliance grounds in two decades.
It also comes during a vastly different political and military environment.
The June 2025 non-compliance finding was adopted just one day before Israel began bombing Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States subsequently joining the attacks.
Iranian nuclear sites have also been targeted during the latest US-Israel war with Iran, while the IAEA has been unable to regain access to key facilities that were struck.
That has left the agency facing significant gaps in its knowledge about Iran's nuclear activities, including the fate of its highly enriched uranium.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has rejected the resolution as politically motivated.
Its mission to the IAEA said that "once again, a political resolution on Iran was adopted without consensus" by the agency's Board of Governors.
Tehran blamed the current situation entirely on what it described as the "criminal acts of aggression" committed by the United States and Israel, adding that Washington's objective of forcing Iran to surrender "will never be achieved".
Iran had warned before the vote that it would respond if the resolution was adopted, although its initial reaction did not specify what measures it might take.
Could the UN Security Council impose new measures on Iran?
In theory, bringing the issue before the Security Council opens another arena for international action against Tehran.
In practice, however, significant measures are considered unlikely.
Russia and China, both allies of Iran, are permanent members of the Security Council and possess veto power.
Both countries voted against Wednesday's IAEA resolution, meaning they could block attempts to impose measures against Tehran at the UN.
The immediate significance of the referral is therefore largely diplomatic: it further escalates the confrontation between Iran and Western powers and places the nuclear dispute formally before the Security Council.
What happened to Iran's enriched uranium?
This remains one of the biggest unanswered questions surrounding Iran's nuclear programme.
Iran has not allowed IAEA inspectors to return to bombed nuclear facilities, including the country's three uranium enrichment sites, which were destroyed or severely damaged in US-Israeli attacks.
Tehran has also not provided an account of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Before the strikes, the IAEA estimated that Iran possessed 440.9kg of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent purity.
That is significantly above the levels normally associated with civilian nuclear energy and relatively close to the roughly 90 percent enrichment associated with weapons-grade material.
According to the IAEA's benchmark, the stockpile would have been sufficient, if further enriched, for around 10 nuclear weapons.
The agency believes more than 200kg of the stockpile remains at one site, although it is unclear how much survived the attacks undamaged.
Grossi has described the uncertainty surrounding the material as a "serious proliferation concern" and called for the situation to be addressed urgently.
Does this mean Iran is building a nuclear weapon?
No. The IAEA's non-compliance finding and the referral to the Security Council do not in themselves establish that Iran is building a nuclear weapon.
The dispute concerns Iran's compliance with its safeguards and reporting obligations, unanswered questions surrounding nuclear material and the IAEA's inability to verify the status of its enriched uranium stockpile.
Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes.
The immediate question is therefore not whether the Security Council will determine that Iran has decided to build a bomb, but whether the referral can increase pressure on Tehran to restore cooperation with inspectors and account for its nuclear material.
With Russia and China likely to oppose punitive Security Council action, the referral may ultimately have greater diplomatic significance than immediate practical consequences.

articles.title: Zelensky Signs Historic 100-Year Partnership Agreement With Carney, Advances Drone Deal, FREYJA Support
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney signed a historic 100-year partnership agreement in Calgary on Thursday, Sept. 10, as Canada also pledged to contribute technology to Ukraine’s European anti-ballistic missile program, FREYJA.
The signing followed Zelensky’s arrival in Canada on Wednesday, Sept. 9, for a three-day visit focused on strengthening bilateral ties, defense and further cooperation between Kyiv and Ottawa.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On Thursday, the two leaders opened their bilateral visit and “very substantive negotiations,” Zelensky said in a statement.
“Today, there is a significant decision from Canada,” Zelensky said. “A very important aid package for air defenses. There is a major shortage of such systems and missiles in the world,” he continued, possibly alluding to the Patriot interceptors Ukraine urgently needs to defend itself against Russia’s aggression, as those are the only weapons capable of deterring ballistic missiles.
Zelensky is scheduled to visit Calgary, Toronto and North Bay through Sept. 11 and is also expected to address members of the Canadian government, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said.
Canada ready to contribute to FREYJA
In a separate, follow-up report, Zelensky announced that Canada would contribute its technologies to FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic program initiated and launched by Ukraine’s FirePoint company.
Russian Strikes Kill 7, Injure 120 Across Ukraine
The program aims to build alternatives to the US-made Patriot interceptors, and includes integrated protection against aerial threats through cooperation among Ukraine, Norway, Denmark, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.
Zelensky said he raised Russia’s “practically constant” ballistic missile and drone strikes with Carney during their meeting, describing the FREYJA commitment and the pending Drone Deal agreement as a “necessary and timely step” in response to the ongoing threat.
Canada committed to providing additional defense supplies, and agreed to help identify financing for Ukraine’s budget throughout 2026-27. “Thank you for the readiness to help find the necessary financing for budget needs and for our soldiers,” Zelensky said.
Further bilateral projects in defense and the economy are also in development Zelensky said, expressing hope for the teams to “reach a full agreement in the near future.”
Strikes continue amid diplomatic push
The commitments come as Ukraine faces repeated, coordinated large-scale strikes nationwide, which have significantly increased following the departure of senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who had visited Kyiv and Moscow throughout the weekend as Washington’s intermediaries.
More than 80 people were injured and at least four killed in Russian strikes across Ukraine on Thursday, with the deadliest strike hitting a shopping center in Pavlohrad.
Although the Kremlin signaled openness for further trilateral talks, the frequency and scale of recent strikes raise doubt about whether the negotiations can deliver meaningful progress.
Before arriving in Canada, Zelensky met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, along with heads of defense companies from partner nations, in Oslo to push forward the FREYJA program. The discussions covered what governments and manufacturers each needed to deliver going forward, and centered on expanding Ukrainian-Norwegian defense cooperation.
On Tuesday, Ukraine announced it was signing contracts with partners for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles for its air defense systems ahead of the winter.
Germany said it would urgently transfer PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks.

articles.title: Trump Promises End to Iran War After Midterms
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said he expects the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran to end “immediately after” the midterm elections.
Trump suggested that Iran is on the verge of collapse, but that its government is holding out in hopes of hurting Republican political prospects in November.
“They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters as he headed to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday.
But “they can’t hold out any longer,” he said.
Trump added that “it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm” for gas prices to come down, but that they would fall once Iran soon seeks an end to the war, which is now in its seventh month.
Trump’s comments come as renewed fighting, including a barrage of tit-for-tat strikes in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, has driven up energy prices to their highest levels since late May. The global benchmark oil price topped $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
The national average for gasoline in the U.S. climbed 7.3 cents to $4.22 a gallon on Wednesday, the largest single day increase since May, according to AAA. Diesel reached a record $5.94 a gallon on Wednesday.
The Trump Administration has sought to tamp down rising energy prices amid growing affordability concerns among Americans. Last month, the Administration extended the Jones Act Waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to transport oil and other commodities between U.S. ports.
U.S. and Iran exchange biggest attack on shipping
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the U.S. and Iran exchanged the largest wave of attacks on shipping since the war began. Iran said it attacked 10 ships, including two U.S. vessels, near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. destroyed five Iranian oil tankers. Iran also launched missiles at a base hosting U.S. forces in Jordan, which U.S. officials reportedly said resulted in limited damage and no casualties.
The U.S. said its tanker strikes were retaliation for two Iranian attempts to hit a U.S. Navy warship.
The latest exchange came after days of escalating attacks. U.S. forces struck Iranian military sites on Sept. 1 in retaliation for attempted Iranian attacks on commercial vessels and U.S. personnel, CENTCOM said. One U.S. strike hit a wedding party in southern Iran, killing at least five people and injuring more than 60 others, according to Iranian officials, and prompting an internal investigation by the U.S. military. On Saturday, Iran fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer. In response, the U.S. destroyed three Iranian oil tankers.
Trump officials have downplayed the nature of the conflict, despite the continued fighting. Last week, Vice President J.D. Vance said he would not call the recent flare up “a war.”
When will the war end?
Trump and his officials initially estimated that the war would last four to six weeks, and have repeatedly said that energy costs will fall quickly once the war is over. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested in July that gas prices could return to $3 a gallon by Labor Day.
But Iran’s hold on the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery in the Persian Gulf through which a fifth of the world’s oil trade flowed before the war, has proved an enduring strategy to disrupt the global economy. Iran militarized the Strait at the start of the war in retaliation against U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28. Iranian leaders have used the Strait as a key point of leverage in now-stalled talks with the U.S., and restarted strikes on ships in the waterway in an attempt to force the U.S. to agree to its demands.
Trump, however, has maintained that he is under no pressure from the economic pain or its potential impact on the midterm elections to strike a deal with Iran, especially one that would be unfavorable to the U.S.
“A negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at,” Trump said on Wednesday.
Trump has insisted that Americans understand the need to continue the war until the U.S. eliminates the possibility of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon.
“I think it’s very easy to explain to America, all you have to do is say: ‘Will you let Iran have a nuclear weapon?’ And the answer is no,” Trump said.
Nevertheless, the public has grown increasingly weary of the war. Just 31% of Americans said they supported U.S. strikes on Iran in a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, while 63% opposed it. And 83% of those polled said they expect U.S. military involvement in Iran to continue for an extended period of time. Americans also appear to be concerned with the economic consequences of the war, with 61% of respondents believing the conflict has made life more expensive for their families, according to a Politico poll in August.
Last month, the Treasury Department launched an economic pressure campaign on Iran in an effort to force its capitulation. Its measures have included a slate of new sanctions on Iran, the ongoing U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports, and the threat of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners.
Iran’s economy has been hit hard by the measures, as well as disruptions and damage from the war. Its already weak currency has spiraled to record lows, while inflation, unemployment, and shortages of essential goods have substantially worsened.
Nevertheless, recent intelligence assessments reportedly indicate that Tehran is prepared to continue fighting for months despite severe economic pressure. Iranian leaders have also signaled a willingness to escalate the war by intensifying attacks on U.S. warships, targeting commercial vessels, and expanding shipping restrictions beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
Analysts have argued that Iran’s leadership might be hoping to inflict greater political and economic costs on the U.S. Administration in an effort to increase its leverage over Washington. Trump advisers, including Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have reportedly discussed with Trump the prospect that the war continues through the remainder of his presidential term.

articles.title: How the U.S. Treasury's New Aviation Sanctions on Iran Extend Beyond Tehran
articles.body:
The U.S. Treasury issued sweeping new sanctions against Iran on Tuesday, targeting the country’s airlines and their international service providers as it ramps up its effort to isolate Tehran from the global economy.
The aviation sanctions form a significant part of the Trump Administration's ”Operation Economic Outcast,” which the White House has described as “an unprecedented campaign to sever every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran.” As negotiations have stalled, and with the U.S. and Iran engaged in active hostilities once more, the economic pressure is intended to push Tehran into a deal to end the war.
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines, accusing them of having “long supported the Iranian regime’s destabilizing activities.” The sweeping measures were largely focused on grounding Mahan Air, which was first sanctioned by the U.S. in 2011 and is also subject to E.U. sanctions. The carrier has long been accused of transporting personnel, equipment, and funds for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
The measures build on OFAC’s April and July actions “targeting persons servicing Mahan Air’s domestic and international flights,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The U.S. also designated firms based outside of Iran that it said had helped Mahan Air maintain operations by providing goods or services. This action specifically targets “covert front companies, foreign intermediaries, and deceptive transshipment routes that Iran relies on to obtain U.S.-origin aircraft and sensitive technology,” according to the Treasury.
The OFAC also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorizations that “allowed for overflights, and for non-U.S. airlines to fly U.S.-origin or U.S.-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran.”
The sanctions, and their international reach, are intended to "intensify Iran's economic isolation, to further degrade their military capability, and push them to some kind of a concession or settlement that favors the United States,” Jack Roush, a PhD candidate affiliated with the Iranian History Initiative at the London School of Economics, tells TIME.
Here’s what to know about the latest sanctions, how they extend beyond the borders of Iran, and the economic pressure mounting against Tehran.
Aviation sanctions target Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Turkey, and UAE-based firms
The U.S. Treasury has accused Iran of using front companies and other pass-through entities in third countries in an attempt to evade aviation links back to Tehran and has extended sanctions to nine internationally-based entities it alleges have aided these efforts.
Measures were imposed on two UAE-based commercial entities and a UAE-based individual, as well as one Turkish-based and one U.K.-based firm.
Four cargo providers and general sales agents were also sanctioned, accused of servicing Mahan Air and coordinating shipments on behalf of the airline. Two are based in Turkey, one in Kazakhstan, and one in Malaysia.
The new sweeping sanctions “will exacerbate challenges that Iran already faces in maintaining its fleet,” says Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House.
With the reliance on foreign entities to maintain Iran’s aging fleet, the measures targeting companies outside of Iran will likely damage Tehran’s aviation capabilities, she says, as it will “restrict Iran's ability to rely on those regional hubs” and could prompt “international carriers [to] further reduce or suspend Iranian services.”
“If that happens, then this becomes a blockade of Iran's aviation infrastructure, which is quite serious,” says Vakil.
U.S. issues warning to anyone doing business with Iran amid effort to choke Tehran off from global economy
The U.S. Treasury has vowed to isolate any international entity that continues to show support to Mahan Air. “Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned,” Bessent said. “You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”
In recent weeks, the U.S. has imposed sanctions on banking institutions in other countries, accusing the lenders of enabling Iran.
On. Aug. 28, the U.S. moved to cut off Egyptian Banque Misr's UAE-located branches from the dollar-based financial system. Banque Misr said it is reviewing the notice from the U.S. Treasury and will communicate with the department “to obtain further information and maintain ongoing cooperation.”
Days later, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Turkey's Golden Global investment bank and two subsidiaries, accusing it of enabling the transfer of oil revenues from China to Iran. Golden Global rejected the allegations, calling them “entirely unfounded and inconsistent.”
The sanctions were significant, marking the first time a bank in a NATO ally had been hit under the current economic campaign, experts told Reuters.
These recent U.S. sanctions on Turkish firms are the latest points of tension between the two countries. In 2019, Turkish state-run lender Halkbank was charged in a Manhattan federal court, accused of participating in a “multibillion-dollar Iranian sanctions evasion scheme.”
The charges—referred to by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan as “ugly”—dragged on for years, before a settlement was reached in March. Halkbank was barred from entering transactions that benefit Iran and had to hire a compliance monitor to review its sanctions and anti-money-laundering programs.
The two NATO allies have also clashed in their differences of opinion related to Israel's operations in Gaza, Trump’s tariff policies, and Washington’s maintained block on F-35 fighter jet sales to Turkey while Ankara still holds Russian-made S-400 air defense systems.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott of Florida earlier this week said “Turkey is not our friend” as he showed support for the sanctions targeting firms in the country. “Bessent had to crack down on them for actively funding Iranian terrorists,” he claimed.
How corporations in other countries respond to the U.S. measures “is an important test” for the Trump Administration, Roush says, noting that despite Washington’s crackdown on international entities supporting the Iranian economy, some have shown they’re willing to continue doing business with Tehran.
"A lot of these smaller, more boutique firms… They're more informal. They tend to continue their trade ties or banking ties with Iran. The UAE has done, or well, they're trying to do a good job of severing these ties with Iran, but other states in the region, like Iraq and Azerbaijan and Turkey, are continuing to trade with Iran,” says Roush. “Iran is an important trading partner for them, and I think it's going to take a significant amount of diplomatic pressure to impose some kind of a full blockade of Iran.”
How Iran has responded to the aviation sanctions
Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations Gholamhossein Darzi on Wednesday argued that Washington’s sanctions amount to “economic terrorism” and “collective punishment,” according to Iran's Mehr news agency.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s Foreign Minister, dismissed the effectiveness of the “economic D-Day” campaign.
“After 47 years of sanctions, the U.S. went to war with Iran on behalf of Israel. The fallout has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide,” he said Tuesday. “After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s ‘novel’ solution is… more sanctions. Seriously?”
But experts say the ramped up economic pressure campaign will undoubtedly impact Iran in some way.
The aviation-related measures alone will “make it harder to transport materiel to keep Mahan Air going, and it'll contribute to regional isolation,” says Roush.
Furthermore, Iran is already feeling the economic impact of the conflict and the U.S. naval blockade on its ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sep. 10, Iran’s Rial currency plummeted in value, hitting a record low open-market rate of 2.34 million rials to the dollar. Inflation has also climbed significantly, with reports indicating rural communities and low-income households are carrying the burden. The country lost around 630,000 manufacturing jobs in the first quarter of 2026, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.
“Ultimately, the Iranian people are likely to suffer, because the regime will continue its predatory practice of absorbing the economic resources of the country and channeling it toward its military efforts,” concludes Roush.

articles.title: Ukraine hits key Russia-Iran logistics hub in Caspian Sea, damages three Russian warships
articles.body:
Ukraine says its forces struck Russia’s Makhachkala port on the Caspian Sea and confirmed damage to three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in a series of long-range attacks.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the Makhachkala Sea Commercial Port in Russia’s Dagestan was hit overnight on 10 September, with a fire recorded at the site. The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The Special Operations Forces (SSO) said Ukrainian units struck oil infrastructure at the port in a joint operation with other Defense Forces. The port’s oil terminal handles tankers with a capacity of up to 10,000 tonnes, while an oil depot is located nearby, according to the SSO.
Makhachkala is Russia’s only ice-free deepwater port on the Caspian Sea and operates year-round. The General Staff said it is an important link in the Russia-Iran logistics corridor, which Moscow uses to bypass Western sanctions.
According to the General Staff, the route is used to transport military-related cargo in both directions, including components and Shahed-type attack drones from Iran to Russia, and explosives, drone components, and ammunition from Russia to Iran. A base of Russia’s Caspian Flotilla is also located near the port.
The SSO said damaging the port’s oil infrastructure could reduce Russia’s ability to use the Caspian Sea to transport and transship energy resources.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian drone manufacturer, said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones in the attack. The company said Makhachkala had been used as a transit point for Iranian attack drones delivered to Russia by sea before being moved onward for use against Ukraine.
Fire Point also said the port handled more than 2.9 million tonnes of cargo in the first eight months of 2026, including more than 2.08 million tonnes of oil.
Three Russian warships hit in Novorossiysk
Ukraine’s General Staff also said further analysis of data confirmed damage inflicted on three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk on 9 September, along with fuel-oil storage facilities at the port.
The General Staff identified the vessels as the small sea minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the frigate Admiral Essen, and the Project 11711 landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
Visual analysis published by Exilenova+ reported strikes on another Russian warship, the Buyan-M-class corvette, as well as confirming strikes on the frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov. The outlet said the Essen was hit in its superstructure and caught fire.
The Buyan-M class is capable of carrying Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. Russia has used such ships to launch strikes against Ukraine.
The Ukrainian General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

articles.title: Ukraine says it hit three Russian warships in Novorossiysk, one had recently launched Kalibr missiles at Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials have reported that three Russian warships capable of launching cruise missiles were hit in a combined missile and drone strike on Novorossiysk overnight into Sept. 9. The vessels in question were a Project 21631 Buyan-M small missile ship, and the frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov.
Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, announced earlier today that the coordinated strike on the naval base in Novorossiysk had caused it to “lose a number of military vessels, including missile carriers.”
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) said the Admiral Essen was hit in its superstructure, causing a fire aboard the ship. The Ukrainian Navy also said a Neptune cruise missile was used in the attack.
The Admiral Essen is a Project 11356 frigate of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet and can carry Kalibr cruise missiles, which Russian forces have repeatedly used in strikes on Ukraine.
It was not the first time Admiral Essen had been targeted. In August, Ukraine’s General Staff reported strikes on the Admiral Essen, Admiral Makarov and the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Satellite images published after the latest attack appear to point to at least two other possible strikes. One target was a Project 21631 Buyan-M small missile ship. Images appear to show a direct hit on the vessel. Ukrainian sources said it lost combat capability after the strike.
Buyan-M ships are a class of small Russian missile vessels armed with the Kalibr-NK missile system. Despite their relatively small size, they can launch long-range cruise missiles at ground targets and have repeatedly been used by Russia to carry out strikes on Ukraine.
The Ukrainian side said the vessel hit in Novorossiysk had taken part in an attack on Kyiv shortly before it was struck.
Another likely target was the frigate Admiral Makarov, which is also capable of launching Kalibr missiles. Ukrainian sources published images that they said show damage to the ship’s port side.
Footage of a possible attack on the Project 11711 large landing ship Pyotr Morgunov was also analyzed. In that case, however, Ukrainian monitoring resources preliminarily assessed that the munition failed to reach its target.
The Novorossiysk strike was carried out overnight into Sept. 9 and involved several types of weapons. Ukraine said it targeted the port and military infrastructure in the city.
Fires in the area were also visible on satellite data from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which detects thermal anomalies. According to the FIRMS map, heat signatures were recorded in the port area from 2:05 a.m. to 3:45 a.m. Moscow time on Sept. 9, with the strongest readings at 3:45 a.m.
After repeated Ukrainian attacks on Sevastopol, Russia relocated a significant part of its Black Sea Fleet to Novorossiysk. In recent years, however, Ukraine has also begun systematically attacking that base with maritime drones, aerial drones, and missiles.

articles.title: Russia rehearsed how to disable Europe’s undersea communications cables near Svalbard. NATO forces drove them off
articles.body:
Russia rehearsed an operation to disable critical undersea cables near Norway’s Svalbard archipelago this spring, according to two Western officials cited by Reuters.
The exercise comes as Russia continues a broader hybrid campaign against European countries, using covert sabotage, cyberattacks, espionage, and surveillance of critical infrastructure alongside its war against Ukraine.
The operation involved Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, known as GUGI, which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate deploying technology designed to disable undersea cables.
British, Norwegian, and US forces tracked the Russian vessels and confronted them at sea, preventing them from completing the exercise, the officials told Reuters. The vessels eventually left the area.
No cables were damaged.
Russian forces rehearsed cable attacks
The operation took place near two 1,400-kilometer fiber-optic cables connecting Svalbard with mainland Norway. The cables carry satellite data from SvalSat, the world’s largest satellite ground station and part of NASA’s Near Space Network.
Britain and Norway disclosed in April that they had uncovered covert Russian activity in Arctic waters, but the details of the operation, including the technology involved and US participation, had not previously been reported.
Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said the joint operation sent Russia a message that covert activity would be detected and face consequences.
The US and UK have sanctioned GUGI over its activities in European waters.
“Will not be tolerated” – UK exposes Russian spy submarine operation targeting its undersea cables
Europe watches its undersea infrastructure
European governments have become increasingly concerned about Russian activity around telecommunications cables, power lines, and pipelines. Reuters reported that since 2023, vessels have increasingly been observed moving slowly over or near sensitive infrastructure, raising concerns that they could be mapping potential targets.
NATO has expanded monitoring in response. Its Baltic Sentry operation increases surveillance around critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea, while the UK-led Nordic Warden monitors northern European waters.
Windward data cited by Reuters showed that vessels classified as “drifting” in the North Sea increased 52% in 2025, to 13,079. At least 11 subsea cables were damaged or cut in the Baltic between October 2023 and the end of 2025.
Western officials are increasingly concerned that Russia could use sabotage against European infrastructure to test NATO's response without immediately triggering open conflict. Some US intelligence officials have raised the possibility that Moscow could eventually test the alliance’s Article 5 mutual-defense commitment, according to Reuters.
Russia’s Defense Ministry did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries.
The Svalbard exercise did not damage infrastructure, but it involved rehearsing capabilities that could be used against critical European infrastructure in a future conflict.

articles.title: Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis seize key Yemen city near Bab el-Mandeb Strait
The Houthis have seized the strategic Yemeni port city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast, government sources said on Thursday, marking a major development in the renewed fighting as tens of thousands have been displaced across the country.
Three Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi forces had entered Mocha and taken control of the coastal city, while local sources told The New Arab that large numbers of residents were fleeing towards the southern city of Aden.
The takeover comes after weeks of escalating Houthi attacks on Mocha and its port and amid a broader offensive by the Iran-backed group across western Yemen.
Mocha is strategically important because of its location on Yemen's western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The city's capture could therefore have wider implications for security around the strait and commercial shipping through the Red Sea, as fighting intensifies across Yemen's western coast.
The Houthis launched a major offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces last week aimed at advancing towards Bab al-Mandab, prompting government-aligned forces to mount counterattacks and expand operations elsewhere in the country.
Mocha had already come under repeated Houthi missile, drone and explosive-laden boat attacks in recent weeks.
The city's port suspended all commercial and maritime operations in mid-August after it was struck by more than 25 Houthi missiles, according to information provided by sources.
The attacks caused civilian casualties and damaged facilities and property, with material losses estimated at around $16 million.
The takeover coincides with an escalation in fighting along Yemen's western coast, particularly in southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, where government and allied forces have been carrying out military movements and withdrawing from several positions.
Yemeni government forces withdrew overnight from Hays district in southern Hodeidah as military units operating around Hays and western Taiz began a process of reorganisation and redeployment, military and local sources said.
It remains unclear how many troops withdrew from Hays and Al-Wazi'iyah or where they have been redeployed. Military sources said the movements were part of preparations for a coordinated field operation.
Tareq Saleh orders western coast forces to regroup
Tareq Saleh, deputy chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said on Thursday that government forces on the western coast had suffered heavy losses in recent days while confronting the Houthi offensive.
Saleh said forces had been ordered to regroup and establish an alternative command centre in a secure location in consultation with the Saudi-led coalition and the Presidential Leadership Council.
Military media affiliated with Saleh's National Resistance said the joint forces had established a command centre south of Mocha following Houthi breakthroughs on several fronts under heavy fire.
The forces involved in the western coast fighting include the National Resistance, the Giants Brigades and Nation's Shield forces, alongside units from the Taiz military axis.
Saleh accused Iran of planning, supporting and participating in the Houthi offensive through what he described as its "various tools", without providing further details about Tehran's alleged involvement.
Iran has rejected accusations that it is interfering in Yemen, saying this week that it supports the country's unity and territorial integrity and a Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.
Meanwhile, military media sources reported air strikes on Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah province.
The National Resistance's military media also said the Houthis had targeted Zuqar Island with two ballistic missiles.
The latest developments come amid the most significant escalation on several Yemeni fronts following years of relative calm. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but clashes resumed in July and have since widened.
Fighting has also spilled across the border into Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh accusing the Houthis of targeting Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities said this week that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.
