articles.title: Russia has eight ships left that can carry Kalibrs. Analysts say Ukraine hit three of them in one night
articles.body:
- The Ukrainian navy says one of its Neptune anti-ship missiles hit the Russian frigate Admiral Essen at Novorossiysk overnight on 8–9 September
- Ukraine's general staff confirms hits on three ships in the raid; open-source analysts read the satellite imagery as showing a second Kalibr carrier, a Buyan-M corvette, knocked out
- It'll take many more strikes to reduce the Russians to zero Kalibr capacity
A Ukrainian Neptune anti-ship cruise missile struck the Russian missile frigate Admiral Essen in the port of Novorossiysk in southern Russia overnight on 8–9 September, the Ukrainian navy claimed. Satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian open-source group Exilenova+ shows fires and apparent damage consistent with the claim. How badly the ship is hurt is unclear.
But if the navy is correct and one of its truck-launched Neptunes hit Admiral Essen, it would be a major victory for Ukraine—and a major loss for Russia. Pummeled by Ukrainian missiles and drones, the Russian Black Sea Fleet has lost or had damaged around a third of its combat strength, by Ukraine's own reckoning. No more than eight of the surviving vessels carry launchers for launching the fleet's best missile: the Kalibr cruise missile.
Taking out those eight Kalibr shooters—two frigates, three corvettes, and as many as three submarines—is a top priority for Ukraine. Preserving the Kalibr ships is one of Russia's top priorities as it escalates its bombardment of Ukrainian cities, factories, warehouses, and power plants.
And the frigate wasn't the only ship in the target set. Ukraine's general staff confirmed hits on three vessels—Admiral Essen, the minesweeper Zheleznyakov, and the landing ship Pyotr Morgunov—along with fuel-oil storage at the port. Exilenova+ reads the imagery as showing two more Kalibr carriers hit: a Kalibr-armed Buyan-M corvette knocked out of action, and fresh damage to sister frigate Admiral Makarov.
Ukraine reported hitting warships and an oil terminal in a Russian port city whose mayor claimed only falling debris
To be clear, it's evident the Ukrainians have already hit Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov. A Ukrainian drone raid targeting Novorossiysk on 12 August resulted in what appeared to be direct hits to the forward missile cells on both ships.
Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov can launch as many as eight of the 2,500-km Kalibrs at a time from these 3S14 cells. Damage the cells, and the frigates can no longer threaten Ukraine. At least until the Russians can effect repairs. Ukraine's military intelligence directorate described this week's damage as a fire on Admiral Essen's deck superstructure—not its missile cells.
Hitting one of the frigates with a 900-km/h Neptune's 260-kg warhead, as opposed to the much lighter warhead on a much slower drone, could do more than temporarily sideline the ship. It may cause irreparable damage, effectively removing the vessel from the Black Sea Fleet's dwindling order of battle.
Recall that a pair of Neptunes from a much earlier batch of the increasingly powerful missile sank the Russian missile cruiser Moskva in April 2022, initiating the ongoing battle over the Black Sea that has seen the Russians gradually lose irreplaceable ships—and gradually pull back surviving vessels into Novorossiysk's protected basin.
Unsafe haven
Novorossiysk, 350 km from the southern front line, is safer for Russian ships than are, say, the ports of occupied Crimea. But it's not actually safe. Ukrainian drones and missiles routinely target the port and the dozens of ships moored inside.
Trending Now
Most of the Ukrainian munitions miss or get shot down. Undeterred, Ukrainian deep strike forces have only intensified their strikes. Launching more Neptunes would represent another escalation. Drones damage. Neptunes destroy.
Even if one or more Neptunes finally took Admiral Essen out of action this week, there's more work left to do. The Russians normally fire fewer than 10 Kalibrs as part of the mix of missiles and drones they hurl at Ukrainian cities once a week or so.
A single frigate can fire eight Kalibrs at a time. So can a single corvette. A submarine might fire four Kalibrs. Even with Admiral Essen off the board, the carriers that may still be combat-capable can put 16 to 20 Kalibrs into the air at once, per Defence Express. Before 2022 the theoretical figure was 76.
Ukraine's navy puts the number in the same range. On 21 August, spokesman Dmytro Pletenchuk counted three surface ships and two submarines able to fire Kalibrs, with both frigates excluded as damaged. He also noted the fleet used its missile carriers once in August, down from three times in July, and now fires from inside protected harbors rather than putting to sea.
But more and better Neptunes may be coming to Novorossiysk. More Kalibr shooters may burn. Ukrainian missile-maker Luch Design Bureau has steadily improved the Neptune with greater range and payload while also increasing production. An open-source tally published by Ukrainska Pravda counted 26 verified Neptune hits on Russian land targets between 2023 and mid-2026.
Ukraine seems determined to eventually reduce the Black Sea Fleet's Kalibr capacity to zero. It will take time and many more strikes, of course. How soon the Ukrainians can send more Neptunes to Novorossiysk may determine how many more Kalibrs blast Ukrainian cities.

articles.title: EU urges Kiev to mobilize women – Moscow
articles.body:
EU urges Kiev to mobilize women – Moscow
Brussels is encouraging Kiev to start mobilizing women amid chronic manpower shortages and has demanded that Ukraine immediately make “a political decision” on the matter, the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) has said.
Kiev launched its mobilization campaign soon after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. Amid mounting frontline losses and desertions, the mobilization drive has grown increasingly violent. Recruitment officers have repeatedly been filmed chasing, beating, and forcibly detaining reluctant conscripts before bundling them into vehicles in what in Ukraine has become known as “basification.”
EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, described the idea of expanding the campaign to include women as “a step in the right direction” at a recent informal EU foreign ministers’ meeting, the SVR said on Thursday, citing information it had obtained. She allegedly warned that Kiev could soon run out of manpower due to a growing shortage of men fit for military service and said that Ukraine should use Israel as a “model to follow.”
The mobilization of women has long been a subject of debate in Ukraine. MP Mariana Bezuglaya argued as early as 2024 that it was time Kiev started targeting women to meet its conscription quota. Last year, the Ukrainian presidential administration’s deputy head, Brigadier General Pavel Palisa, also voiced support for mandatory conscription of women.
According to the SVR, Brussels demanded that Kiev immediately “move from words to action” and make a formal decision to start mobilizing women.
Under current Ukrainian law, men aged 25 to 60 are subject to mobilization, while those aged 23 to 60 are generally barred from leaving the country. Women can serve voluntarily.
Kiev’s brutal mobilization campaign has encountered large-scale draft-dodging and desertion. According to Euronews, around 1.15 million fighting-age Ukrainian men had ended up in the EU as of summer 2026, despite the ban on travelling abroad. According to the SVR, up to 5.6 million Ukrainians are currently residing in various European nations, with women accounting for 43.4% of them.
Many men have proven ready to risk their lives to flee the country illegally through forests, rivers, and mountainous terrain. In February, the head of the Ukrainian border agency, Andrey Demchenko, reported that over 70 apparent draft dodgers had died since 2022, most while trying to cross the Tisza River along Ukraine’s border with Hungary and Romania.
Brussels has reportedly urged EU governments to devise legal mechanisms for sending back Ukrainian refugees residing in the bloc, the Russian intelligence service said, adding that the European Commission sees them as a reason behind the “rise of far-right sentiment” in countries such as Germany or Poland.
Some Western officials have also voiced support for the mobilization of Ukrainian women.
Last year, former British Defense Secretary Ben Wallace said that Vladimir Zelensky should have launched a truly mass mobilization and conscripted all men and women, without sparing the younger generation.
“Zelensky took a view that he was going to preserve the 18 to 28-year-olds, so it’s not a mass conscription,” Wallace said at the time, adding that the Ukrainian leader should have mobilized everyone and “asked Europe to train them because that is not a hard ask.”
Ben Hodges, a former top commander of US forces in Europe, argued earlier that Kiev should consider both drafting women and lowering the mobilization age to 18. “I also think that there is enough work for women in the army,” he stated.
Moscow has repeatedly slammed Ukraine’s NATO backers as pushing the nation into a war “to the last Ukrainian,” describing the conflict as a Western proxy war against Russia fought through Ukraine.

articles.title: Satellite images confirm Ukraine’s strike on Russian warship
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Defense Forces struck Russia's Novorossiysk naval base overnight on September 8-9, hitting the frigate Admiral Essen and starting a fire on its superstructure.
- Ukraine's General Staff also reported hits on the frigate Admiral Makarov, the small missile ship Buyan-M and the patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck Russia’s naval base at Novorossiysk overnight on September 8-9, hitting the Kalibr-missile frigate Admiral Essen and starting a fire on its deck superstructure, according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence agency, known as HUR.
HUR said operators from its Active Operations Department carried out the strike as part of a joint deep-strike operation with other branches of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, targeting both port infrastructure and the Project 11356 frigate. Ukraine’s General Staff separately said the attack also hit a second Kalibr-capable frigate, the Admiral Makarov, the Project 21631 small missile ship Buyan-M, and the Project 22160 patrol ship Vasily Bykov.
Commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces Robert Brovdi said the operation additionally destroyed several Russian missile boats in the port, a Su-33 fighter jet and a Mi-8 helicopter near Anapa, roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) northwest of Novorossiysk, along with two air-defense radar systems near Gelendzhik. Ukraine has not disclosed how many drones or missiles took part in the operation.
Satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian OSINT monitoring group Exilenova+ shows fires and apparent damage at the port consistent with the reported strikes on the Admiral Essen, the Admiral Makarov and the Buyan-M. The same channel said the attack combined drones with at least one Ukrainian Neptune cruise missile, a detail that has not appeared in HUR’s or the General Staff’s own statements on the operation.
Both the Admiral Essen and the Admiral Makarov have been hit before. Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck both frigates in August 2026, along with the Vasily Bykov, in an earlier raid on the same base. Novorossiysk has served as the Black Sea Fleet’s main operating base since repeated Ukrainian strikes pushed Russian warships out of Sevastopol in occupied Crimea.
Russian officials in Novorossiysk said debris from intercepted drones struck a church, industrial sites and residential buildings, killing four people and injuring about 30. Moscow has not issued its own account of damage to the naval vessels named by Ukraine.
The extent of damage to the Admiral Essen, the Admiral Makarov, the Buyan-M and the Vasily Bykov has not been independently confirmed, and Ukraine’s General Staff said assessments of some of the reported strikes were still being finalized.

articles.title: Canada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits
articles.body:
Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.
“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.
The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.
That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.
“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.
In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.
“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.
The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.
Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.
Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.
The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.
Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.
Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”
Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.
But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.
“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.
“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”
After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.
He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.

articles.title: Permanent 5 members clash in UN Security Council over Iran sanctions snapback
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
The five permanent members of the UN Security Council clashed Thursday during a high-stakes session about the legal validity of international sanctions against Iran and the reimposition of UN sanctions under the 2015 nuclear accord's "snapback" provision.
The snapback clause, established under the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was designed to automatically reinstate UN Chapter VII sanctions if Iran breached the deal, intentionally bypassing the veto power of permanent council members.
"The mechanism for reinstating previously adopted Security Council resolutions on Iran, a mechanism set forth in Resolution 2231, was not activated, and this for a whole host of legal and procedural reasons," said the Russian representative, demanding a procedural vote to block a scheduled briefing on the 1737 Sanctions Committee.
Moscow argued that UN Resolution 2231, which endorsed the nuclear deal, expired Oct. 18, 2025, and insisted that the non-proliferation agenda item was struck off the council's list of active matters that day. The Russian envoy maintained that the 1737 Committee ceased to exist in 2015 and that no legal grounds remain to discuss its “so-called work.”
The Chinese representative supported the move, asserting that the council presidency lacks the mandate to draft or deliver a 90-day report. Warning against unilateral action, Beijing stressed, "A few members, in disregard of differences, insist on forcibly reimposing the Council sanctions against Iran and convening Council meetings under a removed agenda item." The envoy warned that the steps deepen institutional division and impede a political settlement, expressing "grave concern" and “strong opposition" against the moves.
Western delegations firmly rejected the challenge, arguing that the sanctions regime had been legally revived following Iranian breaches.
"The United Kingdom, with France and Germany, initiated the snapback mechanism in full accordance with Security Council Resolution 2231," said the British representative, explaining that European powers acted because of Iran's "significant non-performance" under the 2015 nuclear pact. London noted that the process concluded Sept. 28, 2025, leaving six Chapter VII resolutions in effect for nearly a year.
The French representative affirmed that council resolutions were restored alongside the committee's mandate to report every 90 days.
"Regardless of such politically driven matters, the facts are the facts. The 1737 Committee exists," said the US representative, accusing Russia and China of attempting to undermine council decisions to protect Tehran. The American diplomat noted that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed Iran remains non-compliant with its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement.
The council voted 11-2 in favor of adopting the provisional agenda, with two abstentions, defeating the Russian and Chinese bid to halt the meeting. Under UN Security Council rules, procedural votes cannot be blocked by a permanent member's veto and require a minimum of nine affirmative votes to pass.
Permanent members trade accusations after vote
Moscow denounced the briefing as an illegitimate exercise and an "inefficient use" of council resources, with the Russian representative describing it as a “flagrant procedural breach.”
The Russian envoy accused Washington and Israel of conducting strikes on "peaceful" facilities under IAEA safeguards, warning that the "illegal and reckless actions" risked provoking a wider regional catastrophe, while dismissing a new IAEA Board of Governors resolution referring Iran to the council as “politicized.”
Beijing maintained that lasting solutions require addressing the root causes of regional tensions. The "United States’ unilateral withdrawal from the JCPOA, its use of force against Iran twice during the negotiation process, and its pursuit of a policy of maximum pressure against Iran are the primary causes of the current complex and intractable situation in the Middle East and the Iranian nuclear issue," argued the Chinese envoy. China defended lran's "legitimate right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy," and said it acknowledges “Iran's repeated commitments not to develop nuclear weapons.”
"Iran is the only country without nuclear weapons to enrich uranium to this level," said the British envoy, criticizing Tehran for reportedly stockpiling more than 400 kilograms (882 pounds) of uranium enriched to 60% without "any credible civilian justification." London accused Iran of barring UN inspectors from all nuclear facilities since June 2025, sparing only the Bushehr plant, reiterating that a negotiated settlement remains the only durable path.
Rejecting safety arguments raised by Tehran for barring inspectors, the US representative said UN personnel continue to operate safely inside war-torn Ukraine, which IAEA director Rafael Grossi noted as a "worse and more constant war zone." The American diplomat accused Moscow and Beijing of trying to shield a state whose nuclear program is progressing “in the dark.”
France underlined Tehran's stockpile, warning that the amount is potentially sufficient for about 10 explosive nuclear devices.

articles.title: Iran destroys US spy Saildrone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Iran destroys US spy Saildrone in Hormuz (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has destroyed a US Saildrone Explorer reconnaissance vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, releasing footage showing the unmanned craft burning in the water.
The IRGC Navy said on Thursday that the vessel, identified by hull number 5838, was struck while operating near the strategic waterway. Iranian state media described it as an American surveillance drone, but the US military has not confirmed the loss.
“The American terrorist and aggressor army, over the past few days, out of fear of approaching and confronting the fighters of Islam, has dispatched its unmanned vessels to the Strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said.
The Iranian Navy: We have struck a US unmanned vessel, with hull number 5838, at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. pic.twitter.com/WyesLWXI47
— IRIB (Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting) (@iribnews_irib) September 10, 2026
The strategic waterway remains under Tehran’s control and “intelligence surveillance,” the IRGC added, warning that “any hostile presence in this strategic strait will be targeted.”
The roughly seven-meter Saildrone Explorer is an unmanned surface vessel equipped with cameras, sensors and communications systems for maritime surveillance and reconnaissance. The US Navy has previously deployed the platform with the Bahrain-based 5th Fleet’s Task Force 59, which integrates unmanned systems and artificial intelligence into regional operations.
The latest incident comes just two days after the IRGC captured a US underwater drone at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. Footage released by Tehran showed what appeared to be an Anduril-built Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle commissioned in 2025. The Pentagon acknowledged losing the submersible, but said it was old and broken and carried no sensitive data or classified equipment.
The incidents come amid an escalating maritime standoff between Washington and Tehran. The US has destroyed several Iranian oil tankers after accusing the IRGC of firing ballistic missiles at American warships, while Iran has attacked US vessels and commercial tankers it accused of violating restrictions around Hormuz.
The confrontation has severely disrupted traffic through one of the world’s most important energy corridors and pushed Brent crude above $107 a barrel, while farther west, Iran-aligned Houthi forces are tightening their grip on Bab al-Mandeb, another vital chokepoint linking the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.

articles.title: SBI suspects SBU official of organizing ammunition storage in Mila village near Kyiv
articles.body:
Officers of the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) have notified a department head in charge of supply and logistics at the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) of suspicion for overseeing the arrangement and operation of an artillery ammunition depot in the village of Mila near Kyiv.
"It has been established that when deciding to locate the warehouse in a former vegetable storage facility, he failed to take all control measures regarding the security of storing explosives and ammunition. In addition, the warehouse was illegally located near residential buildings. The premises not only failed to meet requirements for weapons storage facilities, but its placement was not coordinated with relevant law enforcement structures and air defense units. The official also failed to take measures to minimize the risks of simultaneous destruction of a large quantity of ammunition by the enemy," the press service of the SBI reported.
Russian unmanned aerial vehicles launched a strike on the facility, triggering ammunition detonation and a fire that spread to neighboring premises.
As a result of the detonation, 35 people were killed. In addition, 191 private residential houses, 14 apartment buildings, a police station, garages, a restaurant, a nursing home, a shop, and a logistics center were damaged, as well as 24 vehicles, including a police service car and a fire truck.
The official has been notified of suspicion of inaction of military authority committed under martial law (Part 4 of Article 426 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
Pechersky District Court of Kyiv remanded him in custody as a preventive measure with an alternative of bail.
The article's sanction provides for punishment in the form of imprisonment for a term of up to 10 years.
His name and the specific department he headed have not been disclosed.
As reported by the Prosecutor General's Office of Ukraine on Thursday, after a similar tragedy in the city of Vyshneve (Kyiv region), measures were initiated to liquidate the depot and remove the ammunition, but as of August 28, when the occupiers attacked the storage facilities with drones, these measures had not been completed. It is emphasized that the depot was located less than 100 meters from residential buildings, and requirements regarding the permissible quantity of ammunition and its dispersal—intended to reduce the risk of simultaneous detonation and damage to surrounding facilities—were not observed.
"The investigation is also examining the circumstances of improper security control over the facility and the failure to take measures to strengthen its air defense cover. Forensic explosives and fire safety evaluations have been ordered in the proceedings... All circumstances are being established, as well as other individuals whose decisions, actions, or inaction may have affected the scale of the consequences of the Russian attack," the agency reported.
Earlier, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that such tragedies are unacceptable, especially after a similar event occurred in Vyshneve near Kyiv, calling it the result of "terrible negligence by those who stored explosives right next to people." He reported that criminal proceedings had been opened regarding the incident and called for a full investigation into all the facts of what transpired.

articles.title: Poland expects Russia to target border crossings as attacks on Ukraine escalate – Russia has already hit crossings with Moldova and Romania
articles.body:
Poland expects Russia to target border crossings with Ukraine as Moscow expands its strikes on trade and logistics routes far from the front line, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on 10 September, according to Reuters.
The warning comes after Russia has already struck at least five Ukrainian border crossings with Moldova and NATO member Romania since late August. The attacks mark a significant escalation in Russia’s targeting of Ukraine’s civilian transport, trade, and logistics infrastructure, far from the front line.
“Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to one of the border crossings was averted,” Tusk said at a press conference in Bratislava, according to Reuters.
He said Poland expected Russia to take similar action against border crossings in other countries, including Poland.
Russia has significantly ramped up its aerial attacks across Ukraine in recent months, increasingly striking civilian transport, energy, industrial, and logistics infrastructure while deploying newer and more capable weapons. The expanded use of drones and missiles has also made these attacks harder to stop, allowing Russia to hit targets farther from the front line with greater frequency and inflict more damage and casualties.
Russia is striking Ukraine’s civilian travel and logistics routes
The Russian attacks have targeted crossings in Ukraine’s southern Odesa Oblast, hundreds of kilometers from the front line.
Four of the crossings hit since late August are on Ukraine’s border with Moldova, while another is on the Romanian border. The sites handle civilian traffic, trade, and logistics that have become increasingly important to Ukraine as the war continues.
On 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing with Moldova, killing two civilians and injuring three others. During the attack, one Russian drone entered Moldovan airspace and flew toward Romania, prompting NATO aircraft conducting air-policing duties to scramble.
Russian drones also struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the Romanian border twice in early September.
Far from any front line: Russia has hit at least five of Ukraine’s western border crossings with Moldova and NATO member since late August
Poland prepares for further escalation
Tusk said he had received a “fairly precise report” from the CIA about possible developments in the coming months, which he said aligned with warnings he had made previously.
“Poland and all of Europe need to be prepared for different possibilities,” Tusk said, including developments not only on the Russian-Ukrainian front but also along the EU’s eastern flank.
The warning comes as Russian strikes increasingly reach toward Ukraine’s borders with NATO and EU countries. The drone incursions into Moldovan and Romanian airspace during attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure have already brought NATO forces into the response.
The latest attacks represent a broader shift in Russia’s targeting: Moscow is not only striking Ukraine’s cities and military infrastructure, but increasingly hitting the trade, transport, and civilian logistics routes that keep the country functioning during the war.

articles.title: Russian drones kill at least nine in strikes targeting warehouses and ports in Ukraine – Europe live
articles.body:
Russia's actions are 'reckless, dangerous and a threat to life,' Nato's Rutte warns, but says they only strengthen resolve to help Ukraine
In his speech, Rutte repeatedly praises Germany’s role within Nato, and then eventually gets to his stark assessment of the situation in Ukraine – and Europe.
He says:
“Russia’s brutal attacks against Ukraine are unrelenting. Russia is suffering enormous losses, now estimated at more than 40,000 killed or seriously wounded every month. Think about it for a moment. Over 40,000 every month.
Despite those heavy losses, Putin shows no willingness to bring the war to an end.
Instead, Russia repeatedly strikes Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, often targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and at the same time, the list of Russia’s malign hybrid activities across Europe grows longer and longer: cyber-attacks, sabotage, arson, airspace violations, drone incidents.
…
The latest hostile actions by Russia are reckless, dangerous and a threat to life. But we are not intimidated. We know these are the tactics of a desperate regime that is failing to meet its objectives in Ukraine. Putin thinks he can divide us, destabilise us and weaken our support for Ukraine. But he will fail. These malicious actions are having the opposite effect.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte has warned that Russia’s “reckless, dangerous” actions in Europe and “unrelenting” attacks on Ukraine will only strengthen the resolve to support Kyiv and invest in European defence (12:01).
Rutte said that Russia’s escalatory behaviour was “a sign of weakness and a symptom of its failure to get its war in Ukraine” (11:45, 12:10).
But European leaders “increasingly understand taking greater responsibility for our own security is not optional,” Rutte said (12:06), even as he insisted he had “no doubt” the US remained fully supportive of European allies (12:28).
Speaking alongside Rutte, German foreign minister Johann Wadephul warned that the Russian threat “has reached our doorstep and it’s tangible” (11:41, 11:53) as he discussed Germany’s lessons from a recent attempted drone attack in Leipzig.
And in the last few minutes, Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk said Poland averted a threat to one of its border crossings with Ukraine overnight and expects its crossings will be targeted in the coming weeks.One to watch.
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Tourists in England face nightly levy under new plans, a model well-proven in Europe
Holidaymakers will face a nightly levy on hotel and Airbnb-style stays across large parts of England in a move welcomed by many mayors but described as risking “irreparable harm” to the tourism industry.
But, as Angela Giuffrida explains, while a nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades.
“Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs.
Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats.
Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors.
Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination.
The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy.”
‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German city where the far right surged
After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend, people in the state capital shared with our correspondent Kate Connolly what they make of the result – and what comes next.
“Asking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday.
The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe.
Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly.
Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said.
Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air.
A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s postwar memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”.
I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past.
Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums.
And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.””
The European Central Bank has raised interest rates for the second time this year, as widely expected, at it tries to bring inflation under control.
The decision was supported by a stronger-than-expected economy that suggests businesses can weather the higher borrowing costs, AP noted.
The central bank for the 21 EU member countries that use the euro currency raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to 2.50% at a meeting held in Berlin, away from the bank’s Frankfurt headquarters, it said.
Poland issues third security alert to residents in areas bordering Ukraine in one day
Poland has warned residents in two south-eastern regions that its air force is monitoring the skies amid ongoing Russian attacks on neighbouring Ukraine.
Locals have received three similar alerts in the past 12 hours – a stark indicator of the intensity of Russia’s attacks and the heightened concern across the border.
Malta warned of corruption crisis after Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict sends ‘chill down the spine’
Juliette Garside
Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017.
At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond.”
“It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added.
Macron meets Stubb for talks on Ukraine, European security
Over in France, it looks like Emmanuel Macron is focusing not only on future space endeavours, but also on very down-to-earth issues of European security.
Aside from his space conference (11:01), he met for talks with Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb on “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, European security, and ways to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy.”
“Finland and France are closer than ever before. France is an important partner for Ukraine and the whole of Europe,” Stubb said.
Despite its low-key format, the meeting is worth noting given Stubb’s central role to all diplomatic efforts on Ukraine, as he is one of the few European leaders that have a genuinely good rapport with the US president, Donald Trump, and so is closely involved in all relevant discussions on Ukraine, Russia and European security.
By the way, we will be liveblogging the Swedish election night for you here on Europe Live, straight from Stockholm, so make sure to join us on Sunday night.
Swedish Muslims challenge far right ahead of key election this weekend
Swedes will vote on Sunday in a tight election that will be another litmus test of whether far-right parties should join the government, as the Sweden Democrats, with roots in the neo-Nazi fringe, poll at around 19% of the vote and could join the ruling centre-right coalition led by Ulf Kristersson.
The Guardian’s Ashifa Kassam visited Sweden recently to take stock of the atmosphere in the country ahead of the vote, and look at how migration and religion are being weaponised for political purposes.
“Not far from one of Scandinavia’s biggest shopping malls, Kashif Virk stood on the pavement, handing out flyers and smiling at those who passed by. On a cloudy Tuesday afternoon, the Swedish-born imam had taken to the street to invite people to ask him anything they had ever wanted to know about Islam.
For years, Sweden’s far right has peddled its own, distorted view of Islam, portraying it as being at odds with Swedish values. The Ask-a-Muslim – or Fråga en Muslim – campaign, conceived by Virk in 2017, was his way of fighting back.”
Rutte’s visit is not the only show in town in Berlin today, as the leader of the United Arab Emirates is paying a state visit to Germany, and is expected to sign off on multi-billion deals on energy, technology, and transport.
Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is getting the full treatment and was welcomed with military honours by president Frank-Walter Steinmeier this morning, before meeting chancellor Friedrich Merz later today.
AFP noted that the UAE is Germany’s largest trading partner in the Gulf, with bilateral trade topping $15bn last year, and many big German companies have a presence there including BMW, Siemens, ThyssenKrupp and rail operator Deutsche Bahn.
The UAE meanwhile has made major investments in Germany, including in the chemical industry and offshore wind power.
Inexplicably, there is no joint press conference scheduled as part of the visit.

articles.title: Zelensky Arrives in Canada for Three-Day Visit Focused on Defense, Energy
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky and First Lady Olena Zelenska arrived in Canada late Wednesday, Sept. 9, for a three-day visit focused on strengthening defense, economic and energy cooperation between Kyiv and Ottawa.
Zelensky will visit Calgary, Toronto and North Bay through Sept. 11 and is expected to address members of the Canadian government, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The talks will focus on expanding cooperation in defense, the economy and energy, while also addressing the human toll of Russia’s war against Ukraine, Carney’s office said.
Zelensky said before the trip that he planned to discuss ballistic missile defense with Canadian officials. He has described ballistic defense as one of Ukraine’s key vulnerabilities as Russia continues its long-range missile and drone attacks.
Kyiv is also seeking to develop its own ballistic missile defense capabilities, Zelensky said.
The Canadian visit follows Zelensky’s trip to Norway, where he attended the funeral of King Harald V and met Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre to discuss air defense and preparations for the coming winter.
Støre later said Zelensky’s plane narrowly avoided a drone while taking off from Moldova en route to Norway.
Zelensky also met Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir on Sept. 9, with talks focusing on strengthening Ukraine’s air defense and preparations for winter.

articles.title: About Nine F-15s and A-10s Damaged in Iranian Strike on U.S. Base in Jordan – CBS
articles.body:
An Iranian missile strike on a U.S. base in Jordan damaged nine U.S. Air Force aircraft.
CBS News reported on this.
Around eight F-15 fighter jets sustained minor damage. After inspections, they were returned to service.
One A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft sustained significantly more serious damage. According to CBS News sources, a missile struck the aircraft and severed its wing.
The strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base took place overnight on September 9, local time.
Iran launched the attack after U.S. forces hit five Iranian oil tankers in response to strikes by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on a U.S. Navy vessel.
Later, Iran claimed to have attacked eight tankers and two warships, as well as U.S. facilities in Jordan.
At the same time, there were no reports of U.S. service members being killed in the attack.
Iran had previously carried out strikes on Muwaffaq Salti. In July, at least two U.S. service members were killed in an attack on the base.
At the time, according to the command, U.S. forces, together with partner forces, provided air defense and repelled a massive Iranian attack.
As of July 16, 2026, the United States had officially confirmed the deaths of 14 service members during Operation Epic Fury.
As of May 2026, the U.S. had lost or sustained damage to at least 42 aircraft.
Among the losses were four F-15E Strike Eagles, one F-35A Lightning II, and one A-10 Thunderbolt II.
The United States also lost or damaged seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft, an E-3 Sentry AEW&C, two MC-130J Commando II special-mission aircraft, and an HH-60W Jolly Green II SAR helicopter.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones strike Makhachkala port and Sochi waterfront, satellite data points to new damage in Russia’s Arctic gas region
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked the commercial seaport in the city of Makhachkala in Russia’s Dagestan overnight into Sept. 10. At around 3 a.m., local residents began reporting explosions and air defense activity near the port. Before the authorities issued any official statements, the independent outlet Astra analyzed witness footage and determined that the commercial seaport was the likely target.
Astra also geolocated one of the explosions to the area of Pushkin Street where the Avar Theater is located.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ published several videos showing drones flying overhead and exploding. Other footage showed smoke rising in the port area and damage in the city. Exilenova+ also published what it said was the apparent moment of a strike on the port’s infrastructure.
Acting Dagestan head Fyodor Shchukin confirmed that fires broke out at the port and at the Avarsky Theater. He said all aerial targets had been destroyed and that the fires were caused by falling debris. However, the theater’s director, Magomed Bisavaliyev, reported that a drone fell directly onto the building’s roof, blowing out windows before a fire started. Shchukin said the fires had been extinguished, no one was killed or injured, and the theater’s damaged roof would be repaired. Airports in Makhachkala, Vladikavkaz, and Grozny suspended operations for three and a half hours.
The Makhachkala Commercial Seaport is Russia’s only ice-free, deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It is used for the shipment of oil, petroleum products, grain, containers, and other cargo moving between Russia, Iran, and countries in Central Asia and the South Caucasus. From January through August 2026, it handled a record 2.9 million metric tons of cargo, according to its own data, up 42.5% from a year earlier. More than 2 million metric tons of that volume was oil.
In addition to the strikes on Makhachkala, the Russian Black Sea city of Sochi was attacked by maritime drones on the evening of Sept. 9. Supernova+ published a full video of one part of the attack, while another clip captured a strike on a pier. Footage posted on social media also appeared to show a cafe building burning near a beach.
Twenty-eight people were injured in the attack, including two children.
Beach infrastructure and a nearby section of the Primorskaya Embankment were damaged. A concert by Russian singer Tatyana Bulanova at the Festivalny concert hall was also interrupted due to the threat of an attack, and performers and audience members were sent to shelter.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that it had intercepted more than 440 fixed-wing drones in the south of the country and over the Black Sea.
New data also emerged about the consequences of yesterday’s Ukrainian drone attack on gas infrastructure in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District, located more than 2,000 kilometers from the border between the two countries.
The open-source intelligence channel Falcon Insight noted that NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) detected several thermal anomalies at the Urengoyskaya compressor station near the Novy Urengoy Condensate Preparation Plant, which was attacked on Sept. 9.
Falcon Insight said such heat signatures are not typical for the compressor station.
The station supports several major gas pipelines, including the Urengoy-Center and Urengoy-Novopskov systems, which transport gas from the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District to other parts of Russia. There had been no previous reports of an attack on the compressor station, and there is still no separate confirmation that the facility was damaged. Satellite monitoring data only shows sources of intense heat and cannot by itself establish what caused them.
Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces claimed responsibility for strikes on two other facilities in the region: the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate processing plants. The Novy Urengoy plant has a design capacity of 19.5 million metric tons of feedstock a year, while the Purovsky plant processed 13.4 million metric tons in 2025. Ukraine’s military did not list the Urengoyskaya compressor station among the targets it said had been hit.

articles.title: Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran attack on base in Jordan damaged American military aircraft, US official says
Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft this week on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, a U.S. official told Reuters.
The U.S. military, the highest-funded in the world, suffered material damage even before Iran's strikes on Tuesday. This includes the destruction of more than two dozen drones, Iran striking fighter jets, and aircraft being lost to accidents.
According to a May report from the Congressional Research Service, 42 U.S. military aircraft had already been lost or damaged in the conflict.
Since the Iran war started in February, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and over 800 injured.
A U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Iran's attack hit one A-10 Thunderbolt II, known as the Warthog, leaving it with a missing wing, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and were returned to service.
Iran's strike on the U.S. base in Jordan came after U.S. forces said they destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers. The U.S. said its strikes were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the previous two days.
The Iranian attack required U.S. forces to fire roughly 30 Patriot interceptors to counter the missiles, the U.S. official said, amid increasing concern about the inventory of U.S. air defence interceptors and other missiles.
While specific inventory numbers are classified, the Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that about 65% of U.S. Patriot interceptors were expended between February and July, with fewer than 850 left on hand, down from 2,330 before the Iran war began.

articles.title: EU lawmakers renew push to seize frozen Russian assets as Ukraine faces its toughest winter yet with a €23 billion defense funding gap
articles.body:
More than 100 European Parliament members are urging EU leaders to revive plans to use frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine, as Kyiv faces a €23 billion shortfall in defense funding, Euronews reports.
Russia is expanding its attacks across Ukraine, with growing numbers of missiles and drones striking cities and critical infrastructure far from the front line. Kyiv expects the coming winter to be the most difficult period of the full-scale war yet, increasing the need for reliable funding to sustain air defenses, energy repairs, and the military.
A letter signed by 122 MEPs from across the political spectrum calls for a new proposal to overcome legal and financial concerns that have stalled the use of the assets. Euronews reported on the letter on 10 September.
The EU holds more than €200 billion in Russian central bank assets, most of them in Belgium. The European Commission previously proposed using the assets to back a zero-interest loan for Ukraine, but EU governments failed to reach an agreement over the legal risks, particularly concerns raised by Belgium.
Ukraine faces a major funding gap
The renewed push comes as Ukraine prepares for another year of war while its defense spending needs continue to grow.
According to the MEPs cited by Euronews, Ukraine has identified a €23 billion gap in defense funding. Kyiv needs sustained financing for weapons, ammunition, air defense, drones, and other military needs as Russia continues its war and expands the scale of its attacks.
The EU has already approved a €90 billion support loan for Ukraine, but lawmakers argue that this will not cover the country’s needs. The estimated cost of damage caused by Russia’s invasion has already surpassed €600 billion, according to the letter.
For Ukraine, securing predictable long-term funding is particularly important as it cannot rely indefinitely on individual EU governments finding additional money in their national budgets.
MEPs seek a way around legal concerns
The proposal is backed by lawmakers from the European People’s Party, Renew Europe, Socialists and Democrats, Greens/EFA, European Conservatives and Reformists, and The Left.
They are calling on the European Commission to create a new mechanism that could take on the legal obligations linked to Russia’s central bank assets. This could allow the funds to be used to support Ukraine without directly transferring the frozen assets to Kyiv.
Belgium has been the main obstacle to the previous proposal because the assets are largely held by Euroclear, a Brussels-based financial institution. The Belgian government is afraid that Russia could pursue legal action against Belgium if Moscow’s assets are used.
Belgium blocks EU’s last-ditch push to unlock €210B of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine
The MEPs argue that Russia should ultimately bear the financial cost of the destruction caused by its invasion.
“Russia should bear the financial consequences of its war of aggression,” the letter says.

articles.title: Ukraine almost ran out of F-16 missiles — Zelensky’s former spokeswoman
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 10. /TASS/. The armed forces of Ukraine have almost run out of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles for F-16 fighter jets, Vladimir Zelensky’s former press secretary Yulia Mendel said.
"In Ukraine, the missiles F-16s use <…> are almost gone. AIM-120s and AIM-9s are running out. Patriot batteries are also critically short of PAC-3 interceptors needed to stop ballistic missiles," she wrote on the X social network.
"І keep coming back to the same thought: without a move toward peace, there is just no way to stop the destruction and keep people alive," Mendel added.

articles.title: Zaluzhny: lack of technology, funding prevents Ukraine from seizing initiative from Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience, but state funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited, which is why private investment can and must become a mutually beneficial solution for both sides, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny notes.
"Ukrainian companies are capable of promptly responding to battlefield needs and developing new types of weaponry based on real combat experience. No other country can offer more relevant experience for developing new arms, modernization, and tactics for their application. However, the lack of technology and funding prevents seizing the initiative from Russia and its partners," Zaluzhnyi said during a speech at the Defence & Resilience Tech Scale Up Showcase in London, the text of which was published in his column on the Interfax-Ukraine agency's website on Thursday.
He called on Ukraine's partners to increase financial and technological investments in arms production in Ukraine, not only to reduce Russia's military potential, but also to strengthen their own defense capabilities.
"State funding for defense innovation in Ukraine is limited. Therefore, private investments can and must become a beneficial solution for both sides. Creating clear mechanisms for cooperation with Great Britain at the institutional level will help attract private capital, technologies, and ultimately create new markets and develop long-term cooperation between the defense industries of Ukraine and its partners," the diplomat said.
Zaluzhnyi stated that Ukraine has gained significant experience in drone production, but the component base, and especially its production, currently remains outside Ukraine, which precludes possibilities for scaling and modernization in the long term, "where marketing gives way to strategy and the outline of victory finally becomes visible." "Even now, these investments are vital in countering urgent threats such as ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones," the former Commander-in-Chief emphasized.
He noted that achieving victory or a dignified peace requires systemic impact on Russia's ability to continue the war, rather than isolated technological solutions.
"Systemic impact means implementing strategies to achieve the main goal: victory over the enemy. Naturally, building such a systemic impact is possible only with appropriate strategies. These strategies must be based on implementing financial and technological policies that enable producing today what is needed tomorrow, or better yet, the day after tomorrow. And what is needed today should be taken from storage facilities as something produced yesterday. Defense production must be part of a war strategy, not the other way around, where war is made to justify someone's promises and profits. Only in this way is it possible to seize the initiative, impose one's will on the enemy, and demand terms from them," Zaluzhny concluded.

articles.title: Defense Forces destroy 128 Russian UAVs – Air Force
articles.body:
On the night of September 10, Russian occupiers attacked the territory of Ukraine with 149 strike UAVs of the Shahed, Herbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drone types, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces shot down/suppressed 128 Russian UAVs of the Shahed, Herbera, and other types," the report on the Telegram channel says.
In addition, hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, and falling debris from shot-down drones was recorded at nine locations.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The attack is ongoing, with enemy UAVs remaining in the airspace.

articles.title: This Is What Ukraine’s Novorossiysk Strike Did to Russia’s Kalibr Fleet
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
This Is What Ukraine’s Novorossiysk Strike Did to Russia’s Kalibr Fleet
Satellite imagery and new visual evidence are revealing the aftermath of Ukraine’s September 9 strike on Novorossiysk, with at least three Russian Black Sea Fleet vessels now confirmed hit and additional missile-carrying warships appearing to have sustained damage.
Ukraine has confirmed that at least three Russian Black Sea Fleet vessels were hit during the September 9 missile-and-drone strike on Novorossiysk, with new imagery providing a clearer picture of the damage inflicted inside one of Russia’s most important naval hubs.
Ukraine’s General Staff said on September 10 that additional analysis confirmed strikes on the minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the missile frigate Admiral Essen and the Project 11711 large landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The updated assessment significantly expands the confirmed results of the overnight operation, which targeted both military and port infrastructure in Novorossiysk.
Fuel-oil storage facilities at the port were also confirmed hit.
The most striking evidence, however, comes from imagery showing the vessels after the attack, published by the OSINT community Exilenova+.
Visual analysis indicates that Admiral Essen, a Russian missile-carrying frigate capable of launching Kalibr cruise missiles, was struck in its superstructure. A fire subsequently broke out on the ship, an effect also reported by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence.
Separate imagery also appears to show another strike on the superstructure of the missile frigate Admiral Makarov. The full extent of damage to that vessel is still being assessed.
A Buyan-M-class small missile ship was also identified among the vessels apparently hit during the operation. Ships of this class are used by Russia as platforms for long-range cruise missiles and have participated in strikes against Ukraine.
One Buyan-M vessel linked to the latest visual evidence had reportedly taken part in a recent Russian missile strike on Kyiv before subsequently coming under Ukrainian attack in Novorossiysk, Exilenova+ noted.
The September 9 operation combined missiles and drones against the port, where Russia has concentrated significant elements of its Black Sea Fleet after Ukrainian strikes made operations from occupied Crimea increasingly dangerous.
Novorossiysk has consequently become particularly important for Moscow as both a naval base and a logistical hub.
Damage assessments remain underway, and Ukrainian authorities have not yet disclosed the full results of every strike recorded during the operation.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian high-speed Mangust patrol boat in temporarily occupied Crimea, along with drone facilities, reconnaissance systems, and ammunition depots across several temporarily occupied regions.

articles.title: Houthis seize strategic Red Sea port near key shipping route – media
articles.body:
Houthis claim control of strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait (VIDEOS)
Yemen’s Houthis have seized the crucial Red Sea city of al-Makha (Mocha), tightening their grip on the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the organisation’s spokesperson told RT on Thursday.
The Houthis pushed Saudi-backed government forces out of Mocha after several days of fierce fighting, reportedly capturing both the city and its port. Videos circulated by OSINT accounts online appear to show Houthi forces entering the strategic port city as the group continues its advance toward full control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The organisation’s spokesperson, Mohammed Al-Bukhaiti, told RT that while it is fighting directly against Saudi forces, it is prepared for a potential expansion of the conflict if any other country “becomes embroiled in the aggression against Yemen.”
“Of course, we now control Bab al-Mandeb, but the goal of our battle remains liberating Yemen and restoring its sovereignty and independence by ending the Saudi aggression and ending the blockade that has caused great suffering to Yemen,” Al-Bukhaiti said.
The Houthis are committed to protecting the freedom of maritime navigation in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, and “do not target any country except the Saudi enemy,” the spokesman added.
Houthi forces captured the key coastal city of Mokha overnight after Saudi/UAE backed forces retreated.
Seen here, Houthi fighters pose with an abandoned M-ATV MRAP at the city’s critical seaport. pic.twitter.com/1WD6l08MVc
“This is one of the most important objectives of our military operations, because the one infringing upon maritime navigation is Saudi Arabia and its allies, as they prevent commercial vessels from travelling to and from Yemen,” he said.
Houthi convoys have reportedly entered the city of Mokha. https://t.co/nKrIOyt0Zypic.twitter.com/wFjvGPzg3H
— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) September 10, 2026
The Houthis have also reportedly landed forces on the strategic Hanish islands after pushing government troops further south. An unnamed military source told Reuters the group seized Zuqar Island after rocket attacks and an amphibious assault. Control of the area would further strengthen the Houthis’ position, potentially cutting government supply routes and depriving Saudi-backed forces of a key logistics hub, sources said.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government has not confirmed Mocha’s capture. However, Lt. Gen. Tareq Saleh, whose forces controlled the city, said earlier Thursday he had ordered them to “reorganize their ranks and establish an alternative command center in a secure location.”
The reported advance marks a sharp escalation after roughly four years of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce in 2022. The Houthis had previously fought Yemen’s internationally recognized government since seizing Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene.
Tensions flared again in July after, according to Yemen’s internationally recognized government, its forces struck Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, declared the de-escalation phase over and subsequently announced a naval blockade of the kingdom. By mid-August, the group was launching coordinated missile and drone strikes on camps belonging to Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which in turn launched counteroffensives across several provinces.
The fighting sharply escalated earlier this week. On Tuesday, the Houthis targeted energy and other infrastructure in Saudi Arabia’s south, including facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco, the country’s largest oil producer. The Houthis called the operation retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen, claiming Riyadh had carried out 121 airstrikes over the previous three days. Saudi aircraft carried out another 40 strikes across four Yemeni provinces on Thursday, according to the Houthi-run Saba news agency.
What is the significance of the Houthis’ advance?
The battle for Yemen’s Red Sea coast has implications far beyond the country. Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean and carries roughly 10% of global seaborne trade. Its importance to energy markets has surged since the US-Israeli war on Iran erupted on February 28 and the Strait of Hormuz came under a de facto blockade, forcing Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, to rely more heavily on Red Sea exports.
Saudi Aramco has increasingly diverted crude through its cross-country pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Loadings have averaged more than 4 million barrels per day since June, more than four times last year’s level. Saudi crude shipments through Bab al-Mandeb between March and mid-July were eight times higher than in the same period of 2025, making disruption to the strait a growing threat to the kingdom’s oil exports.
The Houthis have disrupted the waterway before, repeatedly attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023 in what they said was support for Palestinians during Israel’s war in Gaza.
Despite the renewed hostilities, Riyadh says diplomacy remains possible. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud earlier this week accused the Houthis of prioritizing “their narrow interests” over the interests of Yemen, but insisted that “the road to diplomacy is not closed.”

articles.title: Iran Damages US A-10, F-15s with Missile Attack on Air Base in Jordan
articles.body:
A U.S. Air Force A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft flies in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Aug. 30, 2026. U.S. Air Force photo by Tech. Sgt. Tiffany A. Emery
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
An Iranian ballistic missile attack on a key U.S. air base in Jordan damaged multiple U.S. warplanes, people familiar with the matter confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
One A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft suffered a severely damaged wing and about eight F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were lightly damaged but are considered serviceable after Iran attacked Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on Sept. 8 Eastern Time.
The damage to U.S. aircraft was first reported by CBS News.
A spokesman for U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The attack on the base, known as MSAB, came after the U.S. struck five Iranian tankers Sept. 8, and Iran retaliated by lobbing scores of ballistic missiles at the installation. U.S. and Jordanian forces launched dozens of interceptors at the Iranian missiles. U.S. officials said no American personnel were killed. But Iran was able to harm American materiel. In the hours after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it damaged U.S. aircraft at the base.
The U.S. has dozens of warplanes operating from the base, which acts as a key airpower hub for operations against Iran. Tehran has targeted the facility, near the Jordanian town of Azraq, numerous times since the conflict began in February. Three Army Soldiers were killed in a missile attack on the base in July.
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
One year into a new campaign to boost readiness rates for the B-1B Lancer and B-52H Stratofortress bombers, Air Force Global Strike Command is claiming some early wins and planning to forge ahead with more improvements.
Over the past few months and peaking in August, crews with the 910th Airlift Wing out of Youngstown Air Reserve Station, Ohio, have been running nighttime, low-flying missions to kill a ubiquitous and deadly adversary that’s plagued Americans for centuries—mosquitoes.
General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft.
In the small world of Air Force weather specialists, combat weather specialists are a niche unto themselves, deploying with Army ground units to provide forecasts and, if need be, fight alongside those Soldiers. For Staff Sgt. Francisco Estrada, the hardest part of the job isn’t the possibility of ground combat,…
Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force.
In a dramatic flare-up in the hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan.
After months of delays, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to…
The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.

articles.title: At least three killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine while Zelenskyy is in Canada for talks
articles.body:
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said they had carried out their deepest strike inside Russia, with drones travelling 3,000 km to target two gas condensate plants, the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky plants, located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, one of Russia's key oil and gas regions.
As Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives in Canada for talks with leader Mark Carney, Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange fire.
At least three people were killed in Russian overnight attacks. Ukraine's Armed Forces reported that Moscow attacked Ukraine with 149 drones overnight from Wednesday into Thursday, 128 of which were intercepted. The statement added that they had been launched from Russian cities including Kursk, Millerovo and from the temporarily occupied region of Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea, striking 13 locations.
A late Russian attack on a shopping center car park in Sumy killed at least three people and injured 14 including a teenager, on Wednesday, Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Sumy Oblast Military Administration said on Telegram.
Attacks on the eastern city of Kharkiv have left at least two people injured, after a residential buildings were damaged by drones, according to the city's mayor Ihor Terekhov.
Another large scale attack hitting residential building in the central city of Kryvyi Rih left two people in critical condition, its Head of Kryvyi Rih Defence Council, Oleksandr Vilkul said on Telegram.
Four firefighters have been hospitalised after responding to a blaze on a market in the Western city of Khmelnytskyi, sparked by fallen debris from a Russian drone attack. The firefighters were injured in a secondary explosion, officials reported.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said that they had managed their deepest strike inside Russia, as their drones travelled 3,000 km to strike two gas condensate plants, the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky, located in one of Russia's key oil and gas regions; the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region.
Ukrainian media reported that Russian Telegram media channels had said Ukraine launched a drone attack on the Republic of Dagestan.
The southern coastal city of Sochi also reportedly came under attack by Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels sparking multiple fires, according to Russian authorities. Russian media said residents also reported explosions on the port Caspian sea city of Makhachkala, it is known for its handling of dry and liquid cargo, residents also reported a lack of air raid warnings.
Zelenskyy travels to Canada
As Russia and Ukraine trade fire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy travelled to Canada on Wednesday to hold talks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney as he hopes to build a closer relationship with his allies.
According to a statement by Carney, Zelenskyy's visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic, and energy cooperation."
Carney added:"It will also address the human cost of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries," and that Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defence, recovery, and reconstruction."
Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are scheduled to stay in Canada until Friday, with events in Calgary, Toronto and North Bay on the agenda, as well as a meeting with Cabinet members in Banff, Alberta.
