articles.title: Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm elections, threatens to attack Pickaxe Mountain
articles.body:
Trump says Iran war to end after US midterm vote, Houthis close in on key Strait, sources say
CAIRO/WASHINGTON/DUBAI, Sept 10 - President Donald Trump said he expected the war with Iran to end after the November U.S. midterm elections and threatened again to attack a site associated with the Islamic Republic's nuclear programme after the two sides launched their biggest wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the six-month-old war.
Tensions in the region were high, with Saudi civil defence authorities on Thursday issuing emergency alerts in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours, as clashes flared with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
The Houthis were edging closer on Thursday to gaining more leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world's most important routes for shipping, four Yemeni government military sources said.
Brent crude prices hovered above $100 a barrel as supply routes through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted.
Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the waterway on Wednesday after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, the latest in a series of tit-for-tat strikes that have signalled scant chance of an imminent end to hostilities.
DEADLINES TO END WAR
The war and subsequent increase in fuel prices have helped drive Trump's popularity to record lows. The president said Tehran was trying to influence the November U.S. midterm elections, which will determine whether his Republican Party retains control of Congress.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
Trump has previously set deadlines for the war to end.
The Wall Street Journal reported later that top White House advisers, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have privately warned Trump that the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency, which ends in January 2029. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Trump also said the U.S. may hit Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes near Iran's damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility.
"We notice there's a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard," Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention. Trump has been threatening strikes on Pickaxe Mountain since at least mid-July.
The U.S. and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February partly due to concerns over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Iran says its nuclear activities are for peaceful purposes.
In recent weeks Washington had cited increasing success guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global oil supplies before the war. But a resumption of fighting this month appears to have set back any such gradual reopening. Just seven vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, half the 10-day average, preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Thursday.
RED SEA CLASHES
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen has also escalated in the past few days, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.
Houthi militants have taken control of the Yemeni Red Sea city of Mocha and are launching attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish, the Yemeni sources told Reuters on Thursday.
Government forces and their allies are relocating south to Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait, across from the island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said.
Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most populous areas and much of the north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal or the SUMED pipeline on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
Blocking the narrow passage would isolate Gulf oil-producing countries such as energy superpower Saudi Arabia from their main shipping routes after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — the primary maritime energy artery between Asia and Europe.
Earlier this week, at least 73 people were wounded in four southern Saudi cities, including Khamis Mushait, in recent Houthi strikes on the world's largest oil exporter.
The militant group said it attacked an air base in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Saudi civil defence authorities issued an all-clear on Thursday following another emergency alert declared in Khamis Mushait. REUTERS

articles.title: Two Azerbaijani citizens killed in drone attack on vessel in Black Sea as Russia’s MoD reports striking tug boat escorting ships to Odesa
articles.body:
Two Azerbaijani citizens were killed and two others suffered burns in a drone strike on the tug boat TEDY near the port of Odesa in southern Ukraine on Sept. 9. Russia’s Defense Ministry said the same day that its forces had struck a tug escorting ships into the Odesa port. The ministry did not identify the vessel, but the ship type, location, and timing match reports of the attack on TEDY.
The attack was first reported by the public association Support for Azerbaijani Sailors, which said drones had attacked TEDY in the Black Sea near Odesa on the morning of Sept. 9. After the first strike, the damaged vessel headed toward the Romanian port of Constanța, but it came under attack twice more during the night.
There were 10 people aboard: four Azerbaijani citizens, three Turkish citizens, two Germans, and one Ukrainian. Azerbaijani sailors Aslan Aliyev and Asim Gasimov were killed. Two other Azerbaijani citizens, Imran Novruzov and Rauf Aliyev, suffered burns and were taken to a hospital in Chornomorsk.
Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry later confirmed the deaths and injuries. The ministry said it was in contact with Ukrainian authorities and diplomatic missions to assist the injured and arrange for the return of the bodies of those killed. It also advised Azerbaijani citizens to avoid working aboard vessels whose routes pass through areas of active fighting.
On the evening of Sept. 9, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Russian forces had carried out coordinated strikes on Ukrainian seaports and vessels. Among the targets, it listed a tug that had been escorting dry cargo ships into the port of Odesa. The Russian military did not name the vessel or report any crew deaths. There is no direct confirmation so far that the ministry’s statement referred to TEDY.
TEDY (IMO 9059200) is a roughly 30-meter tug and supply vessel built in 1995 and registered under the Somali flag. The Insider reviewed data provided by the vessel tracking platform Starboard Maritime Intelligence. On Sept. 7 at 12:58 p.m. UTC, TEDY departed the Romanian port of Midia and headed northeast toward Odesa at a speed of 14 to 15 kilometers per hour. At 4:41 p.m., the ship stopped transmitting its tracking signal for nearly a day.
Then, on Sept. 8 at 4:03 p.m., it reappeared in the tracking system about 40 kilometers southwest of Snake Island (Zmiinyi Island) and had effectively stopped. TEDY transmitted its last signal from that location at 4:24 p.m.
The group Support for Azerbaijani Sailors identified the Turkish company Mert Marine Corporation as TEDY’s owner. Data reviewed by The Insider supports that claim. TEDY’s vessel record lists Mert Marine as both the owner and operator of the tug. The same information appears in all available Automatic Identification System (AIS) records from June through September 2026.
Ships with foreign crews operating in the Black and Azov seas have repeatedly been targeted by Russian and Ukrainian drones in recent months. In June, drones attacked the vessels Natra and Circon in Taganrog Bay. According to updated figures from Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry, four Azerbaijani sailors were killed and four others were injured. One Azerbaijani citizen initially listed among the dead was later identified as a Russian national. Ukraine’s military effectively confirmed the strikes, saying the vessels had been used to transport stolen grain, military cargo, and fuel. An analysis of their routes by The Insider found that both ships had sailed between the Russian ports of Kavkaz and Rostov-on-Don.
On July 14, Russian drones attacked two merchant ships near Odesa. On the dry cargo vessel Atlas Bey, which was sailing from Chornomorsk to Turkey with a cargo of meal, the captain, an Azerbaijani citizen, and another crew member were killed. Three people were injured.
Several more foreign vessels were hit between July 17 and 19. One sailor was killed and three were injured in an attack on the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged dry cargo ship Venturo. A strike on the Guinea-Bissau-flagged dry cargo ship Golden Leo, which was carrying corn, killed 10 people — nine crew members and a Ukrainian pilot. The vessel later sank. Four Indian citizens were among those killed, prompting New Delhi to summon Russia’s chargé d’affaires.
Ukraine has also attacked vessels linked to Russian ports. Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said that as of Aug. 8, a total of 218 vessels had been struck in an operation launched in July. That figure has not been independently verified. The Insider found that not all of the vessels attacked were under Ukrainian sanctions, and one was sailing under the Turkish flag.
After attacks on the Yasar and Nadezhda, which had departed Novorossiysk, Turkey’s Foreign Ministry warned that strikes on commercial shipping risked triggering uncontrolled escalation in the Black Sea.

articles.title: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels seize strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha
Yemen’s Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday as their offensive against Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Saudi Arabia launched dozens of airstrikes over the past 24 hours, the Houthis said, after the Iran-backed group carried out attacks on Saudi territory that wounded dozens of people.
Yemen's Houthis seized control of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday, with witnesses telling AFP of fighters marching on the area chanting "death to America, death to Israel".
Saudi Arabia meanwhile launched dozens of airstrikes in the last 24 hours, according to the military spokesman for the Houthis, who control large parts of northwest Yemen and launched a large-scale offensive last week against Riyadh-backed Yemeni government forces.
The Houthis launched attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens of people wounded, in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
A Yemeni military source told AFP on Thursday that the Iran-backed Houthis were advancing towards the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait "after having taken control of Mocha".
The waterway, which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal, has gained importance as a transit route since the start of the wider Middle East war, which saw Iran blockade the Strait of Hormuz.
The regional war has disrupted maritime traffic in the Gulf, causing oil prices to soar.
On Thursday, the US oil contract WTI surpassed $100, after Brent North Sea crude -- the main international benchmark -- already did so on Wednesday.
After Mocha's capture, the leader of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, said the protection of the country's coasts and restoring state control of them was an "Arab and international interest".
The military source said the Houthis also seized Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea, "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters".
In a statement, Tarek Saleh, who heads the Yemeni National Resistance Forces that controlled Mocha, said he moved his command centre "to a safe location" to regroup.
Government forces have paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran", he added.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'Maritime coercion'
Before the offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north, including the capital Sanaa, as well as the major port city of Hodeidah on the Red Sea.
But they did not yet hold any areas directly overlooking Bab al-Mandab.
With their drones and missiles, the Houthis have been able to disrupt traffic in the Red Sea.
But "controlling the coast would strengthen Houthi maritime coercion", said Andreas Krieg, a security expert at King's College London.
The advance of the Houthis in Mocha, as well as in the nearby areas of Khokha and Hays, has driven many people to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the port city.
Mujahid Tahami, who also set off for Aden, said some families had fallen victim to "looting by gangs as they tried to flee".

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Hundreds dead
Yemen relapsed into war in July after years of relative calm punctured by sporadic violence and deepening poverty.
Since last week, the fighting in Yemen has left more than 500 dead, mostly combatants, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
It has also forced nearly 20,000 people to flee their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition battling the Houthis said the group fired ballistic missiles and drones at several cities in southern Saudi Arabia.
On Thursday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi Arabia had launched 64 strikes on Yemenover the previous 24 hours.
Their Al-Masirah TV channel reported 10 strikes on Taiz province in western Yemen.
The United Nations Security Council met Thursday to discuss the conflict with its Yemen envoy, Hans Grundberg, who called for "the active investment of every member of this body to contain what could be the precipice for a far more dangerous conflict".
The emergency meeting was brought together by the United Kingdom, which called on the Security Council to "send a clear and consistent message: the Houthis must de-escalate, cease their attacks, and return to a path towards peace".
The hostilities kicked off in July when the Houthis let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
The government retaliated by striking Sanaa airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital and forcing out the government, fought the Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: IAEA exposes North Korea's secret nuclear enrichment facility, expansion of weapon infrastructure
articles.body:
North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report that the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea's nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations.
In the report, dated August 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang's nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009.
It identified a new two-story building at Yongbyon as the site's second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building's construction.
Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs.
Expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material
The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024.
The IAEA said the developments in North Korea's nuclear program violated UN Security Council resolutions.
"The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern," IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
The report accompanied Grossi's statement.
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency's authority. North Korea's mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had "no legal right… to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT," referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

articles.title: Iran arms, advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranian arms and advice helped Yemen's Houthis seize key Red Sea city, sources say
The lightning Houthi advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran's Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Iran's war with the U.S., according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources.
By seizing the southwestern port city of Mocha, the Houthis have strengthened their chokehold on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway whose disruption further constricts global energy supplies after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Six months into the wider regional conflict between the Houthis' Iranian allies and the United States, the group now looks focused on consolidating that grip on the strait even as opposing government forces backed by Saudi Arabia focus on an offensive in the north.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a close U.S. ally, and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy".
Several senior Revolutionary Guards commanders had already travelled to Yemen to oversee and command Houthi attacks directed against Saudi Arabia after weeks of discussions over military strategy, a regional diplomat briefed by Tehran said.
A third Iranian source, an official, said Iran had held several meetings with allies including the Houthis and that the move on Mocha was a Houthi rather than Iranian decision. However, it had helped Iran by putting upward pressure on oil prices and hurting the United States and Saudi Arabia, the official added.
Inside Yemen, five military sources from the Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government said the Revolutionary Guards had directed the new Houthi campaign along the Red Sea coast, a flat, narrow plain known as the Tihama, starting with a blitz of rocket fire.
Citing communications intercepts and the accounts of captured Houthi prisoners, the Yemeni military sources said they believed the Iranian effort was being directed by Abdolreza Shahlaei, a top Revolutionary Guards commander.
Iranian sources were not immediately able to confirm that, though they had previously described Shahlaei, who is in the Guards' specialist Quds Force unit, as having spent time in Yemen in recent years.
The Guards were still able to move weapons and personnel in and out of Yemen despite an aerial and maritime blockade of Houthi areas, the Iranian sources said without elaborating on how they did so.
"If we look at their offensive on the west coast, it's not something prepared just last week or last month," said Ahmed Nagi, Yemen analyst at International Crisis Group, describing the seizure of Mocha as a significant milestone in the war.
"The evolution of the Houthis was basically because of the new weapons they gained, either through the Iranians directly or through the different smuggling networks that they are counting on," Nagi said, pointing specifically at their use of drones in the latest offensive.
As the Houthis began an advance towards Mocha last week, Yemen's government requested more air support and other help from the Saudis, two more Yemeni officials said.
It was seeking a Saudi air campaign against Houthi targets in the Houthi heartland including Sanaa and key strategic assets such as oil depots, they said.
However, the kingdom stuck to providing logistical, armament and intelligence support with only limited air strikes that were focused on northern battlefronts in Jawf and Marib provinces, areas the government regarded as less important.
The officials' own assessment was that Riyadh was anxious to avoid a major escalation with the Houthis for fear of provoking heavier drone strikes on Saudi territory.
Saudi officials did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Riyadh's military focus on the northern front rather than the Red Sea coast and other big Houthi targets.
The overall military situation in Yemen is hard to gauge after a years-long pause in major warfare since a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. Both Iran and Saudi Arabia have invested in forces they back there. But the pro-government coalition has suffered from internal splits.
Although previous rounds of warfare in the Tihama had produced sudden advances and retreats, it remains unclear if Saudi-backed forces can easily dislodge the Houthis this time, Nagi said.
"Maybe we can see some advances from the government if they get the necessary support from the Saudis. But that could be a bit difficult this time," he said.

articles.title: Government again commits not to extend Dreadnought sub life
articles.body:
The Government has confirmed that it has accepted a Strategic Defence Review recommendation not to extend the service lives of the Royal Navy’s Dreadnought-class ballistic missile submarines beyond their intended end-of-service dates from the mid-2050s.
The position was confirmed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked whether ministers had committed to Recommendation 34 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard replied: “The Government accepted this 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommendation and is in the process of implementing it.”
Recommendation 34 explicitly calls on the Government to avoid repeating the costs associated with extending ageing submarine fleets and to begin planning for the system that will eventually replace Dreadnought.
The Strategic Defence Review stated: “To avoid the costs of the past, the Government must commit to not extending the life of the Dreadnought class submarines beyond their intended end-of-service dates from the mid-2050s. It should start to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought nuclear deterrent within this Parliament.”
The Government has also confirmed separately that work to define Dreadnought’s eventual successor is beginning as part of wider investment in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise.
In a written answer in July, Obese-Jecty asked what plans the MOD had to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought strategic deterrent.
Pollard said: “As announced in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government will invest over £20 billion more in the Defence Nuclear Enterprise over the next four years than the previous four years to modernise and sustain our nuclear deterrent, the cornerstone of our national security.”
He added: “This will fund our new deterrent submarines and warheads, establish a nuclear fuels programme, start defining the Dreadnought successor, and upgrade our infrastructure across the defence nuclear estate.”
Pollard said this would allow the Government to meet its commitment to begin defining the future system during the current Parliament, stating: “This will allow us to meet the Government’s commitment to start to define the requirement for the post-Dreadnought strategic deterrent within this Parliament.”
The Dreadnought class is being built to replace the Royal Navy’s existing Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines and will carry the UK’s strategic nuclear deterrent through much of the middle of the century.
The Strategic Defence Review recommendation is intended to avoid the additional cost and complexity that can arise when major platforms remain in service significantly beyond their originally planned lives. Rather than relying on a later life-extension programme for Dreadnought, the review calls for work on its eventual successor to begin decades in advance, with the requirement-definition process now being funded through the wider Defence Nuclear Enterprise programme.

articles.title: Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
Iran's capture of a US military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril.
The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter.
After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design.
More recently, the U.S. military moved swiftly to prevent Iranian forces from taking possession of uncrewed maritime technology. In 2022, a US Navy patrol ship and MH-60S Seahawk helicopter were deployed after an Iranian naval vessel attempted to tow away a Saildrone surface vessel in the Gulf, according to the Navy.
Analysts say Iran is unlikely to gain a decisive military advantage from the captured drone, but the episode nonetheless represents a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington's efforts to project technological superiority.
Iranian embassies mock US
Iranian embassies around the world have mocked the US for losing its drone. Iran's embassy in Ghana, in a post on X, boasted about picking the submersible up in "a strait controlled by people who can hear a shrimp sneeze," adding that, "Our guys picked it up like a plastic bottle in a fishing net. Fully intact. Still blinking like an idiot. Condolences to whoever was holding the joystick."
US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins of US Central Command said the "defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment." Anduril did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"Of course Iran will take every opportunity as a propaganda win," said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. "It can help the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) make better versions of their own designs."
Iran will almost certainly try to pry open the drone's hardware, but the drone's software carries built-in defenses, said Bryan Clark, a senior fellow and director of the Center for Defense Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute. Iranian engineers "could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems," he said, pointing to Tehran's track record with captured American aircraft.
"Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!" Iran's embassy in Hyderabad wrote on X.
The incident has also highlighted a disconnect between the messaging of Anduril and its customer, the US Navy.
Navy officials said the Dive-LD was an older-model vehicle that suffered a malfunction and was recovered by Iranian forces after being left "dead in the water."
Anduril has promoted the Dive-LD as "the most reliable and flexible" large autonomous underwater vehicle available, saying it is capable of operating for up to 10 days in demanding conditions. In addition to its use by the US Navy, the Dive-LD was the testbed vehicle for the development of Australia's new Ghost Shark large underwater drone.
"This is something that Iran has proven very adept at exploiting for its own benefit in terms of seeking to frame the narrative as one of US, in this case, ineptitude and their ability to sort of retain control over the Strait of Hormuz," said Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred drones: there were strikes at 13 locations
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred drones: there were strikes at 13 locations
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian Federation launched attack drones from the territory of the Russian Federation and the occupied Crimea and Donetsk regions. Air defense shot down or suppressed 128 UAVs; strikes were recorded at 13 locations.
During the night of September 10, the Russians attacked Ukraine with Shahed-type attack UAVs (half of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, as well as decoy drones of the "Parody" type. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
The enemy launched drones from the Russian cities of Millerovo, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk, as well as from the occupied Crimea and Donetsk.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Air defenses shot down/suppressed 128 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types.
Hits by the enemy's air attack weapons were recorded at 13 locations, as well as the falling of downed drones (debris) at 9 locations.

articles.title: Ukraine and Canada agree on 100-year partnership: declaration signed
articles.body:
Ukraine and Canada agree on 100-year partnership: declaration signed
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have signed a declaration on a 100-year partnership, which envisages the two countries' intention to raise bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership in various spheres, including defence and assistance to Ukraine's armed forces.
Source: European Pravda, with reference to the statement
Details: In the statement, the leaders condemned Russia's war in Ukraine and paid tribute to the courage of the Ukrainian people and their defenders.
Both leaders stressed the importance of continuing reforms in Ukraine on the path to full membership of the European Union and NATO.
"Canada remains a committed partner in supporting these efforts," the statement emphasised.
The statement stressed that Canada will continue to "meet Ukraine's most urgent military needs and support Operation UNIFIER, which has been extended until 2029".
Canada will also continue to strengthen the Armed Forces of Ukraine, paying particular attention to the "urgent need for air defence systems and interceptors, and will provide training, military equipment, ammunition and other critically important military support".
"Both countries will deepen cooperation in the areas of intelligence, cyber defence, counter-drone and electronic jamming systems, as well as in countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation. Canada will continue to work with partners to establish a system of politically and legally binding security guarantees to prevent any future aggression by the Russian Federation," the statement stressed.
The statement also notes that Canada and Ukraine will establish a long-term defence industry partnership for the joint production of unmanned systems, counter-drone and electronic jamming systems, as well as ammunition.
In addition, the countries will expand trade and investment under the modernised Free Trade Agreement, promote the development of public-private partnerships and mobilise capital and de-risking solutions needed to support Ukraine's recovery and reconstruction.
Separately, Canada and Ukraine agreed to deepen cooperation in the areas of energy security and critical minerals, industry and sustainable forest resource management, and will strengthen ties between innovators and researchers in the fields of AI, cybersecurity, space, biotechnology and digital governance.
The countries will also cooperate to ensure reliable and safe navigation in the Black Sea, as well as to further disrupt the activities of and deter Russia's shadow fleet.
In addition, Canada has pledged to maintain and strengthen economic pressure on Russia.
Background:
- Zelenskyy is on a three-day visit to Canada together with First Lady Olena Zelenska.
- On the same day, Zelenskyy stated that Canada had prepared a new aid package with air defence systems for Ukraine.

articles.title: Australia declares its new air defense missile system combat ready
articles.body:
- Australia's Army declared Final Operational Capability for NASAMS on September 9, 2026, with 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery as the first operational unit.
- The system, built under the SRGBAD project with Raytheon Australia and Norway's Kongsberg, uses Australian CEA Technologies radar and Hawkei-mounted launchers.
Australia’s Army has declared Final Operational Capability for its National Advanced Surface to Air Missile System, confirming the ground-based air defense system is ready to support Australian Defence Force operations. Defence announced the milestone on September 9, 2026.
NASAMS is built to detect, track and destroy cruise missiles, aircraft, helicopters and drones. The system was delivered under the Short Range Ground Based Air Defense project, known as SRGBAD, part of a broader air and missile defense setup that also draws on ships and fighter aircraft to protect ADF personnel and infrastructure.
Soldiers from Adelaide’s 16th Regiment, Royal Australian Artillery, are the first operational unit to field the system. The regiment, based at Woodside in South Australia, ran live-fire trials and qualification training as part of the phased rollout that led to this week’s declaration.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability for NASAMS marks a significant milestone in strengthening Australia’s integrated air and missile defence capability,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence Richard Marles. “NASAMS provides Army with a modern, highly capable air defence system that enhances our ability to protect Australian Defence Force personnel, critical assets and infrastructure from a range of airborne threats.”
Raytheon Australia is the prime contractor on SRGBAD, running under the Army’s long-standing LAND 19 Phase 7B program. NASAMS itself was co-developed by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, and Kongsberg Defence Australia built the system’s Fire Distribution Centres locally before handing final units to Raytheon Australia last year. The SRGBAD program is valued at roughly A$2.5 billion.
The Australian version pairs the Norwegian NASAMS design with locally built CEA Technologies radar, the CEATAC and CEAOPS active electronically scanned array systems, mounted alongside launchers on Hawkei protected mobility vehicles. Raytheon’s AN/AAS-52 Multispectral Targeting System adds day and night optical tracking. The setup replaces the Army’s older RBS-70 man-portable air defense missiles.
“The achievement of Final Operational Capability delivers a world-leading capability for Defence and provides a major boost to Australia’s integrated air and missile defence,” said Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy. “Australian-designed radar technology is a key part of this capability, highlighting the important contribution local industry makes to Australia’s national security.”
NASAMS is in service with, or on order for, more than a dozen countries. Ukraine has used the system in combat against Russian cruise missiles and drones since 2022, giving the design an operational record beyond Australia’s own trials. Defence has not disclosed how many NASAMS batteries or launchers 16th Regiment will ultimately operate; the regiment is expected to field two batteries once full capability is reached.
Each NASAMS troop is built around a Fire Distribution Centre, a CEATAC radar, an optronic sensor vehicle and several launchers, with the Hawkei launchers and canisters carried on MAN/Rheinmetall HX77 trucks. The missile load is a mix of AIM-120 AMRAAM and Sidewinder missiles, the same interceptors used on Australian and allied fighter jets.
Sustainment of the system will run primarily through Australian-based support contracts already in place with CEA Technologies and Raytheon Australia.

articles.title: Netanyahu vows Iran will not obtain nuclear weapons while he is prime minister
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday vowed that Iran would not obtain nuclear weapons as long as he remains prime minister, after US President Donald Trump said that Tehran was attempting to rebuild its nuclear weapons capabilities.
“President Trump announced this evening that Iran is trying to arm itself again with nuclear weapons. That is true,” Netanyahu said.
“After we destroyed its immediate ability to produce nuclear bombs, both during Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion, they are trying again.”
Speaking at the Western Wall ahead of Rosh Hashanah, Netanyahu pledged that Israel would prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
"I pledge to you here at the Western Wall, ahead of the New Year: As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons," he said.
Netanyahu also announced that the IDF was "dealing with the Ali Taher Ridge" shortly before he announced that the IDF destroyed Hezbollah's underground infrastructure there.
Trump: US 'noticed there's a little activity at Pickaxe'
It is important to note that Trump never directly said that Tehran was attempting to rebuild nuclear weapons; rather, he stated that the US had "noticed there's a little activity at Pickaxe."
Trump also stressed that if US forces saw activity the president did not approve of, he would order CENTCOM to strike Pickaxe.
"We're leading in space. We know everybody that's moving at Pickaxe, we know everybody that's moving everywhere, all over Iran, and if anything goes bad, we hit them. We hit them hard," Trump said.
He also downplayed the situation, calling it a "military conflict" instead of a war.
"It's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits 8 Russian War Sites From Arctic to Caspian
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities supporting Moscow’s war effort in a sweeping campaign stretching from the Arctic to the Caspian Sea, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, Sept. 10.
In a Telegram post, Zelensky said the targets included an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Russia’s Republic of Dagestan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions also came under attack, according to the president.
“Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a just response,” Zelensky said.
Shahed supply route hit on the Caspian
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones attacked the Makhachkala port, which Russia allegedly used to receive Iranian-made Shahed attack drones transported across the Caspian Sea.
A strike and subsequent fire were recorded within the port, RBC-Ukraine reported, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
The Makhachkala facility is Russia’s only ice-free deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It operates throughout the year and connects Russia with other countries in the region, including Iran.
Shahed drones delivered through the port were reportedly transported onward to deployment areas before being launched against Ukraine.
During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons (3.2 million tons) of cargo, including over 2.08 million tons of oil.
Russia Sets Eye on Zaporizhzhia's Orikhiv With 150,000-Troop Formations
Eight targets across six Russian regions
Along with the Makhachkala port, Zelensky confirmed that a refinery had been hit in the Yamalo-Nenets region of Russia’s Arctic. He did not identify the facility or describe the damage there, but the reported attacks covered six Russian federal subjects.
The president did not provide details about the sites attacked in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries, ports, logistics hubs, and other infrastructure Kyiv says supplies Moscow’s military or generates revenue used to finance Russia’s invasion.
Zelensky thanked the Ukrainian personnel involved in the latest operations and those supporting the country’s ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russia.
“I thank every warrior and everyone who ensures our long-range capability and precision,” he said.

Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities supporting Moscow’s war effort in a sweeping campaign stretching from the Arctic to the Caspian Sea, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, Sept. 10.
In a Telegram post, Zelensky said the targets included an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Russia’s Republic of Dagestan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions also came under attack, according to the president.
“Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a just response,” Zelensky said.
Shahed supply route hit on the Caspian
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 long-range drones attacked the Makhachkala port, which Russia allegedly used to receive Iranian-made Shahed attack drones transported across the Caspian Sea.
A strike and subsequent fire were recorded within the port, RBC-Ukraine reported, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
The Makhachkala facility is Russia’s only ice-free deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It operates throughout the year and connects Russia with other countries in the region, including Iran.
Shahed drones delivered through the port were reportedly transported onward to deployment areas before being launched against Ukraine.
During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million metric tons (3.2 million tons) of cargo, including over 2.08 million tons of oil.
Russia Sets Eye on Zaporizhzhia's Orikhiv With 150,000-Troop Formations
Eight targets across six Russian regions
Along with the Makhachkala port, Zelensky confirmed that a refinery had been hit in the Yamalo-Nenets region of Russia’s Arctic. He did not identify the facility or describe the damage there, but the reported attacks covered six Russian federal subjects.
The president did not provide details about the sites attacked in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan, and Bryansk regions.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries, ports, logistics hubs, and other infrastructure Kyiv says supplies Moscow’s military or generates revenue used to finance Russia’s invasion.
Zelensky thanked the Ukrainian personnel involved in the latest operations and those supporting the country’s ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russia.
“I thank every warrior and everyone who ensures our long-range capability and precision,” he said.

articles.title: How Russia Is Targeting Ukraine’s Food Chain, From Factories to Store Shelves
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
How Russia Is Targeting Ukraine’s Food Chain, From Factories to Store Shelves
Russian strikes on Ukraine's food production and logistics are increasingly reaching supermarket shelves, where shortages have begun to surface. What began as attacks on distant warehouses is now registering at the checkout, in thinner produce aisles and in new limits on how much shoppers can buy.
The retail chain ATB, among Ukraine's largest supermarket networks, has introduced temporary purchase limits on several categories of goods. Customers can buy no more than six units or kilograms of groceries, eggs, and bulk products in a single transaction, the company reported on Facebook.
It attributed the limit to the fallout from Russian strikes and a surge in speculative buying, describing resellers who make wholesale purchases in stores and pile additional pressure on already-stretched logistics. ATB stressed that the restrictions are temporary and that it is doing everything possible to keep shelves supplied.
The squeeze is visible in Kyiv, where fresh fruit, vegetables, sugar and dairy have intermittently vanished from some supermarkets as strikes disrupt the depots that feed them.
Ninety percent of food retail logistics is destroyed
The pressure on retailers follows weeks of intensifying attacks on warehousing and delivery infrastructure. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, cited by Reuters, told reporters in Kyiv that roughly 90% of the food logistics run by retail chains had been wiped out.
"As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn't mean Ukrainians will be left without food," Vysotskyi noted.
Both sides have stepped up strikes on economic targets in recent weeks, with Russia concentrating on warehouses tied to Ukraine's leading supermarkets, its top postal service and home-goods stores. The blows have rippled beyond food: a wave of attacks delayed trains across several regions and left passengers stranded, while Kyiv spent close to 15 hours under air-raid alert on a single day.
Food producers are hit directly
The strikes have repeatedly struck food producers themselves. In Dnipro, Mayor Borys Filatov reported on Telegram that a recent attack had damaged, for the second time in the full-scale war, an oil-extraction plant belonging to the US agribusiness Bunge, maker of the Oleina cooking-oil brand.
Filatov emphasized that the plant stands in the city center and that US Senator Richard Blumenthal had visited it shortly before the strike.
On September 8, a Russian drone hit a food plant operated by Euro Food Service in Bila Tserkva, south of Kyiv. The company stated on LinkedIn that its production and storage facilities had been significantly damaged and that manufacturing and shipments were halted. No staff were injured, and the firm indicated it was working to keep its products on store shelves while it assessed the destruction.
American-owned plants in the crosshairs
American-owned facilities have featured prominently in the campaign. On September 3, Russian drones set fire to a Coca-Cola plant outside Kyiv, near Brovary, an attack President Volodymyr Zelenskyy framed as a message to Washington.
"It's a clear Russian signal to America. The Russians cannot be unaware that this is an American facility," Zelenskyy declared in his nightly video address. The strikes on Bunge and Coca-Cola, together with the senator's earlier visit, have sharpened Ukrainian appeals for a firmer US response.
The disruption now reaches ordinary consumers. McDonald's reported on September 10 that frequent, prolonged air-raid alerts and delivery delays had forced some Ukrainian outlets to reduce their menus, with items to be restored as supply stabilizes.
Couriers, retailers and aid stockpiles
The wider wave has swept up couriers, retailers and humanitarian stockpiles alike. Reuters reported that recent strikes destroyed Nova Poshta sorting centers near Kyiv and in Sumy, wounded at least four people at an Epicenter home-improvement store in Zaporizhzhia, and gutted a warehouse shipping thousands of book titles a day.
A shopping center in Kharkiv was struck for the second time in two days, while drone attacks on the Kyiv region damaged more than a dozen warehouses and killed one person.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi wrote on Telegram that 16 people had been killed across Ukraine in a single day of attacks. "They are hitting civilian businesses, food warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals, warehouses where books are stored," he added.
The World Health Organization (WHO), cited by Reuters, confirmed that one of its main medical-supply warehouses in the Kyiv region was struck overnight in early September.
Spokesperson Christian Lindmeier told reporters in Geneva that at least 20 attacks had hit warehouses storing humanitarian supplies during 2026, 15 of them holding health-related goods. An earlier August strike on a WHO depot in Dnipro destroyed half the supplies intended for an estimated 225,000 people in front-line areas.
A deliberate strategy, officials contend
Ukrainian officials have characterized the campaign as a deliberate effort to grind down daily life rather than a run of stray hits. Andriyy Kovalenko, who heads Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, described waves of jet-powered drones aimed at paralyzing the capital and exhausting its defenders and residents.
"The aim—to wear down the air defenses and the population," he indicated. The choice of food depots, hypermarkets and postal terminals, in Vyhivskyi's account, points to civilian supply as the intended pressure point.
What shoppers are being told
Authorities are also advising residents to prepare for potential supply and utility disruptions. Kyiv has begun stockpiling essential food and drinking water ahead of possible prolonged winter blackouts, while maintaining emergency reserves for vulnerable residents and Points of Invincibility.
The city can currently provide hot meals for up to 25,000 people and plans to purchase another 20,000 emergency food kits as Russia continues targeting critical infrastructure.
Vysotskyi has urged households to keep a modest one-week food reserve while ruling out any need for month-long stockpiling, warning that wartime disruptions could recur. Even so, he maintained that goods that are interrupted on the shelf tend to reappear once logistics adapt.

articles.title: Over the past day, the Defense Forces struck eight infrastructure facilities in the Russian Federation, including an oil refinery and a commercial port, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Over the past day, the Defense Forces struck eight infrastructure facilities in the Russian Federation, including an oil refinery and a commercial port, Zelenskyy says
Kyiv • UNN
The Makhachkala Commercial Sea Port in Dagestan, through which Iranian Shaheds were delivered, came under attack.
Over the course of a day, Ukrainian forces struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities. In particular, they hit an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and the Sea Trade Port in Dagestan. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported this, UNN writes.
Over the course of this day, our warriors struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities that support the war. An oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region was hit, as was the Sea Trade Port in Dagestan. Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan and Bryansk regions were also targeted. Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a just response
The president also thanked the warriors who ensure our long-range strike capability and accuracy.
As the manufacturer of the strike drones Fire Point reported, the Sea Trade Port in Dagestan was hit by FP-1 drones. Hits and a subsequent fire were recorded on the port’s premises.
Makhachkala Sea Trade Port is Russia’s only ice-free deep-water port on the Caspian Sea. It operates year-round and provides maritime connections between Russia and the countries of the Caspian region, including Iran. Makhachkala was also used as one of the delivery points for Iranian strike UAVs to Russia across the Caspian Sea, from where they were subsequently transported to areas of deployment against Ukraine.
During the first eight months of 2026, the port handled more than 2.9 million tonnes of cargo, of which more than 2.08 million tonnes was oil.

articles.title: AFU General Staff confirms strikes on Russia’s Makhachkala seaport and three ships in Novorossiysk
articles.body:
AFU General Staff confirms strikes on Russia’s Makhachkala seaport and three ships in Novorossiysk
As reported by Ukrinform, the press service of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
“Overnight on September 10, 2026, units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Makhachkala Commercial Seaport in the Republic of Dagestan, Russian Federation. A fire was recorded at the facility. The extent of the damage is being clarified,” the statement said.
In addition, based on an analysis of additional data, the General Staff confirmed that on September 9, 2026, fuel-oil storage facilities in Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Krai, Russian Federation, were struck, as well as at least three enemy vessels: the Zheleznyakov minesweeper, the Admiral Essen frigate, and the Project 11711 Pyotr Morgunov large landing ship, the General Staff noted.
The Makhachkala Commercial Seaport is the only ice-free deep-water port of the Russian Federation on the Caspian Sea and an important transport and logistics hub.
The port plays a key role in the Russia-Iran logistics corridor across the Caspian Sea, which is used to circumvent Western sanctions. Military-related supplies are transported in both directions along this route: components and Shahed-type attack UAVs from Iran to Russia, and explosives, drone components and ammunition from Russia to Iran. A base of the Russian Caspian Flotilla is located near the port.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets region as well as a seaport in Dagestan during the night.

articles.title: Russia and Vietnam to strengthen military cooperation and intelligence sharing on “hostile” countries
articles.body:
Russia and Vietnam have agreed to deepen cooperation in defense, security, and military technology, as well as to exchange information on the activities of “hostile forces and foreign special agencies,” according to a joint statement issued following talks between Vladimir Putin and Vietnamese President To Lam in Moscow on Sept. 9. Additionally, Putin announced that Russia will soon introduce a visa-free regime for Vietnamese nationals.
The two sides agreed to “enhance cooperation between military branches” and cooperate in maritime security, military personnel training, science, technology, and engineering. After the talks, To Lam stated that Russia and Vietnam intend to “deepen defence, security, and military technical cooperation as a strategic pillar of our ties.”
A separate clause in the joint statement addresses cooperation in the field of information security. Russia and Vietnam agreed to intensify the exchange of information and expertise “in countering the conspiracies, intentions, and activities of hostile forces and foreign special agencies,” which, in the document’s wording, are aimed at interfering in internal affairs and influencing state, political, and legislative institutions. The two sides also stated their readiness to expand cooperation “in combating crime in all its forms and manifestations, including cybercrime” and to continue cooperation between law enforcement agencies.
In addition, Moscow and Hanoi intend to expand cooperation in the oil and gas sector. The joint statement describes energy and fossil fuels as areas of “strategic breakthrough in Vietnam-Russia relations.” The two sides agreed to speed up work on possible supplies of Russian oil and liquefied natural gas to Vietnam and on building infrastructure on the Vietnamese side for receiving, processing, and storing hydrocarbons.
Putin said the Russian side had even proposed creating strategic fuel reserves in Vietnam. “Our companies are also interested in establishing transit deliveries of energy resources through Vietnamese territory to neighboring states,” he said. During the visit, the two sides signed agreements on oil and gas projects on the Vietnamese shelf and a framework agreement between Zarubezhneft and Petrovietnam regarding the strategic oil reserve.
Nuclear energy remains another area of cooperation. This past March, Russia and Vietnam signed an intergovernmental agreement on building a Russian-designed nuclear power plant in Vietnam. Putin called the initiative “a truly flagship project.” The two sides also intend to build a Nuclear Science and Technology Center in Vietnam.
In the context of expanding political and security cooperation, Putin announced the potential liberalization of Russia’s visa regime for Vietnamese citizens. “For our part, we are working to introduce reciprocal visa-free travel for our Vietnamese friends in the near future,” he said. Russians no longer need a visa for short trips to Vietnam, and according to Putin, almost 700,000 Russians visited the country in 2025, and another 800,000 in the first half of 2026.
In the final statement, Moscow and Hanoi called their development a “long-term strategic choice and one of the priorities in the foreign policy of each country.” During the meeting with Putin, To Lam called the Russian leader “a great friend of our country and a close brother to the Vietnamese people.” The joint statement also says that Russia “highly appreciates” Vietnam’s position regarding the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Zelensky’s plane nearly collides with drone during takeoff in Moldova, Norwegian PM states
articles.body:
The plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky nearly collided with a drone during takeoff on its way from Moldova to Norway, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere told the broadcaster NRK on Sept. 9, as quoted by Reuters. Stoere did not specify the source of this information nor how close the drone had come to Zelensky’s plane.
“His plane was nearly hit by a drone as it was about to take off from Moldova. That’s the reality he’s facing,” Stoere said.
On Sept. 8, Zelensky flew to Oslo for King Harald V’s funeral and met with Stoere that same evening. The Norwegian government’s official statement on the talks does not mention the drone incident.
Around the same time, a drone flew over Moldova and Romania; Moldovan authorities initially identified the object as a Shahed of the sort commonly used by Russian forces. According to Moldova’s Defense Ministry, the aircraft entered the country’s airspace from Ukraine at 4:20 p.m., headed through the Chisinau area toward Romania, and left Moldovan territory 17 minutes later.
Romania’s Ministry of Defense said that at 4:33 p.m. its radars detected an aerial target west of Chisinau, and at 4:37 p.m. it entered Romanian airspace roughly 30 kilometers southeast of Iasi. Two Spanish F-18s were scrambled to track the drone, which advanced further into Romania, reaching the vicinity of Roman before turning back. It was detected again over Moldova at 5:08 p.m. The aircraft eventually crashed near the village of Mihaileni Vechi, roughly 25 kilometers from the Romanian border.
On Sept. 9, Moldovan police said that the debris found at the site featured a turbojet engine and other elements characteristic of UAVs commonly used by Russia. The impact caused an explosion that left a large crater; at the scene, investigators found shrapnel in the form of metal balls. Experts are still determining the drone’s exact type and the size of its warhead. No casualties were reported.
The OSINT project Oko Hora (Eye of Horus) ✙ News and Analysis claims that the UAV was a jet-powered Geran-4 that had flown about 500 kilometers over Moldova and Romania at an altitude of 7,000-8,000 meters before it ran out of fuel and crashed.
Violations of Romanian airspace by Russian drones have happened before. Since the start of the full-scale war, the country’s Ministry of Defense has recorded 45 unauthorized drone incursions — 26 of them in 2026. In July, Romanian troops destroyed three drones over the course of three days, and in late May a Russian Geran-2 crashed into a residential building in Galati, injuring two people.

articles.title: South Lebanon trembles as Israel destroys Ali al-Taher tunnels
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Tremor recorded in southern Lebanon as Israel destroys Ali al-Taher tunnels
Israel said Thursday it demolished key tunnels built by the Iran-backed Hezbollah group beneath the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, with a 4.1 magnitude tremor recorded in the area.
AFP journalists in the area heard several explosions. In a video shared by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, a huge fireball can be seen rising into the night sky.
The explosion comes a few days after Israeli authorities claimed to have taken control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, claiming that Hezbollah had dug numerous tunnels there.
Israeli troops occupy swathes of southern Lebanon, establishing a so-called "security zone" along the entire border region.
A joint statement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Katz said the tunnels were strategic infrastructure "built over two decades, with Iranian funding and planning."
The destruction "completes the achievement of operational control over the Ali al-Taher ridge -- above and below ground", the statement added.
The United States Geological Survey meanwhile reported a 4.1 magnitude tremor in the area, after Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that Israel carried out a "massive explosion" on the Ali al-Taher ridge in the Nabatiyeh region, "causing tremors and a powerful rumble".
AFP journalists in south Lebanon also said they heard "huge explosions" on Thursday evening.
"We were sitting there and everything shook," Joelle Fares, who recently moved to Marjaayoun, told AFP.
Israel announced last week that it had captured the Ali al-Taher ridge. Hezbollah has remained silent on the matter.
The Israeli army said the Hezbollah infrastructure extended for more than two kilometres (1.2 miles) and contained "dozens of Iranian-made rockets, missiles, and UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), as well as machine guns, dozens of anti-tank missiles, and hundreds of mines and explosive devices".
The underground compound also included a command centre of Hezbollah's "Badr" unit, the army added.
A military official told AFP that some of the militants that had operated in the area of the ridge had abandoned it, while others were "eliminated by aerial strikes and artillery fire".
The official said Hezbollah members had dug eight underground routes to move safely beneath the ridge, and several dozen explosive drones and hundreds of mines were seized by the Israeli army.
An all-out war resumed on 2 March when Hezbollah fired rockets into northern Israel in support of its backer Iran. Israel had already been violating a November 2024 ceasefire with daily attacks on Lebanese soil. The wider conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023.
There had been a lull in violence after the agreement reached between Lebanon and Israel in June, and talks are set to resume next week. But Israeli strikes have increased in intensity in recent days, killing dozens of people.
During negotiations, the United States, which is sponsoring the talks, proposed that the Lebanese army take control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, but Hezbollah refused, a source close to the parties told AFP.
Beirut authorities say Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people in total since March, and more than 8,500 since October 2023. Israeli forces continue to occupy a so-called "security zone" in the south and have wiped out dozens of towns and villages.

articles.title: Ukrainian Ballistic Missiles To Strike Russia in Just a Few Weeks — Fire Point CEO
articles.body:
Ballistic missiles manufactured by Fire Point will strike targets on Russian territory in just a few weeks.
Iryna Terekh, the company’s CEO, announced this on the sidelines of the “Photonics4Defense 2026: Technology Exchange & Matchmaking” event.
According to her, the FP-7 has already successfully completed two stages of testing. The company is now preparing to test the product under combat conditions. This stage is also part of the missile’s certification process.
“We expect it to be ready for deployment very soon. We’re talking about weeks, not months,” Terekh noted.
She explained that the initial stages of missile testing involve ground and laboratory tests, during which each system and subsystem—including the rocket engine and navigation equipment—is tested separately.
This is followed by flight tests, during which the company collects data on the missile’s performance and compares its actual characteristics with the calculated ones.
The third stage, which the company is currently preparing for, involves testing under combat conditions. In late November 2025, it was announced that the company planned to complete the codification process for the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile with the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense by the end of 2025.
In early February 2026, Denys Shtilierrman clarified in an interview with DW that, despite hopes that the missile would enter service by the end of 2025, a “series of events” had prevented this from happening—‘we hope to complete all tests in February’.
At the same time, the FP-9 is currently undergoing flight tests, meaning it is in the second phase.
The developers note that testing the FP-9 is harder to organize because of its long range. The missile has a minimum ballistic flight distance beyond which it can no longer be programmatically stopped.
Because of this, Ukraine’s territory is insufficient for a full-scale test of the FP-9. Therefore, once the current phase is complete, its military testing may immediately proceed to operations against Russian targets.
Militarnyi previously reported that in July 2026, Denys Shtilierman, Fire Point’s chief designer, stated that the only thing standing between the start of FP-9 ballistic missile tests—involving strikes on Russia—and their implementation is the testing of the solid-fuel engine.

articles.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia.
The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded.
🔴Czy w razie ewentualnej agresji ze strony Rosji, Polska powinna pomóc Litwie, Łotwie i Estonii?
➡️tak – 77,8% 
➡️nie – 16,1%  #sondaż @IBRiS_PL dla @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/6jiBgOW5v3
— IBRiS (@IBRiS_PL) September 9, 2026
In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed.
Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid.
Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”.
That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government.
In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.”
The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred.
“We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.”
With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”.
🇵🇱🇺🇸🇪🇪🇱🇹🇱🇻@mblaszczak @pisorgpl o zobowiązaniach sojuszniczych wynikających z artykułu 5 @NATO 👇
Źródło: @BogRymanowski @Radio_ZET pic.twitter.com/gfQz4QyD1D
— WarNewsPL (@WarNewsPL1) September 1, 2026
Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked.
“A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”.
In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission.
“NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added.
Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. 
Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek…
— Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026
On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade.
“Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.”
“We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.”
📍 Ādaži 🇱🇻
Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent.
The Polish contingent in Latvia serves as part of NATO’s allied presence, strengthening deterrence and defence… pic.twitter.com/tKMIix2h9L
— Ministry of Foreign Affairs 🇵🇱 (@PolandMFA) September 9, 2026
